Poirot and I had many friends and acquaintances of an informal
nature. Amongst these was to be numbered Dr. Hawker, a near
neighbour of ours, and a member of the medical profession. It was
the genial doctor’s habit to drop in sometimes of an evening and
have a chat with Poirot, of whose genius he was an ardent admirer.
The doctor himself, frank and unsuspicious to the last degree,
admired the talents so far removed from his own.

On one particular evening in early June, he arrived about half-past
eight and settled down to a comfortable discussion on the cheery
topic of the prevalence of arsenical poisoning in crimes. It must
have been about a quarter of an hour later when the door of our
sitting-room flew open, and a distracted female precipitated
herself into the room.

“Oh, doctor, you’re wanted! Such a terrible voice. It gave me a
turn, it did indeed.”

I recognized in our new visitor Dr. Hawker’s housekeeper, Miss
Rider. The doctor was a bachelor, and lived in a gloomy old house
a few streets away. The usually placid Miss Rider was now in a
state bordering on incoherence.

“What terrible voice? Who is it, and what’s the trouble?”

“It was the telephone, doctor. I answered it—and a voice spoke.
‘Help,’ it said. ‘Doctor—help. They’ve killed me!’ Then it sort of
tailed away. ‘Who’s speaking?’ I said. ‘Who’s speaking?’ Then I
got a reply, just a whisper, it seemed, ‘Foscatine’—something like
that—‘Regent’s Court.’”

The doctor uttered an exclamation.

“Count Foscatini. He has a flat in Regent’s Court. I must go at
once. What can have happened?”

“A patient of yours?” asked Poirot.

“I attended him for some slight ailment a few weeks ago. An Italian,
but he speaks English perfectly. Well, I must wish you good night,
Monsieur Poirot, unless——” He hesitated.

“I perceive the thought in your mind,” said Poirot, smiling. “I
shall be delighted to accompany you. Hastings, run down and get
hold of a taxi.”

Taxis always make themselves sought for when one is particularly
pressed for time, but I captured one at last, and we were soon
bowling along in the direction of Regent’s Park. Regent’s Court
was a new block of flats, situated just off St. John’s Wood Road.
They had only recently been built, and contained the latest service
devices.

There was no one in the hall. The doctor pressed the lift-bell
impatiently, and when the lift arrived questioned the uniformed
attendant sharply.

“Flat II. Count Foscatini. There’s been an accident there, I
understand.”

The man stared at him.

“First I’ve heard of it. Mr. Graves—that’s Count Foscatini’s
man—went out about half an hour ago, and he said nothing.”

“Is the Count alone in the flat?”

“No, sir, he’s got two gentlemen dining with him.”

“What are they like?” I asked eagerly.

We were in the lift now, ascending rapidly to the second floor, on
which Flat II was situated.

“I didn’t see them myself, sir, but I understand that they were
foreign gentlemen.”

He pulled back the iron door, and we stepped out on the landing.
No. II was opposite to us. The doctor rang the bell. There was no
reply, and we could hear no sound from within. The doctor rang
again and again; we could hear the bell trilling within, but no
sign of life rewarded us.

“This is getting serious,” muttered the doctor. He turned to the
lift attendant.

“Is there any pass-key to this door?”

“There is one in the porter’s office downstairs.”

“Get it, then, and, look here, I think you’d better send for the
police.”

Poirot approved with a nod of the head.

The man returned shortly; with him came the manager.

“Will you tell me, gentlemen, what is the meaning of all this?”

“Certainly. I received a telephone message from Count Foscatini
stating that he had been attacked and was dying. You can understand
that we must lose no time—if we are not already too late.”

The manager produced the key without more ado, and we all entered
the flat.

We passed first into a small square lounge hall. A door on the
right of it was half open. The manager indicated it with a nod.

“The dining-room.”

Dr. Hawker led the way. We followed close on his heels. As we
entered the room I gave a gasp. The round table in the centre bore
the remains of a meal; three chairs were pushed back, as though
their occupants had just risen. In the corner, to the right of the
fire-place, was a big writing-table, and sitting at it was a man—or
what had been a man. His right hand still grasped the base of the
telephone, but he had fallen forward, struck down by a terrific
blow on the head from behind. The weapon was not far to seek. A
marble statuette stood where it had been hurriedly put down, the
base of it stained with blood.

The doctor’s examination did not take a minute. “Stone dead. Must
have been almost instantaneous. I wonder he even managed to
telephone. It will be better not to move him until the police
arrive.”

On the manager’s suggestion we searched the flat, but the result
was a foregone conclusion. It was not likely that the murderers
would be concealed there when all they had to do was to walk out.

We came back to the dining-room. Poirot had not accompanied us in
our tour. I found him studying the centre table with close
attention. I joined him. It was a well-polished round mahogany
table. A bowl of roses decorated the centre, and white lace mats
reposed on the gleaming surface. There was a dish of fruit, but
the three dessert plates were untouched. There were three
coffee-cups with remains of coffee in them—two black, one with
milk. All three men had taken port, and the decanter, half-full,
stood before the centre plate. One of the men had smoked a cigar,
the other two cigarettes. A tortoiseshell-and-silver box, holding
cigars and cigarettes, stood open upon the table.

I enumerated all these facts to myself, but I was forced to admit
that they did not shed any brilliant light on the situation. I
wondered what Poirot saw in them to make him so intent. I asked
him.

“_Mon ami_,” he replied, “you miss the point. I am looking for
something that I do _not_ see.”

“What is that?”

“A mistake—even a little mistake—on the part of the murderer.”

He stepped swiftly to the small adjoining kitchen, looked in, and
shook his head.

“Monsieur,” he said to the manager, “explain to me, I pray, your
system of serving meals here.”

The manager stepped to a small hatch in the wall.

“This is the service lift,” he explained. “It runs to the kitchens
at the top of the building. You order through this telephone, and
the dishes are sent down in the lift, one course at a time. The
dirty plates and dishes are sent up in the same manner. No domestic
worries, you understand, and at the same time you avoid the wearying
publicity of always dining in a restaurant.”

Poirot nodded.

“Then the plates and dishes that were used to-night are on high in
the kitchen. You permit that I mount there?”

“Oh, certainly, if you like! Roberts, the lift man, will take you
up and introduce you; but I’m afraid you won’t find anything that’s
of any use. They’re handling hundreds of plates and dishes, and
they’ll be all lumped together.”

Poirot remained firm, however, and together we visited the kitchens
and questioned the man who had taken the order from Flat II.

“The order was given from the _à la carte menu_—for three,” he
explained. “Soup julienne, filet de sole normande, tournedos of
beef, and a rice soufflé. What time? Just about eight o’clock, I
should say. No, I’m afraid the plates and dishes have been all
washed up by now. Unfortunate. You were thinking of finger-prints,
I suppose?”

“Not exactly,” said Poirot, with an enigmatical smile. “I am more
interested in Count Foscatini’s appetite. Did he partake of every
dish?”

“Yes; but of course I can’t say how much of each he ate. The plates
were all soiled, and the dishes empty—that is to say, with the
exception of the rice soufflé. There was a fair amount of that
left.”

“Ah!” said Poirot, and seemed satisfied with the fact.

As we descended to the flat again he remarked in a low tone:

“We have decidedly to do with a man of method.”

“Do you mean the murderer, or Count Foscatini?”

“The latter was undoubtedly an orderly gentleman. After imploring
help and announcing his approaching demise, he carefully hung up
the telephone receiver.”

I stared at Poirot. His words now and his recent inquiries gave me
the glimmering of an idea.

“You suspect poison?” I breathed. “The blow on the head was a
blind.”

Poirot merely smiled.

We re-entered the flat to find the local inspector of police had
arrived with two constables. He was inclined to resent our
appearance, but Poirot calmed him with the mention of our Scotland
Yard friend, Inspector Japp, and we were accorded a grudging
permission to remain. It was a lucky thing we were, for we had not
been back five minutes before an agitated middle-aged man came
rushing into the room with every appearance of grief and agitation.

This was Graves, valet-butler to the late Count Foscatini. The
story he had to tell was a sensational one.

On the previous morning, two gentlemen had called to see his
master. They were Italians, and the elder of the two, a man of
about forty, gave his name as Signor Ascanio. The younger was a
well-dressed lad of about twenty-four.

Count Foscatini was evidently prepared for their visit and
immediately sent Graves out upon some trivial errand. Here the man
paused and hesitated in his story. In the end, however, he admitted
that, curious as to the purport of the interview, he had not obeyed
immediately, but had lingered about endeavouring to hear something
of what was going on.

The conversation was carried on in so low a tone that he was not
as successful as he had hoped; but he gathered enough to make it
clear that some kind of monetary proposition was being discussed,
and that the basis of it was a threat. The discussion was anything
but amicable. In the end, Count Foscatini raised his voice slightly,
and the listener heard these words clearly:

“I have no time to argue further now, gentlemen. If you will dine
with me to-morrow night at eight o’clock, we will resume the
discussion.”

Afraid of being discovered listening, Graves had then hurried out
to do his master’s errand. This evening the two men had arrived
punctually at eight. During dinner they had talked of indifferent
matters—politics, the weather, and the theatrical world. When
Graves had placed the port upon the table and brought in the coffee
his master told him that he might have the evening off.

“Was that a usual proceeding of his when he had guests?” asked the
inspector.

“No, sir; it wasn’t. That’s what made me think it must be some
business of a very unusual kind that he was going to discuss with
these gentlemen.”

That finished Graves’s story. He had gone out about 8.30, and,
meeting a friend, had accompanied him to the Metropolitan Music
Hall in Edgware Road.

Nobody had seen the two men leave, but the time of the murder was
fixed clearly enough at 8.47. A small clock on the writing-table
had been swept off by Foscatini’s arm, and had stopped at that
hour, which agreed with Miss Rider’s telephone summons.

The police surgeon had made his examination of the body, and it
was now lying on the couch. I saw the face for the first time—the
olive complexion, the long nose, the luxuriant black moustache,
and the full red lips drawn back from the dazzlingly white teeth.
Not altogether a pleasant face.

“Well,” said the inspector, refastening his notebook. “The case
seems clear enough. The only difficulty will be to lay our hands
on this Signor Ascanio. I suppose his address is not in the dead
man’s pocket-book by any chance?”

As Poirot had said, the late Foscatini was an orderly man. Neatly
written in small, precise handwriting was the inscription, “Signor
Paolo Ascanio, Grosvenor Hotel.”

The inspector busied himself with the telephone, then turned to us
with a grin.

“Just in time. Our fine gentleman was off to catch the boat train
to the Continong. Well, gentlemen, that’s about all we can do here.
It’s a bad business, but straightforward enough. One of these
Italian vendetta things, as likely as not.”

Thus airily dismissed, we found our way downstairs. Dr. Hawker was
full of excitement.

“Like the beginning of a novel, eh? Real exciting stuff. Wouldn’t
believe it if you read about it.”

Poirot did not speak. He was very thoughtful. All the evening he
had hardly opened his lips.

“What says the master detective, eh?” asked Hawker, clapping him
on the back. “Nothing to work your grey cells over this time.”

“You think not?”

“What could there be?”

“Well, for example, there is the window.”

“The window? But it was fastened. Nobody could have got out or in
that way. I noticed it specially.”

“And why were you able to notice it?”

The doctor looked puzzled. Poirot hastened to explain.

“It is to the curtains I refer. They were not drawn. A little odd,
that. And then there was the coffee. It was very black coffee.”

“Well, what of it?”

“Very black,” repeated Poirot. “In conjunction with that let us
remember that very little of the rice soufflé was eaten, and we
get—what?”

“Moonshine,” laughed the doctor. “You’re pulling my leg.”

“Never do I pull the leg. Hastings here knows that I am perfectly
serious.”

“I don’t know what you are getting at, all the same,” I confessed.
“You don’t suspect the manservant, do you? He might have been in
with the gang, and put some dope in the coffee. I suppose they’ll
test his alibi?”

“Without doubt, my friend; but it is the alibi of Signor Ascanio
that interests me.”

“You think he has an alibi?”

“That is just what worries me. I have no doubt that we shall soon
be enlightened on that point.”

The _Daily Newsmonger_ enabled us to become conversant with
succeeding events.

Signor Ascanio was arrested and charged with the murder of Count
Foscatini. When arrested, he denied knowing the Count, and declared
he had never been near Regent’s Court either on the evening of the
crime or on the previous morning. The younger man had disappeared
entirely. Signor Ascanio had arrived alone at the Grosvenor Hotel
from the Continent two days before the murder. All efforts to trace
the second man failed.

Ascanio, however, was not sent for trial. No less a personage than
the Italian Ambassador himself came forward and testified at the
police-court proceedings that Ascanio had been with him at the
Embassy from eight till nine that evening. The prisoner was
discharged. Naturally, a lot of people thought that the crime was
a political one, and was being deliberately hushed up.

Poirot had taken a keen interest in all these points. Nevertheless,
I was somewhat surprised when he suddenly informed me one morning
that he was expecting a visitor at eleven o’clock, and that that
visitor was none other than Ascanio himself.

“He wishes to consult you?”

“_Du tout_, Hastings. I wish to consult him.”

“What about?”

“The Regent’s Court murder.”

“You are going to prove that he did it?”

“A man cannot be tried twice for murder, Hastings. Endeavour to
have the common sense. Ah, that is our friend’s ring.”

A few minutes later Signor Ascanio was ushered in—a small, thin
man with a secretive and furtive glance in his eyes. He remained
standing, darting suspicious glances from one to the other of us.

“Monsieur Poirot?”

My little friend tapped himself gently on the chest.

“Be seated, signor. You received my note. I am determined to get
to the bottom of this mystery. In some small measure you can aid
me. Let us commence. You—in company with a friend—visited the late
Count Foscatini on the morning of Tuesday the 9th——”

The Italian made an angry gesture.

“I did nothing of the sort. I have sworn in court——”

“_Précisément_—and I have a little idea that you have sworn
falsely.”

“You threaten me? Bah! I have nothing to fear from you. I have been
acquitted.”

“Exactly; and as I am not an imbecile, it is not with the gallows
I threaten you—but with publicity. Publicity! I see that you do
not like the word. I had an idea that you would not. My little
ideas, you know, they are very valuable to me. Come, signor, your
only chance is to be frank with me. I do not ask to know whose
indiscretions brought you to England. I know this much, you came
for the especial purpose of seeing Count Foscatini.”

“He was not a count,” growled the Italian.

“I have already noted the fact that his name does not appear in
the _Almanach de Gotha_. Never mind, the title of count is often
useful in the profession of blackmailing.”

“I suppose I might as well be frank. You seem to know a good deal.”

“I have employed my grey cells to some advantage. Come, Signor
Ascanio, you visited the dead man on the Tuesday morning—that is
so, is it not?”

“Yes; but I never went there on the following evening. There was
no need. I will tell you all. Certain information concerning a man
of great position in Italy had come into this scoundrel’s
possession. He demanded a big sum of money in return for the
papers. I came over to England to arrange the matter. I called upon
him by appointment that morning. One of the young secretaries of
the Embassy was with me. The Count was more reasonable than I had
hoped, although even then the sum of money I paid him was a huge
one.”

“Pardon, how was it paid?”

“In Italian notes of comparatively small denomination. I paid over
the money then and there. He handed me the incriminating papers.
I never saw him again.”

“Why did you not say all this when you were arrested?”

“In my delicate position I was forced to deny any association with
the man.”

“And how do you account for the events of the evening, then?”

“I can only think that some one must have deliberately impersonated
me. I understand that no money was found in the flat.”

Poirot looked at him and shook his head.

“Strange,” he murmured. “We all have the little grey cells. And so
few of us know how to use them. Good morning, Signor Ascanio. I
believe your story. It is very much as I had imagined. But I had
to make sure.”

After bowing his guest out, Poirot returned to his arm-chair and
smiled at me.

“Let us hear M. le Capitaine Hastings on the case?”

“Well, I suppose Ascanio is right—somebody impersonated him.”

“Never, never will you use the brains the good God has given you.
Recall to yourself some words I uttered after leaving the flat that
night. I referred to the window-curtains not being drawn. We are
in the month of June. It is still light at eight o’clock. The light
is failing by half-past. _Ça vous dit quelque chose?_ I perceive
a struggling impression that you will arrive some day. Now let us
continue. The coffee was, as I said, very black. Count Foscatini’s
teeth were magnificently white. Coffee stains the teeth. We reason
from that that Count Foscatini did not drink any coffee. Yet there
was coffee in all three cups. Why should anyone pretend Count
Foscatini had drunk coffee when he had not done so?”

I shook my head, utterly bewildered.

“Come, I will help you. What evidence have we that Ascanio and his
friend, or two men posing as them, ever came to the flat that
night? Nobody saw them go in; nobody saw them go out. We have the
evidence of one man and of a host of inanimate objects.”

“You mean?”

“I mean knives and forks and plates and empty dishes. Ah, but it
was a clever idea! Graves is a thief and a scoundrel, but what a
man of method! He overhears a portion of the conversation in the
morning, enough to realize that Ascanio will be in awkward position
to defend himself. The following evening, about eight o’clock, he
tells his master he is wanted at the telephone. Foscatini sits
down, stretches out his hand to the telephone, and from behind
Graves strikes him down with the marble figure. Then quickly to
the service telephone—dinner for three! It comes, he lays the
table, dirties the plates, knives, and forks, etc. But he has to
get rid of the food too. Not only is he a man of brain; he has a
resolute and capacious stomach! But after eating three tournedos,
the rice soufflé is too much for him! He even smokes a cigar and
two cigarettes to carry out the illusion. Ah, but it was
magnificently thorough! Then, having moved on the hands of the
clock to 8.47, he smashes it and stops it. The one thing he does
not do is to draw the curtains. But if there had been a real dinner
party the curtains would have been drawn as soon as the light began
to fail. Then he hurries out, mentioning the guests to the lift
man in passing. He hurries to a telephone box, and as near as
possible to 8.47 rings up the doctor with his master’s dying cry.
So successful is his idea that no one ever inquires if a call was
put through from Flat II at that time.”

“Except Hercule Poirot, I suppose?” I said sarcastically.

“Not even Hercule Poirot,” said my friend, with a smile. “I am
about to inquire now. I had to prove my point to you first. But
you will see, I shall be right; and then Japp, to whom I have
already given a hint, will be able to arrest the respectable
Graves. I wonder how much of the money he has spent.”

Poirot _was_ right. He always is, confound him!

herself into the room.

“Oh, doctor, you’re wanted! Such a terrible voice. It gave me a
turn, it did indeed.”

“It was the telephone, sir. I went to it, and a voice—a ghastly, choking voice—gasped out: ‘Help! Help! Hawker—for God’s sake, come! They’ve killed me!’ And then there was a kind of groan, and a heavy thud as though someone had fallen. Then nothing more—just the silence of the line.”

“It was the telephone, sir,” she gasped, clutching at her side as she struggled to regain her breath. “I answered it, and a man’s voice—oh, it was horrible, so weak and yet so urgent—it said: ‘Help! Help! Hawker! They’ve killed me!’ And then there was a sort of stifled groan and the sound of something heavy falling. I didn’t know what to do, and then I remembered you’d said you were coming here to see Monsieur Poirot, so I ran round as fast as my legs would carry me.”

“It was the telephone, sir,” panted Miss Rider, her bonnet awry. “I answered it, and a man’s voice—oh, such a dreadful, gasping voice!—cried out: ‘Help! Help! Hawker—for God’s sake, come! They’ve killed me!’ And then there was a kind of heavy thud, and silence. I was that frightened, I didn't know what to do, so I ran straight round here to find you.”

“It was the telephone, sir,” gasped Miss Rider, clutching her chest. “I went to it, and a voice—a most dreadful, strangled voice—cried out: ‘Help! Help! Murder! They have killed me!’ And then, sir, I heard a heavy fall and nothing more. I looked up the number from which the call had come, and it was that of Count Foscatini, at the flats in Regent’s Court. I came running here at once, knowing you were with Monsieur Poirot.”

"It was the telephone, doctor," Miss Rider gasped, her hands fluttering like agitated birds. "It rang just now, and when I answered it, a voice—a most dreadful, strangled voice—cried out: 'Help! Help! Murder!' Then there was a heavy fall and nothing more. I was that frightened, I ran straight here knowing you were with Monsieur Poirot."

“It was the telephone, doctor. I answered it—and a voice spoke.
‘Help,’ it said. ‘Doctor—help. They’ve killed me!’ Then it sort of
tailed away. ‘Who’s speaking?’ I said. ‘Who’s speaking?’ Then I
got a reply, just a whisper, it seemed, ‘Foscatine’—something like
that—‘Regent’s Court.’”

The doctor uttered an exclamation.

“Count Foscatini. He has a flat in Regent’s Court. I must go at
once. What can have happened?”

“A patient of yours?” asked Poirot.

“I attended him for some slight ailment a few weeks ago. An Italian,
but he speaks English perfectly. Well, I must wish you good night,
Monsieur Poirot, unless——” He hesitated.

“I perceive the thought in your mind,” said Poirot, smiling. “I
shall be delighted to accompany you. Hastings, run down and get
hold of a taxi.”

The lift stopped at the second floor, and the attendant, whose face now betrayed a certain degree of apprehension, led us to the door of Flat II. He pressed the bell twice, but there was no response. Dr. Hawker's face grew more serious. "He may be beyond answering," he said grimly. The attendant produced his passkey and opened the door. We stepped into a small, square hall. On the right, a door stood ajar, and a bright light shone from within. Dr. Hawker hurried forward and pushed the door open, only to recoil with a sharp cry of "My God!"

The lift stopped, and we stepped out into the carpeted corridor. Dr. Hawker led the way to the door of Flat 11 and pressed the electric bell. We waited, but there was no sound of footsteps from within. The doctor rang again, a long, insistent peal, yet the silence remained unbroken. With an impatient exclamation, he seized the door-handle and turned it. To our profound surprise, the door was not locked. It yielded at once, and we passed into the small, dimly lit hallway of the flat. No one was in sight, but from the room beyond—the dining-room, as it proved to be—there came a strange, muffled sound that made our pulses quicken.

The lift stopped, and Dr. Hawker led the way down the corridor to the door of Flat II. He rang the bell with a sharp, insistent touch, but no one came to answer it. After a moment’s hesitation, he turned the handle; the door was unfastened, and we passed into the small, square hall. All was silent. From a door on the right, a beam of light fell across the floor. The doctor pushed it open and we followed him into a dining-room where the table was laid for three. But it was the figure in the armchair that caught our breath—a man with a dark, olive complexion, his head lolled back at a grotesque angle and his eyes staring sightlessly at the ceiling. A heavy marble paperweight, stained with blood, lay on the floor beside him.

The lift came to a standstill, and the attendant led the way to the door of Flat II. He rang the bell, but there was no response from within. After a moment's pause, he rang again, more insistently, and we waited in a silence that felt increasingly ominous. Finally, at the doctor's urgent request, the man produced his passkey and turned it in the lock. We stepped into a small, darkly panelled hall. From a room just ahead of us, the door of which stood slightly ajar, a bright stream of light fell across the floor. Dr. Hawker pushed it open and then fell back with a sharp cry.

The lift came to a standstill, and the attendant threw back the metal gates. We stepped out into the thickly carpeted corridor, and Dr. Hawker led the way to the door of Number 11. He pressed the electric bell, but there was no response from within the silent apartment. He waited a few moments and then rang again, more insistently this time. Still there was no sound of approaching footsteps, nor any indication of life. With a muttered exclamation of impatience, the doctor tried the door-handle. To our surprise, the door was not locked; it yielded beneath his touch and swung slowly inwards, revealing a small, dimly-lit entrance hall.

He pulled back the iron door, and we stepped out on the landing.
No. II was opposite to us. The doctor rang the bell. There was no
reply, and we could hear no sound from within. The doctor rang
again and again; we could hear the bell trilling within, but no
sign of life rewarded us.

“This is getting serious,” muttered the doctor. He turned to the
lift attendant.

“Is there any pass-key to this door?”

“There is one in the porter’s office downstairs.”

“Get it, then, and, look here, I think you’d better send for the
police.”

Poirot approved with a nod of the head.

The man returned shortly; with him came the manager.

“Will you tell me, gentlemen, what is the meaning of all this?”

“Certainly. I received a telephone message from Count Foscatini
stating that he had been attacked and was dying. You can understand
that we must lose no time—if we are not already too late.”

The manager produced the key without more ado, and we all entered
the flat.

We passed first into a small square lounge hall. A door on the
right of it was half open. The manager indicated it with a nod.

“The dining-room.”

We had just completed our survey of the premises when the sound of a key turning in the outer door reached our ears. A moment later, a man stood in the doorway, his eyes traveling in bewilderment from the body of his master to the group of strangers. He was a man of middle age, with the quiet, expressionless face of the trained servant. This was evidently Mr. Graves. His composure, however, vanished at the sight of the slumped figure at the desk, and he let out a stifled cry of horror.

We had hardly completed our brief survey when the sound of heavy footsteps in the hall announced the arrival of the police. It was Inspector Japp himself who entered, his eyes widening with a mixture of professional interest and weary resignation at the sight of Poirot. “You again, moosior?” he remarked, before turning his attention to the grim tableau at the desk. While Japp’s men began the routine work of measuring and photographing, the front door opened once more to admit a middle-aged man of quiet, deferential appearance. This was Mr. Graves, the Count’s valet. Upon being informed of the tragedy, he collapsed into a chair, his face a mask of horrified bewilderment, and it was some minutes before he was composed enough to explain that he had been sent out by his master on a specific errand shortly after the dinner had commenced.

We had hardly finished our cursory inspection when the front door opened and a man entered. He stood momentarily transfixed, staring at the unexpected assembly in the hall. He was a man of middle age, with a discreet, clean-shaven face and the unmistakable bearing of a well-trained servant. The manager stepped forward and addressed him. “Ah, Graves, this is a terrible business. Your master—” The man’s eyes widened. “The Count, sir? Has something happened to him?” He pushed past us into the dining-room, only to recoil with a smothered cry at the sight of the figure slumped over the desk. “Oh, my God! The Count! He’s—he’s dead!”

Poirot, however, was not looking at the body. He had wandered over
to the dinner table and was looking at the remains of the meal.
There were three plates, and it appeared that the meal had been a
simple one, consisting of a soup, a main dish of some kind of
stew, and dessert. Poirot’s eyes were fixed on the plates with a
peculiar intensity. Suddenly he turned. The sound of a key was
heard in the outer door. A moment later a man entered the room,
stopped dead, and stared at us in amazement. He was a tall, dark
man of middle age, dressed in a quiet suit of blue. This,
evidently, was Mr. Graves.

The arrival of Inspector Japp was not long delayed. The Scotland Yard official was an old friend of ours, and he greeted Poirot with a comical mixture of respect and professional jealousy. After a brief briefing from Dr. Hawker, Japp began his survey of the room, but he had barely commenced when the sound of a key turning in the front door announced a new arrival. A tall, thin man of middle age, with a discreet and slightly melancholy face, stood frozen on the threshold of the dining-room. This was Mr. Graves, the Count’s valet, and the expression of horrified bewilderment that crossed his features as he took in the scene—the huddled figure at the desk and the presence of the police—seemed, at first glance, entirely genuine.

We came back to the dining-room. Poirot had not accompanied us in
our tour. I found him studying the centre table with close
attention. I joined him. It was a well-polished round mahogany
table. A bowl of roses decorated the centre, and white lace mats
reposed on the gleaming surface. There was a dish of fruit, but
the three dessert plates were untouched. There were three
coffee-cups with remains of coffee in them—two black, one with
milk. All three men had taken port, and the decanter, half-full,
stood before the centre plate. One of the men had smoked a cigar,
the other two cigarettes. A tortoiseshell-and-silver box, holding
cigars and cigarettes, stood open upon the table.

I enumerated all these facts to myself, but I was forced to admit
that they did not shed any brilliant light on the situation. I
wondered what Poirot saw in them to make him so intent. I asked
him.

“_Mon ami_,” he replied, “you miss the point. I am looking for
something that I do _not_ see.”

“What is that?”

“A mistake—even a little mistake—on the part of the murderer.”

He stepped swiftly to the small adjoining kitchen, looked in, and
shook his head.

“Monsieur,” he said to the manager, “explain to me, I pray, your
system of serving meals here.”

The manager stepped to a small hatch in the wall.

The manager signaled his assent, and we were soon whisked up to the top floor in the service lift. The kitchens were vast and well-organized, though the heat was somewhat oppressive to my mind. Poirot, however, seemed entirely in his element. He addressed the head chef with a polite flourish of his hand, explaining that he wished to see the plates and remains of the dinner served to Flat II. The chef, though clearly harried by the late hour, led us to a side table where a stack of dishes awaited the dishwasher's attention. With a small pair of tweezers he produced from his pocket, Poirot began to turn over the fragments of food—the bones of three grouse, the remains of a _soufflé grand marnier_, and the skins of three peaches—as though each morsel held a secret of profound significance.

The manager escorted us to the lift, and we ascended to the top floor. The kitchens were large and well-appointed, though at this hour the bustle was beginning to die down. At a word from the manager, the head chef came forward. Poirot wasted no time. “The dinner for Flat 11—it was for three persons, was it not?” “Yes, Monsieur,” replied the chef, consulting a ledger. “Soup, _sole meunière_, _tournedos_, and a savory. All served for three.” Poirot inspected the remains on the dirty plates with meticulous care, his eyes darting from one piece of cutlery to another. “Everything appears to be in order,” he remarked, yet I noticed he seemed particularly interested in the quantity of food consumed from each plate.

The manager, somewhat mystified by Poirot’s request, led us to the top of the building. The communal kitchens were a scene of organized chaos, though the dinner rush had largely passed. Poirot was introduced to the head chef, and after a brief exchange in French that seemed to establish an immediate rapport, he was shown the stacks of crockery recently returned from the service lift of Flat II. With meticulous care, Poirot examined each plate, noting the remains of the meal—a clear soup, a dish of sea kale, and a main course of _noisettes d’agneau_. He seemed particularly interested in the quantities of food left on the plates, murmuring to himself as he counted the various utensils.

The manager conducted us to the top floor. The kitchens were large
and well-ordered, bustling with the activity of clearing away the
evening’s service. At Poirot’s request, the head chef pointed out
the remains of the meal that had been sent down to Flat II. Poirot
fell to examining the plates with an extraordinary intentness. He
seemed especially interested in the debris of the second course—a
dish of _Risotto de Volaille_—and he carefully counted the number
of cutlets that had been consumed from the silver platter, his
brows knit in deep concentration.

The manager complied, leading us to the top of the building where the communal kitchens were located. It was a scene of late-night efficiency, with staff beginning to tidy away for the evening. At a word from our guide, a kitchen-clerk brought forward the tray containing the used dishes from Flat II. Poirot bent over them, his nose almost touching the cold remains of the feast. He noted the three plates, each with the remnants of a savoury, followed by the bones of three portions of chicken. He seemed particularly interested in the contents of the bread-basket and the number of used wine glasses. I watched him, wondering what could possibly be gained from the study of dirty plates, while Dr. Hawker fidgeted with his watch, clearly anxious to return to the scene of the crime.

“Oh, certainly, if you like! Roberts, the lift man, will take you
up and introduce you; but I’m afraid you won’t find anything that’s
of any use. They’re handling hundreds of plates and dishes, and
they’ll be all lumped together.”

Poirot remained firm, however, and together we visited the kitchens
and questioned the man who had taken the order from Flat II.

“Every dish was returned, and by the looks of it, he and his
guests had done full justice to them. The plates were practically
licked clean.”

“Aha!” Poirot murmured. “That is most interesting. A gourmand,
this Count. It is a pity his life was cut short so abruptly.
Now, Hasting, let us return to the scene of the tragedy.”

When we got back, Inspector Japp had arrived with two of his men.
The Inspector greeted us with his usual breezy cordiality.

“Always in it, aren’t you, Mr. Poirot? Well, we’ve got a clear
case this time, I think. We know the men we’re after.”

“Indeed?”

“Yes. A couple of Italian scoundrels. They’ve been seen about
here lately. Political job, I should say. This Count Foscatini
wasn’t his real name—we’ve had our eye on him for some time. He
was a bit of a mystery, but we’ve reason to believe he was mixed
up in several shady transactions.”

“And you think his friends from Italy paid him a visit to settle
accounts?”

“That’s about the size of it. They were seen entering the building
at half-past seven. They didn’t come out by the front, but there’s
a back entrance they could easily have used. We’ve got their
descriptions. One’s a tall, thin man with a black beard, the other’s
shorter and stouter.”

“Well, sir, as to that, the empty dishes go up, as you see, and
certainly none of them came back full. They were as clean as plates
usually are after a meal—that is, the ones from the soup and the
fish. There was a little of the beef left, and a good bit of the
soufflé.”

“Aha! That is very interesting. A small eater, then, this Count
Foscatini? Thank you, monsieur. We will return down.”

We found Inspector Japp of Scotland Yard already in the dining-room.
He greeted Poirot with a grin.

“Another of these ‘mysteries’ that you like so much, eh? A regular
top-hole business, this. Count Foscatini—well known to the
Italian Embassy as a man of some social standing, but not above
suspicion in certain political directions. We’ve had our eye on
him for some time. It looks as though his ‘friends’ have got even
with him at last.”

“His friends? Two of them, were there not?”

“That’s it. Both Italians, by the description the lift man gave
of them. They’ve made a clean getaway—but we’ll have them before
long. We’re on their track already.”

“You have their names, then?”

“One of them, at all events. Signor Ascanio. He’s the man we want.”

“Ascanio? A tall man, was he, of middle age?”

“That’s it. How did you know?”

“I did not know. I guessed. It is a common name in Italy.”

“Is it?” said Japp. “I didn’t know that. But we’ve got something
to go on. This man Ascanio was at the Italian Embassy this
morning, asking for the Count’s address. We can get a full
description of him there.”

“Then you think it is a political assassination?”

“Looks like it. Some secret society business, I should say.
They’re a rare lot, these Latins!”

“What about the man-servant—this Graves?” asked Poirot.

“He returned just as we arrived. He seems a decent, reliable
sort of fellow. He’d been given the evening out by his master.
The Count, it appears, was expecting two friends to dinner, and
intended to do his own waiting.”

“Wait a moment,” I interrupted. “That is slightly unusual, is it
not? A man of the Count’s position waiting on his own guests?”

“It was on account of the privacy of their conversation, so
Graves says,” explained Japp. “The Count was particularly
anxious that no one should overhear what they had to say. He
did not even want the service-lift man to see his guests, and
gave orders that the courses were to be left in the lift, and
that he would take them out himself.”

Poirot’s eyes twinkled.

“Very interesting,” he murmured. “A man of some ingenuity, the
late Count Foscatini.”

“He did, sir. He’s a good customer, and always has his little
dinner in style. Everything was sent up in due course, and the
trays returned empty—well, not empty, of course, but the plates
showed that the dishes had been properly appreciated.”

Poirot’s eyes twinkled. “Ah, he had a fine appetite, this Count of
yours! And the two other gentlemen? They also, I presume, had
justice done to them?”

“As far as I know, sir. The portions sent up were for three, and
all returned as usual. Is there anything else you’d like to know?”

“No, I thank you. Our business is finished.”

We returned to the second floor. A few minutes later a sharp-faced
young man arrived from Scotland Yard, and was soon deep in talk
with the doctor and the manager. Poirot and I stood together in
a corner.

“Well, Hastings,” said my friend, “what do you make of it?”

“A very simple case,” I replied. “The Count was obviously
blackmailed by these two men. He invited them to dinner to discuss
terms. They could not agree, and they killed him. They were
probably out of the flat and away before the Count was even able
to reach the telephone. As for the man, Graves, it’s a bit
suspicious his being out just then, but he may be speaking the
truth.”

“And the telephone call?”

“A last dying effort. He must have had just strength enough to
crawl to the phone and gasp out those few words.”

Poirot shook his head.

“You are very rapid, my friend. But there are one or two points
that do not fit in. If the Count was expecting a visit from
blackmailers, why did he have such a—well, such a _comfortable_
dinner? Why the soup, the fish, the entrée, and the sweet? A man
who is going to be murdered does not usually display such a fine
unprejudiced appetite.”

“He might not have known they were going to murder him,” I
suggested.

“Perhaps not. But it is a little unusual, all the same. And then
there is another point. The man, Graves. He says his master had
two visitors to dinner. The lift man says he didn’t see them. That
is possible, of course. They might have come by the stairs. But
it is a point to be noted. And then, there is the question of the
menu. It is a very—what shall I say?—well-balanced menu. But did
you notice one thing? There was no salad.”

“Good heavens, Poirot!” I cried. “What has a salad to do with it?”

“Everything, my friend. To a man of my nationality, a dinner
without a salad is—is—inconceivable! And yet, there was no salad
provided for in that order.”

I looked at him in amazement. Sometimes I really believe Poirot
is a little mad. But at that moment the young man from Scotland
Yard came up to us.

“Inspector Japp,” he introduced himself. “I believe you are
Monsieur Poirot? I’ve heard of you. I’d be glad of a word with you,
if you don’t mind.”

The two moved away together, and I was left to my own reflections.
It was not long, however, before Poirot rejoined me. His face was
grave.

“The plot thickens, Hastings,” he said. “It seems that Count
Foscatini was a man of some importance in certain circles—circles
that are not always above-board. And he was not a Count at all.
His name was—well, never mind what his name was. But he was a
very useful man to certain people.”

“A spy?” I whispered.

“Something of the sort. And now he is dead. It is a very pretty
little problem—very pretty indeed.”

He was silent for a moment, then he added:

“We must find this man Graves. He is the key to the mystery.”

But Graves was not to be found. He had vanished as completely as
though the earth had swallowed him up. Inquiries at his club—he
belonged to a small club in Soho—failed to produce any
information. He had not been there that evening.

It was not until the following day that we had any news. And then
it was Japp who brought it.

“We’ve got him!” he announced triumphantly. “Found him in a
lodging-house in Bloomsbury. He was just packing his bag to start
for the Continent.”

“And what does he say?” asked Poirot.

“He’s got a very fine story. Says he was told by the Count that
he wouldn’t be wanted that evening, as he was expecting two friends
to dinner. He says he went out about half-past seven, and didn’t
come back until nearly eleven. He says he was quite surprised to
find the police there.”

“And the two friends?”

“He says he doesn’t know who they were. He’d never seen them
before. They were Italians, he says, and spoke in their own
language most of the time.”

“A very likely story,” I remarked.

“But there’s one thing,” Japp went on. “He had a large sum of
money on him—nearly five hundred pounds in notes. He can’t
account for it—says it’s his savings. But that’s a bit thin, isn’t
it?”

“It is certainly—suggestive,” said Poirot. “And the two Italians?
Have you any clue to them?”

“We’re looking for them. We’ve got a description of sorts. One
was a tall man with a beard, and the other was shorter and
dark-haired. Not much to go on, I’m afraid.”

“Wait a moment,” said Poirot. “A tall man with a beard, and a
shorter, dark-haired man. Where have I heard that before?”

He thought for a moment, then his face cleared.

“I have it! The two men who were seen leaving the building shortly
after nine o’clock. The porter remembered them when Japp questioned
him.”

“That’s right,” said Japp. “But they might be anyone. It’s a large
building, and people are always coming and going.”

“True,” said Poirot. “But it is a coincidence, all the same. And
now, Japp, I have a little suggestion to make. I should like to
have a word with this man Graves—if you have no objection.”

“None at all. You’ll find him at the police station. But I don’t
think you’ll get much out of him. He’s a cool customer, I can tell
you.”

“We shall see,” said Poirot, with a smile. “Come, Hastings, let
us go and see what Monsieur Graves has to say for himself.”

The man stared. “I couldn’t tell you that, I’m sure, sir. The
plates that come back are generally pretty clean, I should say. It
was a good little dinner, that. The Count was a gentleman as
appreciated good cooking. He usually ordered for two, but to-night,
as I say, it was for three.”

Poirot’s eyes twinkled. “For three? You are sure of that?”

“Oh, yes, sir. Three of everything—three portions of soup, three of
fish, three of tournedos, and three portions of soufflé. All
served together.”

Poirot seemed satisfied. He led the way back to the lift. As we
descended, we met the police arriving. Inspector Japp was among
them, and he greeted Poirot with a friendly grin.

“Another of your little cases? Not much doubt about this one, I
should say. Those two foreign gentlemen did for him between them.
I shouldn’t be surprised if they were gone out of the country by
now. We’ll have a job to find them.”

“You think so?” said Poirot softly.

“I do. It’s the usual thing. A quarrel—the Count’s a bit of a
mystery, isn’t he?—they get to high words, and one of them picks
up the first thing handy and brained him. Then they made off as
fast as they could. It’s a plain, common or garden case. Nothing
for you here, Monsieur Poirot.”

“I am not so sure,” said Poirot. “There are several points of
interest.”

“For instance?”

“The coffee,” said Poirot. “One cup with milk, two without. The
fact that there were three of everything. And the telephone call.
Why did the Count telephone to the doctor instead of the police?”

“He’d had the doctor lately—natural to think of him,” said Japp.
“And as to the coffee—well, people have their different tastes.”

“Yes,” said Poirot. “It is very interesting.”

“Everything,” said the man. “I’m sure of it, because the dishes
were always quite empty when they came back. There wasn’t a bit of
food left on them.”

Poirot’s eyes shone with a sudden light.

“_C’est intéressant!_” he murmured.

He turned away, and we descended to the second floor again.

The police had arrived, and with them a sharp-looking man in plain
clothes who was introduced as Inspector Japp of Scotland Yard. I
was glad to see that our old friend was in charge of the case.
He was already busy taking notes, and he greeted us with a
cheerful nod.

“Glad to see you, Monsieur Poirot. There’s something in your line
here, I think. This looks like a nasty business.”

Poirot drew him aside and whispered something in his ear. Japp’s
eyebrows rose.

“You think so?” he said. “Well, it’s worth trying, anyway.”

He turned to the manager.

“I want to see the lift-man who was on duty this evening.”

The man was soon found.

“I was only on duty from eight o’clock,” he explained. “At half-past
eight I took Mr. Graves—the Count’s man—down. He said he was going
out for the evening.”

“And the Count’s guests?”

“I didn’t see them. They must have come in before eight.”

“Did you see anyone else go into the flat?”

“No one, sir.”

“You are sure of that?”

“Positive. I’ve been in the lift all the time.”

“Then,” said Japp, “it seems fairly certain that the murderers
were the two men who were dining with the Count. But where are they?
They couldn’t have vanished into thin air.”

The manager stepped forward.

“There’s a fire-escape at the back of the building,” he said. “It
leads down from the kitchen of each flat to the courtyard below.”

Japp nodded.

“That explains it. They must have made their escape that way. But
who were they? That’s the question.”

Poirot, who had been listening intently, now spoke.

“I think,” he said, “that I can give you a little information on
that point. One of the guests was a tall, dark man with a beard;
the other was shorter and had a slight moustache.”

Japp stared at him.

“How do you know that?” he asked.

Poirot smiled.

“It is a little deduction of my own,” he said. “But let us see if
I am right. Is there anyone here who saw the Count’s guests this
evening?”

No one had seen them.

“Then we must look elsewhere for our information,” said Poirot.
“But I think you will find that I am right.”

Japp looked at him doubtfully.

“Well,” he said, “we’ll see. In the meantime, I’ll have a look at
the Count’s papers. There may be something there to give us a
clue.”

He turned to the writing-table and began to turn over the papers.
Suddenly he gave a cry of surprise.

“Look here!” he said. “What do you make of this?”

He held up a small, square piece of paper. On it were written two
names: “Signor Ascanio” and “Signor Paolo.”

“Those must be the two guests!” I cried.

“It looks like it,” said Japp. “But who are they?”

“Ascanio is a well-known name in Italy,” said Poirot. “As for
Paolo, it is a common enough Christian name.”

“Well,” said Japp, “I’ll get on to the Italian Embassy and see if
they can help us. In the meantime, I’ll have a look round the rest
of the flat.”

We followed him as he went through the rooms. Everything was in
the most perfect order. The Count was evidently a man of means,
and the flat was furnished with great taste.

In the bedroom we found a large trunk, packed and ready for
departure. On the labels was the name “Count Foscatini,” and the
destination “Rome.”

“He was going away, then,” said Japp.

“So it appears,” said Poirot.

He was standing by the dressing-table, looking at a small
photograph in a silver frame. It was the portrait of a very
beautiful woman.

“Who is this, I wonder?” he said.

“I don’t know,” said Japp. “But I’ll find out.”

He turned to the manager.

“Do you know who this lady is?”

The manager shook his head.

“I’ve never seen her before,” he said.

Poirot replaced the photograph on the dressing-table.

“A very beautiful woman,” he repeated.

We returned to the dining-room. Japp was still busy with his
investigations. Suddenly he looked up.

“Wait a minute!” he said. “I’ve just remembered something. Signor
Ascanio! Wasn’t there a Signor Ascanio who was involved in that
big financial scandal in Rome a few years ago?”

“You are right,” said Poirot. “I remember the case well. He was
acquitted, but many people believed that he was guilty.”

“Then it’s more than likely that he’s our man,” said Japp. “I’ll
get on to the Embassy at once.”

He went to the telephone and was soon in communication with the
Italian Embassy. After a few minutes’ conversation he hung up the
receiver and turned to us.

“I’ve got some news,” he said. “Signor Ascanio is in London at the
present moment. He’s staying at the Ritz. And what’s more, he was
seen this evening in the company of a man who answers to your
description, Poirot—short, with a slight moustache.”

“Aha!” said Poirot. “And the other man—the tall one with the
beard?”

“They don’t know anything about him,” said Japp. “But I think we’ve
got enough to go on. I’ll go round to the Ritz at once and see if
I can find Signor Ascanio.”

“I will accompany you,” said Poirot.

“And I too,” I said.

We left the flat and drove to the Ritz. On arrival there we were
informed that Signor Ascanio was in his room. We went up and found
him alone.

He was a tall, handsome man of middle age, with dark, piercing
eyes and a distinguished appearance. He seemed surprised to see us.

“To what do I owe the honour of this visit?” he asked, in
excellent English.

Japp introduced himself and explained the object of our visit.
Ascanio’s face went pale.

“Count Foscatini murdered!” he cried. “It is impossible!”

“I’m afraid it’s only too true,” said Japp. “And I understand that
you were dining with him this evening.”

Ascanio hesitated for a moment.

“It is true,” he said at last. “I was dining with him. But I left
early—about half-past eight.”

“And your companion?” asked Poirot.

Ascanio looked at him in surprise.

“My companion? I was alone.”

“But I understood that there were two guests,” said Japp.

Ascanio shook his head.

“No,” he said. “I was the only guest.”

“Then who was the other man?” asked Japp. “The man with the slight
moustache?”

Ascanio’s face went even paler.

“I—I don’t know,” he stammered.

“Come, come, Signor Ascanio,” said Japp. “It’s no use denying it.
We know that you were seen in his company this evening.”

Ascanio was silent for a moment. Then he spoke.

“Very well,” he said. “I will tell you the truth. The other man
was my secretary, Signor Paolo. But he did not dine with us. He
waited for me in the hall of the flat.”

“And did he stay there all the time?” asked Japp.

“As far as I know, yes,” said Ascanio.

“And what time did you leave?”

“At half-past eight, as I told you.”

“And where did you go then?”

“We went back to the hotel.”

“And you were there for the rest of the evening?”

“Yes.”

Japp looked at him suspiciously.

“Well,” he said, “I’ll have to ask you to come with me to the
station and make a statement.”

Ascanio protested, but Japp was firm, and in the end he was forced
to comply.

We returned to the flat, where we found the doctor and the manager
waiting for us.

“Well?” asked the doctor. “Any news?”

Japp told him what had happened.

“It looks bad for Ascanio,” said the doctor.

“It does,” said Japp. “But there’s one thing that puzzles me.
If Ascanio and his secretary were the murderers, why did they
leave their names on the writing-table?”

“Perhaps they didn’t,” said Poirot. “Perhaps it was the Count
himself who wrote them.”

“But why should he do that?” asked Japp.

“I don’t know,” said Poirot. “But it’s a possibility.”

He turned to the manager.

“Tell me,” he said. “Was there anyone else in the flat this
evening? Anyone at all?”

The manager shook his head.

“No one,” he said. “Only the Count and his guests.”

“And the man Graves?”

“He went out at half-past eight, as I told you.”

“And what time did he return?”

“He hasn’t returned yet.”

“That’s strange,” said Japp. “I’ll have a word with him when he
comes back.”

He turned to the doctor.

“Well, doctor, I think that’s all we can do for the moment. I’ll
let you know if anything else turns up.”

The doctor thanked him and left. Poirot and I followed him.

As we walked down the street Poirot was very silent. I knew the
signs, and I did not disturb him. At last he spoke.

“Hastings,” he said, “there is something about this case that I do
not like.”

“What is it?” I asked.

“The dinner,” he said. “The dinner of three.”

“But what’s wrong with it?”

“Everything,” said Poirot. “It is a very strange dinner indeed.”

“I don’t see anything strange about it,” I said.

“No,” said Poirot. “But then you do not see as I see. You look,
but you do not observe.”

He was silent for a moment. Then he spoke again.

“Hastings,” he said, “I want you to do something for me.”

“What is it?”

“I want you to go back to the flat and find out everything you can
about the man Graves. Find out where he goes, what he does—
everything.”

“But why?” I asked.

“Because,” said Poirot, “I have a little idea. And if I am right,
Mr. Graves is a very important person in this case.”

I did as he requested, and for the next few days I spent my time
following Graves. I found out that he was a very quiet, respectable
man who lived a very simple life. He went to the same club every
evening, and he never seemed to see anyone or do anything out of
the ordinary.

I reported all this to Poirot, but he did not seem surprised.

“Good,” he said. “It is as I thought.”

“But what does it mean?” I asked.

“It means,” said Poirot, “that we are getting nearer to the truth.
But there is still one thing that I do not understand.”

“What is that?”

“The telephone call,” he said. “The telephone call to Dr. Hawker.”

“But what’s wrong with it?”

“Everything,” said Poirot. “It is the most mysterious thing of
all.”

He was silent for a moment. Then he spoke again.

“Hastings,” he said, “I think it is time that we had another talk
with Signor Ascanio.”

We went to the Ritz and found Ascanio in his room. He seemed very
nervous.

“Well, Signor Ascanio,” said Poirot. “I hope you have had time to
think things over.”

“I have told you the truth,” said Ascanio. “I have nothing more to
say.”

“Are you sure of that?” asked Poirot. “Are you quite sure?”

Ascanio was silent.

“Because,” said Poirot, “I have found out something. Something very
interesting.”

Ascanio looked at him in alarm.

“What is it?” he asked.

“I have found out,” said Poirot, “that you were not the only guest
at the Count’s dinner-table.”

Ascanio’s face went white.

“What do you mean?” he asked.

“I mean,” said Poirot, “that there was a third person there.
A person whose name was not on the writing-table.”

Ascanio was silent for a moment. Then he spoke.

“Very well,” he said. “I will tell you the truth. There was a
third person. A woman.”

“Aha!” said Poirot. “And who was she?”

“She was the woman in the photograph,” said Ascanio. “The woman in
the Count’s bedroom.”

“And who is she?”

“She is my wife,” said Ascanio.

“Your wife!” I cried.

“Yes,” said Ascanio. “She was the Count’s mistress. I found out about
it, and I went to the flat to confront them.”

“And what happened?” asked Poirot.

“We had a quarrel,” said Ascanio. “A very violent quarrel. And
then—and then I killed him.”

“You killed him?” said Japp, who had just entered the room.

“Yes,” said Ascanio. “I killed him.”

Japp stepped forward and arrested him.

“Well,” said Japp, as we walked away. “That seems to be the end of
that. A very simple case, after all.”

“Do you think so?” said Poirot.

“Of course,” said Japp. “He’s confessed, hasn’t he?”

“Yes,” said Poirot. “He’s confessed. But I wonder why.”

“Because he’s guilty, of course!” said Japp.

“Perhaps,” said Poirot. “But I am not so sure.”

He was silent for a moment. Then he spoke again.

“Hastings,” he said, “I want you to come with me to Dr. Hawker’s.”

We went to the doctor’s house and found him in his study. He seemed
very surprised to see us.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” he said. “What can I do for you?”

“I want to ask you a few questions about the telephone call you
received on the night of the murder,” said Poirot.

The doctor looked at him in surprise.

“But I’ve already told you everything I know,” he said.

“I know,” said Poirot. “But I want to ask you one more question.
Are you quite sure that it was the Count’s voice you heard?”

The doctor hesitated for a moment.

“Well,” he said, “I thought it was. But I couldn’t be sure.
It was just a whisper, you know.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And did you hear anything else? Anything at
all?”

“No,” said the doctor. “Nothing.”

“Thank you,” said Poirot. “That is all I wanted to know.”

We left the doctor’s house and walked back to our rooms.

“Poirot,” I said. “What is all this about?”

“It is very simple, my friend,” said Poirot. “But I cannot tell you
yet. I must wait until I have all the facts.”

The next morning Poirot received a letter. He read it and then
handed it to me. It was from Japp.

“Dear Poirot,” it ran. “We’ve got some more news about the Foscatini
case. It seems that Ascanio was lying. His wife was not in London
on the night of the murder. She was in Rome. And what’s more, she
has an alibi that is absolutely unshakable.”

“Aha!” said Poirot. “So Ascanio was lying. But why?”

“Because he was trying to protect someone, of course!” I said.

“Perhaps,” said Poirot. “But who?”

“His secretary, Signor Paolo?” I suggested.

“Maybe,” said Poirot. “But there is another possibility.”

“What is that?”

“The man Graves,” said Poirot.

“Graves!” I cried. “But he was out all the evening.”

“So he says,” said Poirot. “But have we any proof of that?”

“No,” I said. “But why should he kill the Count?”

“I don’t know,” said Poirot. “But I have a little idea.”

He was silent for a moment. Then he spoke again.

“Hastings,” he said, “I want you to go back to Regent’s Court and
find out if anyone saw Graves on the night of the murder.”

I did as he requested, but I could find no one who had seen him.

I reported this to Poirot, but he did not seem surprised.

“Good,” he said. “It is as I thought.”

“But what does it mean?” I asked.

“It means,” said Poirot, “that we are very near to the truth.
And now, my friend, I think it is time that we had a little talk
with Miss Rider.”

“Miss Rider!” I cried. “The doctor’s housekeeper?”

“Yes,” said Poirot. “Miss Rider.”

We went to the doctor’s house and found Miss Rider in the kitchen.
She seemed very surprised to see us.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” she said. “What can I do for you?”

“I want to ask you a few questions about the night of the murder,”
said Poirot.

Miss Rider looked at him in surprise.

“But I’ve already told you everything I know,” she said.

“I know,” said Poirot. “But I want to ask you one more question.
Are you quite sure that it was the Count’s voice you heard on the
telephone?”

Miss Rider hesitated for a moment.

“Well,” she said, “I thought it was. But I couldn’t be sure.
It was just a whisper, you know.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And did you hear anything else? Anything at
all?”

“No,” said the doctor. “Nothing.”

“Thank you,” said Poirot. “That is all I wanted to know.”

We left the doctor’s house and walked back to our rooms.

“Poirot,” I said. “What is all this about?”

“It is very simple, my friend,” said Poirot. “But I cannot tell you
yet. I must wait until I have all the facts.”

The next day Poirot received another letter. He read it and then
handed it to me. It was from Japp.

“Dear Poirot,” it ran. “We’ve got some more news about the Foscatini
case. It seems that Graves was not out all the evening. He was seen
by one of the other servants in the building. He was seen coming
out of the Count’s flat at about a quarter to nine.”

“Aha!” said Poirot. “So Graves was in the flat after all.
And what’s more, he was there at the very time that the murder
must have been committed.”

“Then he’s the murderer!” I cried.

“Perhaps,” said Poirot. “But we must be sure. And I think I know
how to find out.”

He was silent for a moment. Then he spoke again.

“Hastings,” he said, “I want you to come with me to Regent’s Court.”

We went to the flat and found Japp and the manager there.

“Well, Japp,” said Poirot. “I think I can tell you who the
murderer is.”

Japp looked at him in surprise.

“You can?” he said. “Who is it?”

“It is Mr. Graves,” said Poirot.

“Graves!” said Japp. “But why should he kill the Count?”

“Because,” said Poirot, “the Count was not a Count at all.
He was a common blackmailer. And Graves was one of his victims.”

Japp stared at him in amazement.

“A blackmailer!” he said. “Are you sure?”

“Quite sure,” said Poirot. “I have been making some inquiries in
Italy. It seems that Foscatini was well known there as a
professional blackmailer. He had several victims in England, and
one of them was Mr. Graves.”

“But how did you find out?” asked Japp.

“It was the dinner,” said Poirot. “The dinner of three.”

“What about it?” asked Japp.

“It was a very strange dinner,” said Poirot. “You will remember
that all three men had eaten every dish. Now, that is very unusual.
Most people have their likes and dislikes. But these three men had
all eaten everything.”

“Well?” said Japp.

“Then there was the coffee,” said Poirot. “Three cups of coffee.
Two black and one with milk. And three different kinds of tobacco.
One cigar and two cigarettes. It all seemed to point to three
different people. But then I realized something. If there were
three people at the table, why were there no finger-prints on the
plates and glasses?”

“No finger-prints?” said Japp.

“No,” said Poirot. “I checked them myself. There were no
finger-prints at all. And that could only mean one thing. The table
had been set by someone who was wearing gloves.”

“Graves!” said Japp.

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “Graves had set the table himself.
He had eaten all the food himself, to make it look as though
three people had been there. He had even smoked the cigar and the
cigarettes himself. And then he had killed the Count.”

“But why did he do it?” asked Japp.

“Because,” said Poirot, “the Count was blackmailing him. Graves
had a secret—a very dark secret. And the Count had found out about
it. He was demanding a large sum of money, and Graves couldn’t pay.
So he decided to kill him.”

“And the telephone call?” asked Japp.

“That was the cleverest part of all,” said Poirot. “Graves knew
that the doctor was with me. So he called the doctor’s house,
knowing that Miss Rider would answer the phone. He disguised his
voice and pretended to be the Count. He knew that Miss Rider would
immediately tell the doctor, and that we would all come rushing to
the flat. That way, he would have a perfect alibi.”

“But how did he get out of the flat?” asked Japp.

“Through the fire-escape,” said Poirot. “It was very simple.”

Japp nodded.

“Well,” he said, “it looks like you’ve solved it again, Poirot.
I’ll go and arrest Graves at once.”

He left the room, and Poirot and I were left alone.

“Well, Poirot,” I said. “That was a very clever piece of work.”

“It was nothing, my friend,” said Poirot. “A very simple case,
after all.”

“But there is one thing that I still don’t understand,” I said.

“What is that?”

“Why did Ascanio confess?”

Poirot smiled.

“Because,” he said, “he was also being blackmailed by the Count.
And he thought that if he confessed, it would stop any further
investigation into his own affairs. He knew that his wife had a
perfect alibi, so he thought he was safe.”

“I see,” I said. “And the woman in the photograph?”

“She was just another of the Count’s victims,” said Poirot.
“He had many of them.”

He was silent for a moment. Then he spoke again.

“Well, Hastings,” he said. “I think that is the end of the
Foscatini case. Let us go and have some dinner.”

And so we did.

“Yes; but of course I can’t say how much of each he ate. The plates
were all soiled, and the dishes empty—that is to say, with the
exception of the rice soufflé. There was a fair amount of that
left.”

“Ah!” said Poirot, and seemed satisfied with the fact.

As we descended to the flat again he remarked in a low tone:

“We have decidedly to do with a man of method.”

“Do you mean the murderer, or Count Foscatini?”

“The latter was undoubtedly an orderly gentleman. After imploring
help and announcing his approaching demise, he carefully hung up
the telephone receiver.”

I stared at Poirot. His words now and his recent inquiries gave me
the glimmering of an idea.

“You suspect poison?” I breathed. “The blow on the head was a
blind.”

Poirot merely smiled.

“The Count, sir, was a gentleman who lived very simply,” he began.
“But he had many friends, and some of them—well, sir, they were
rather strange to my thinking. About a week ago a gentleman
called, a Signor Ascanio. They had a long talk together, and once
or twice I heard their voices raised as though in anger. At the
end, however, they seemed to have come to an understanding, for
the Count invited him to dinner to-night. He said he would bring
a friend with him.”

“Did you see this friend?” asked the inspector.

“No, sir. I’ve never seen him. The Count had given me the evening
off, and as I was going out I met Signor Ascanio on the stairs.
He was alone.”

“What time was that?”

“Just about eight o’clock, sir. He stopped me and asked me if the
Count was at home, and I told him yes. I then went on my way, and
only returned five minutes ago to find—this!”

The man was overcome by his feelings.

“What was this Signor Ascanio like?”

“A tall, thin man, sir, with a very dark complexion and a
melancholy expression. He spoke with a strong Italian accent.”

“We must find this Signor Ascanio,” the inspector said, with some
decision. “He was with the Count at eight o’clock, and at a
quarter-past eight the Count was dead.”

Graves nodded his head.

“I only wish I’d never gone out, sir. But the Count was most
insistent.”

“You say there were three for dinner?”

“Yes, sir. But only Signor Ascanio arrived while I was there. I
understand that the other gentleman was to come a little later.”

“I see. Well, we must get on his track as soon as possible.”

The inspector turned to Poirot.

“I suppose you’ll be wanting to have a look round, Monsieur
Poirot?”

“If I may.”

“Go ahead, then. I’ll just get a few notes from the doctor and
the manager.”

Poirot’s first move was to the writing-table. He examined the
blood-stained statuette with interest. Then he turned his
attention to the telephone.

“Ah! A most convenient instrument,” he murmured. “And what have
we here?”

He had picked up a small scrap of paper that lay on the floor near
the dead man’s hand. On it was written a name and address:

_Signor Ascanio, Hotel de l’Europe._

“A clue!” I cried.

“Possibly,” said Poirot. “But why should the Count write it down?
He knew where the man was staying, since he had invited him to
dinner.”

He looked at the dead man again, and then at the telephone.

“It is a problem,” he said. “A very pretty little problem.”

The inspector now joined us.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot, anything to suggest?”

“Only that you should find Signor Ascanio as soon as possible.”

“That’s what I’m going to do. I’ve already sent a man to the
Hotel de l’Europe. We’ll soon see what he has to say for himself.”

But when we reached the Hotel de l’Europe a fresh surprise
awaited us. Signor Ascanio had left the hotel that afternoon, and
his whereabouts were unknown.

About three weeks before, he said, his master had been visited by
a tall, dark man of Italian appearance, who had called himself
Signor Ascanio. On his departure the Count had appeared to be
greatly agitated, and had told Graves that he was in some trouble.
This morning he had received a letter, which he had read and then
promptly burnt. He told Graves that Signor Ascanio was coming to
dinner that night, and that he was bringing a friend.

“The Count told me to go out for the evening,” Graves explained.
“He said he would not need me. I was to go to the first house of
a music-hall, and then he gave me some money for my supper. I
think he wanted me out of the way.”

The inspector’s face took on an expression of importance.

“Now, Graves, I want you to tell me if you can describe this
Signor Ascanio.”

“Well, sir, he was a tall, dark man, as I said, and he had a
pointed black beard. He spoke English very well, but with a slight
accent. The friend I didn’t see. They must have come just after I
left.”

“What time was that?”

“Eight o’clock, sir.”

“And you returned—when?”

“About eleven o’clock. I let myself in with my latch-key. I
noticed nothing until I went into the dining-room to see if anything
was wanted. Then I saw—that!”

The man gave a sob and buried his face in his hands.

“Well, that seems clear enough,” said the inspector. “The Count
was being blackmailed by this Signor Ascanio. He was forced to
invite him to dinner. The friend was probably an accomplice.
They killed the Count and then decamped. We must get on the track
of this Ascanio at once. He shouldn't be hard to find.”

“One moment, Inspector,” said Poirot’s quiet voice. “There is one
point that I should like to be clear about. Did Count Foscatini
have much money in the flat?”

“I don’t know, sir. He had a small safe in his bedroom, but I
don’t know what was in it.”

“Well, we’d better have a look at it,” said the inspector.

He led the way to the bedroom. The safe was a small one of a
well-known make. It was locked, but the key was found in the
Count’s pocket. The inspector opened it. It contained a certain
amount of jewellery, but no money.

“This is strange,” he said. “Graves, did your master usually keep
much money in the safe?”

“I don’t know, sir. He never spoke to me about his money affairs.”

“Well, it looks as though robbery was the motive, after all. Now,
Graves, I want you to come with me to the station and give a
detailed description of this Signor Ascanio.”

“The Count had been much worried lately,” he told us. “About ten
days ago a gentleman called—a Signor Ascanio. They were together
for some time, and I could hear their voices raised in anger. Since
then the Count has been nervous and jumpy. This morning he had a
letter—also from Signor Ascanio. He read it and then burnt it.
But he stayed at home all day, and at about half-past seven the
Count told me he was expecting two gentlemen to dinner. He gave me
the evening off, but I was to stay and see them in. They arrived at
about five minutes to eight—Signor Ascanio and another gentleman.”

“What was the other one like?” asked the inspector.

“A tall, thin man, with a very dark face—a very unpleasant-looking
gentleman, if I may say so, sir.”

“And Signor Ascanio?”

“Oh, he was a different type altogether. A short, stout man, with
a very loud voice and a very florid complexion. He had a big
diamond ring on his finger.”

“The Count appeared to be on friendly terms with them?”

“Well, sir, I can’t say that. He seemed very nervous and
constrained. But he’d ordered a very good dinner—one of his
favourites.”

“And then?”

“Then, sir, the Count told me I could go. I went out at about five
minutes past eight. I’ve been to the cinema, and just got back.”

“The lift man says he saw you leave,” said the inspector. “How did
you get in just now? Have you a key?”

“No, sir, the door was ajar.”

“Ajar?”

“Yes, sir.”

The inspector’s eyes met those of the manager.

“That’s very strange,” the latter remarked. “The door has a
Yale lock. It shouldn’t have been left ajar.”

“But it was,” the valet insisted. “I’m sure of it.”

“And you saw no one on the stairs?”

“No, sir.”

“Signor Ascanio!” muttered the inspector. “It’s a good lead. We
must find him. What was the address on the letter the Count
received this morning?”

“I only saw the postmark, sir. It was Richmond.”

“Richmond! That’s a bit vague. Still, we’ve got his name. Signor
Ascanio. We should find him easily enough.”

“And the other man?” I asked.

The valet shook his head.

“The Count didn’t mention his name, sir. I’ve never seen him
before.”

“I arrived back at about half-past nine,” he explained. “I had been
given the evening out by the Count, who was expecting two friends
to dinner. When I came in, the flat was in darkness. I went
straight to the Count’s bedroom, but he wasn’t there. Then I
noticed the dining-room door was ajar, and I saw—that!”

He pointed with a shaking finger to the figure of his master.

“I only wish I had been here. I might have saved him. Those men—I
didn’t like the look of them from the first.”

“You saw them, then?” asked the inspector.

“Yes, sir. I showed them in. They came about eight o’clock. Two
gentlemen, Italians, I should say. One of them I’d seen before.
A Signor Ascanio. He’d been here before to see the Count. The
other was a much older man, very thin, with a long grey beard. I
didn’t catch his name.”

The inspector’s note-book was busy.

“And you were given the evening out?”

“Yes, sir. The Count often did that when he had friends to dinner.
He liked to be alone. He’d tell me to go at half-past seven, and
not to come back until ten.”

“But you came back at half-past nine?”

“Yes, sir. I’d been to the pictures, and I didn’t much care for the
film, so I thought I’d come back early.”

“Now, about this Signor Ascanio. You say you’d seen him before.
When was that?”

“About three weeks ago, sir. He came to see the Count one morning.
They had a bit of a row, I think. I heard their voices raised in the
study.”

“Can you give us a description of him?”

“A tall man, sir, very dark, with a small black moustache. Very
smartly dressed.”

The inspector nodded.

“And the other?”

“A much older man, as I said. Very thin, with a long grey beard.”

“What about the Count? Was he in his usual health and spirits?”

“I think he was a bit nervous, sir. He seemed to be expecting
somebody—or something.”

The inspector turned to Poirot.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot, what do you think of it?”

Poirot smiled.

“I find it very interesting,” he said. “A most interesting case.
Tell me, Monsieur Graves, did the Count ever mention this Signor
Ascanio to you?”

“No, sir. He never mentioned any of his friends. He was a very
reserved gentleman.”

“And you say he was in his usual health?”

“Yes, sir, as far as I know. He’d been seeing a doctor lately—Dr.
Hawker, I believe—but it was only for some small thing.”

Poirot nodded.

“I should like to have a look at the Count’s papers, if I may,” he
said to the inspector.

“I don’t see any objection. We’ll have to go through them anyway.”

The search was a short one. The Count’s papers were neatly
arranged, and there was very little of interest among them. A few
letters from friends in Italy, some bills, and a small diary.
Poirot turned the pages of the diary.

“Nothing much here,” he remarked. “Wait a minute. Here’s an entry
for to-day: ‘A. 8 p.m.’ That would be Ascanio, I suppose.”

He handed the diary to the inspector.

“I think we’d better get a move on,” said the latter. “I’ll have a
description of this Signor Ascanio circulated at once. We ought to
be able to pick him up before long.”

“His lordship,” he began, “had for some time past been extremely
nervous. He was a gentleman who lived very simply, and his tastes
were small. He spent much of his time at his club, the Marlborough.
He would frequently go there for lunch, and sometimes for dinner.
Lately, however, he had stayed at home. Only yesterday, sir, he
spoke of a change—of some great danger that was hanging over his
head. ‘Graves,’ he said, ‘there are men in London who seek my life.
But for the present they are held in check. I have friends—great
friends.’

“He then went on to speak of two gentlemen who were coming to see
him this evening. ‘I must have everything of the best, Graves.
Spare no expense. They are people of importance—vast importance.’

“I understood from his lordship that they were coming on business
of the utmost gravity. He was particularly anxious that I should
not be in the flat while they were here. He gave me the evening
