off, and I was to return at eleven o’clock. But I felt uneasy, sir,
and I came back early—to find—this!”

The poor fellow’s voice broke.

“Did you see these gentlemen?” asked the inspector.

“Yes, sir, I did. They arrived just as I was leaving. One was a
tall, dark man with a very long nose, and the other was a shorter,
stouter gentleman. Both looked like foreigners.”

“Could you identify them, do you think?”

“I am sure of it, sir.”

“They would be the men the lift-boy saw,” I put in.

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “And their names?”

“I don’t know their names, sir, but one of them was addressed as
Signor Ascanio.”

“Signor Ascanio,” repeated Poirot, as though the name were
familiar to him. “That is very interesting. And the other?”

“I didn’t hear his name, sir.”

The inspector turned to the valet.

“You are sure the Count seemed in fear of his life?”

“Positive, sir.”

“Then we have a very clear case. These two men come here, they
quarrel with him, and one of them kills him. We must find this
Signor Ascanio. I suppose you can’t give us his address?”

“No, sir, I’m afraid not.”

“Well, we’ll soon find him. A man like that shouldn’t be difficult
to trace.”

Poirot, meanwhile, had been wandering about the room. He now
stopped in front of the writing-table.

“This is the Count’s diary, I see. He seems to have been a man of
method. See, here is the entry for to-day: ‘8 p.m. Dinner. Signor
Ascanio and friend.’ And here is a name and address on the blotter:
‘Signor Ascanio, 14, Berkeley Square.’”

“Capital!” cried the inspector. “We’ll get on his track at once.
And in the meantime, Graves, you’d better come with me to the
station and give us a full description of the two men.”

On the previous morning, two gentlemen had called to see his
master. They were Italians, and the elder of the two, a man of
about forty, gave his name as Signor Ascanio. The younger was a
well-dressed lad of about twenty-four.

He had heard high words—threats. The word “money” had been mentioned more than once, and also the phrase “the price of silence.” Then, it seemed, a compromise had been reached. The visitors were to return for dinner that evening, when the Count promised to have certain “documents” ready for them. Signor Ascanio, the elder man, had been particularly vehement, gesturing wildly and speaking in a low, hissed Italian that Graves could only partially understand. The valet’s eyes shifted as he spoke, as though he were still afraid of what he had overheard.

"The voices were raised, though I could not catch every word," Graves continued, his eyes darting toward the silent figure at the desk. "The Count sounded desperate. I heard him say, 'I have not the sum you require,' and the older man, this Signor Ascanio, replied with a laugh that made my blood run cold. 'Then you know the consequences,' he said. Before they left, it was arranged that they should return for dinner at eight o'clock. The Count was most particular that I should leave the flat once the table was laid; he said he would attend to the service lift himself, as the matters to be discussed were of a highly confidential nature."

“I heard the Count’s voice raised in anger,” Graves continued, his hands trembling slightly. “He was shouting at Signor Ascanio, saying that he would not be bled any longer and that the demands were outrageous. Signor Ascanio's voice was lower, more cold and menacing; he spoke of ‘consequences’ and ‘the price of silence.’ It seemed to me that they were discussing some matter of a political or perhaps a financial nature—I couldn't be sure which. Eventually, however, the Count appeared to yield, for I heard him suggest that they should return this evening to dine and conclude their business in a more amicable fashion. It was then that I thought it best to retire, lest I be caught playing the eavesdropper.”

"I heard high words, monsieur," Graves continued, his voice trembling with what seemed to be a genuine agitation. "The Count was speaking in Italian, which I do not understand, but the tone was unmistakable—it was a threat. Then Signor Ascanio spoke in English. He said, 'It must be tonight, or the consequences will be on your own head.' The Count replied with a laugh that sounded more like a snarl. They stayed for an hour, and when they left, the Count was as white as a sheet. He told me then that he would be having two guests for dinner the following evening and that I was to have the night off after the meal was served, as the matters to be discussed were of a private and diplomatic nature."

"The Count’s voice was raised in anger," Graves continued, his eyes darting towards the silent figure in the chair. "I heard him cry out quite clearly: 'I have the papers here, and they are worth a fortune to the right people!' Then the older man—Signor Ascanio—spoke in a low, cold tone that made my flesh creep. 'You will never live to sell them, Foscatini,' he said. 'The organization has ways of dealing with traitors.' I was so terrified of being discovered that I beat a hasty retreat, and I thought no more of it until tonight, when those same two gentlemen arrived for dinner."

The conversation was carried on in so low a tone that he was not
as successful as he had hoped; but he gathered enough to make it
clear that some kind of monetary proposition was being discussed,
and that the basis of it was a threat. The discussion was anything
but amicable. In the end, Count Foscatini raised his voice slightly,
and the listener heard these words clearly:

“I have no time to argue further now, gentlemen. If you will dine
with me to-morrow night at eight o’clock, we will resume the
discussion.”

The Inspector nodded curtly and began a systematic search of the room, while Poirot remained by the table, his eyes fixed upon the three coffee-cups with a singular expression. “Tell me, Graves,” he said suddenly, “when you served the coffee, did you also serve the port?” “Yes, sir, I placed the decanter on the table as I always do.” “And the Count, he was in good spirits?” “He seemed a little preoccupied, sir, but otherwise much as usual.” Poirot turned his attention to the writing-desk where the body lay. He pointed to the telephone. “A most convenient instrument,” he murmured, “but it can be a double-edged sword, can it not, Hastings?” I did not quite follow his meaning, but I knew better than to interrupt his train of thought when he was in such a mood.

The inspector nodded, his pencil flying over the pages of his notebook. "A very clear statement, Graves. We shall lose no time in tracing this Signor Ascanio and his companion. It seems a typical case of a political or financial vendetta." Poirot, who had been prowling around the room like a cat, suddenly came to a halt behind the victim’s chair. He did not seem to be looking at the body, but rather at the heavy silk curtains that draped the window. "Tell me, Graves," he said softly, "when you left the flat at half-past eight, were these curtains drawn or open?" The valet hesitated for a moment, his brow furrowing in thought. "They were drawn, sir. I always draw them as soon as I have served the first course of dinner." Poirot’s eyes flickered with a strange light, but he made no comment, merely turning his attention back to the remains of the rice soufflé on the table.

The inspector made a note of the address. “We shall see what Signor Ascanio has to say for himself. It is a pity you did not see them leave, Graves.” The valet sighed. “I wish I had, sir. To think that while I was enjoying myself at the Music Hall, my poor master was being done to death! It’s a wicked world, sir, a very wicked world.” Poirot, who had been standing by the window, turned back into the room. “Tell me, Graves,” he said softly, “was it the Count’s custom to dine so—shall we say—precisely? The order from the kitchen was for three, and yet, looking at these plates, one might almost say that the appetite of the party was remarkably uniform.”

The inspector made a few rapid notes. “A tall man with a dark beard, and a younger, slight man, clean-shaven. We should have little difficulty in tracing them if they are still in London. Now, Graves, tell me this: when you left the flat at half-past eight, where were the three gentlemen?” “They were still at the table, sir, just finishing their coffee. My master told me I might go then.” Poirot stepped forward, his eyes twinkling with that green light that always betokened internal excitement. “One little moment, Monsieur l’Inspecteur. Graves, you say they were finishing their coffee? Then the four courses of the dinner—the soup, the fish, the tournedos, and the rice soufflé—had all been served and consumed?” “Yes, sir,” replied Graves, looking slightly surprised. “The last of the dishes had been sent up the lift just before I left.”

The inspector nodded as he completed his notes on the descriptions of the two mysterious guests. Signor Ascanio, it appeared, was a man of middle height, with a dark, sallow complexion and a small black moustache; his companion was a younger man, tall and fair. When Graves had finished his recital, Poirot, who had been listening with his eyes half closed, suddenly intervened. “One moment, Monsieur Graves. You say that you left the flat at half-past eight? At that time, had the meal reached its conclusion?”

Nobody had seen the two men leave, but the time of the murder was
fixed clearly enough at 8.47. A small clock on the writing-table
had been swept off by Foscatini’s arm, and had stopped at that
hour, which agreed with Miss Rider’s telephone summons.

Our first steps were to search the room for any trace of the two
mysterious guests. There were no cards or anything of that sort
to be found, but we did find a single glove, and on the table
was a small card with the name “Signor Ascanio” printed on it.
The police were already on his track. No. 100, Bury Street, St.
James’s, was the address on the card, and we were not surprised
when, in the small hours of the morning, we received word that
Signor Ascanio had been arrested.

The inspector was highly delighted.

“A quick piece of work, that,” he remarked to us with
unconcealed satisfaction. “He was found at his hotel, packed and
ready for flight. He denies all knowledge of the affair, but
admitted that he had dined with the Count that evening. He can’t
account for the time after nine o’clock, and when we searched him
we found a heavy, loaded stick in his possession.”

“And the younger man?” asked Poirot.

“He is still at large. We have no description of him, beyond
Graves’s statement that he was a well-dressed young fellow of
about twenty-four. We shall get him, though.”

Poirot did not seem so sure. He was deep in thought.

“Ascanio? Ascanio? I seem to know that name.”

The inspector’s face took on a superior smile.

“Of course you do. Why, it’s one of the best-known names in Italy.
The Count was a well-connected man, I understand.”

Poirot shook his head.

“No, it’s not that. Where have I seen it recently? Ah, I have it!”

He pulled a small pocket-book from his pocket and turned over the
leaves.

“Ascanio. Of course. Why, he’s one of the attachés at the Italian
Embassy.”

The inspector’s face fell.

“If that’s so, we’ve got into a pretty mess. It will lead to all
sorts of international complications.”

Poirot smiled.

“I shouldn’t worry. If he’s the man you want, his being an attaché
won’t save him.”

“No; but it will make things more difficult. Well, we must just
hope for the best.”

Next morning there was a full account of the “Regent’s Court
Murder” in all the papers. The police had already discovered a
great deal about the late Count Foscatini. He was a man of
mystery, and his past was shrouded in obscurity. He had been
living in Regent’s Court for about six months, and had apparently
plenty of money. He was a man of cultured tastes, and his flat
was full of beautiful things. Among them was a collection of
valuable old coins, which was found to be intact. This seemed to
dispose of robbery as a motive.

Poirot, who had been listening to Graves with the closest
attention, now began a cross-examination of the witness.

“You say that your master and his guests had finished their meal
when you left?”

“Yes, sir.”

“They had already had their coffee?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Now, what did they have for dinner?”

“Soup julienne, filet de sole normande, tournedos of beef, and
rice soufflé.”

“And they all partook of these dishes?”

“Yes, sir.”

“You are quite sure of that?”

“I am quite sure, sir.”

“But they did not have any dessert?”

“No, sir.”

“Why not?”

“I don’t know, sir. The Count said they would not require it.”

“How much of the rice soufflé was left?”

“Oh, about half of it, sir.”

“And how many of the tournedos?”

“Three, sir.”

“You are quite sure there were three?”

“Quite sure, sir.”

“And three portions of fish?”

“Yes, sir.”

“And three plates of soup?”

“Yes, sir.”

Poirot’s face took on a look of extreme satisfaction.

“I think I have everything I want,” he said. “I think I see light.”

“_I_ don’t,” I confessed. “It seems to me as dark as ever it was.”

“On the contrary, it is remarkably clear.”

“What about the two men?”

“We shall see them in good time,” he answered.

The next morning, we found him in high good humour. He had already
visited Scotland Yard, and had interviewed Inspector Japp.

“I have given him a hint,” he said, “and I have no doubt that he
will act upon it. We shall hear something before long.”

And we did. In the afternoon we received a visit from Inspector
Japp. He was in a state of great excitement.

“I’ve got them!” he cried. “Both of them! They were at the Ritz.
Ascanio and the other. They’ve been followed ever since they left
Regent’s Court last night.”

“And you have arrested them?” I asked.

“Not yet. We want to be sure of our ground. But they are under
observation.”

“Have you any evidence?”

“Plenty. We have found a blood-stained handkerchief in Ascanio’s
pocket, and he has a scratch on his hand.”

“That seems conclusive enough,” I said.

“Wait a bit,” said Japp. “There’s one very curious point. Ascanio
denies having been at Regent’s Court at all last night. He says
he was at his hotel all the evening.”

“That’s a very foolish lie,” I remarked.

“Wait a bit,” said Japp again. “His story is that he was to have
dined with Count Foscatini, but that at the last moment he was
taken ill and could not go. He says he sent a note by his
secretary.”

“And the secretary?”

“The secretary confirms his story. He says he took the note to
Regent’s Court and left it there.”

“And the blood-stained handkerchief?”

“Ascanio says he cut his hand with a razor this morning.”

“A very likely story,” I said.

“Wait a bit,” said Japp for the third time. “The most curious
thing is that the lift man at Regent’s Court says he didn’t see
either of them last night.”

“But Graves says they were there.”

“Yes, Graves says so. But then Graves may be mistaken. Or he may
be lying.”

“But why should he lie?”

“That’s what we’ve got to find out.”

“I think I can help you there,” said Poirot quietly. “I think I
can show you that Graves’s story is a tissue of lies from
beginning to end.”

“What!” I cried.

“Listen,” said Poirot. “Last night, when we were in the flat, I
went up to the kitchen and made some inquiries. I found that the
order for dinner had been for _three_ people. I found also that
every dish had been partaken of by _three_ people. Now, Graves
tells us that he left the flat at half-past eight, and that the
three men had then finished their dinner. But the murder did not
take place until 8.47. Therefore, if Graves’s story is true, the
murderers must have stayed in the flat for seventeen minutes
after they had killed their victim. Why should they do that? To
smoke a cigar and a couple of cigarettes? It is not likely. And
there is another point. Graves says there were three tournedos.
But the cook told me there were only _two_.”

“Two!” I cried. “Then there were only two people at dinner!”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “Count Foscatini and one other. And that
other was not Signor Ascanio or his secretary. It was Graves
himself!”

“Graves!” I cried.

“Yes. Graves is the murderer. He killed his master, and then, to
provide himself with an alibi, he invented the story of the two
Italian guests. He himself ate the third portion of everything,
to make it appear that there had been three people at dinner. Then
he went out, leaving the telephone off the hook, so that he could
call up the doctor and make it appear that his master was still
alive. It was he who spoke to Miss Rider. He has a very good
imitation of his master’s voice.”

“But the voice on the telephone said ‘Foscatini’,” I objected.

“No,” said Poirot. “Miss Rider said it said ‘Foscatine’—or
something like that. What it really said was ‘Foscari’—the name
of a famous Venetian family. Graves had been reading a book about
them, and the name was in his mind. It was a very clever touch,
but it was his undoing.”

“And the clock?”

“He set it back, of course. He is a very clever man, is Graves.
But he made one mistake. He forgot that the cook would remember
how many tournedos he had sent down.”

“Well, I’m damned!” said Japp. “I must go and see about this at
once.”

He hurried out of the room. Poirot turned to me with a smile.

“You see, Hastings? The little grey cells! They never fail one.”

“And now for the Italian gentlemen,” said Poirot. “Where are they
to be found? There’s no doubt they are our men. Dr. Hawker,
perhaps you can tell us something about them?”

The doctor shook his head.

“I know no one of the name of Ascanio. I should have thought that,
with such an Italian name, he would be at the Embassy. That’s a
good idea. I’ll go and find out.”

“Quite so,” said Poirot. “And, if you don’t mind, I’ll come with
you.”

“Have you any idea who the men were?” the inspector asked Graves.

The man shrugged his shoulders.

“One of them—the elder—was a Signor Ascanio. He is a gentleman of
wealth and position in Italy, I believe. The other I have never
seen before.”

The inspector looked at Poirot.

“What do you think of it, Monsieur Poirot?”

“It is a very simple case,” said my friend, with a little shrug of
his shoulders.

“Simple!” the inspector and I cried together.

“I have no doubt that Signor Ascanio is the man you seek. If I
might offer a suggestion, I should keep a sharp lookout at all the
ports.”

“The inspector is of my opinion,” Poirot remarked as we walked
home. “Ascanio is the man, and he’ll be out of the country before
we can say ‘Jack Robinson’—if we’re not careful.”

“But,” I said, “if he was a gentleman of wealth and position in
Italy, why should he want to murder a fellow-countryman?”

“Ah! my dear Hastings, that is the question. The Italian is a
passionate and impulsive being. He does not always stop to count
the cost of his actions.”

“And you think that Ascanio is the man?”

“I have no doubt of it.”

The following morning, on the arrival of Inspector Japp, our
old friend of Scotland Yard, the case was put into his hands. I
accompanied him to the scene of the tragedy. Poirot was not
disposed to go. He had some other matters he wished to attend to.
The search for the two Italians, Signor Ascanio and the younger
man, was pushed with all possible speed. We were at the Yard when
news of the elder man’s arrest came through. He had been found
at a small hotel in Soho, and was brought to the Yard for
interrogation.

He was a thick-set man of about forty, with a dark, oily
complexion. He was not exactly an attractive-looking person. In
reply to Japp’s questions, he denied any knowledge of the crime.
He admitted having dined with Count Foscatini on the previous
evening, but stated that he and his friend had left the flat about
ten minutes before nine. No; they had not been at all on bad terms
with the Count. On the contrary, their relations were of the
friendliest. He refused to give his friend’s name or address.
He said he had met him in Italy some time previously, but did not
know where he lived in London.

“_Cui bono?_” said Japp, as we walked out into the street. “He had
every motive for it, but the thing that beats me is how he thinks
to escape. He was known to have been there. He must have known
that suspicion would fall upon him.”

The police surgeon had made his examination of the body, and it
was now lying on the couch. I saw the face for the first time—the
olive complexion, the long nose, the luxuriant black moustache,
and the full red lips drawn back from the dazzlingly white teeth.
Not altogether a pleasant face.

The inspector was already busy with his notebook. “Signor Ascanio,” he muttered. “We must lay our hands on him without delay. Did he leave no address, Graves?”
“None, sir. But I believe he mentioned he was staying at the Hotel Victoria.”
The inspector nodded to one of his men, who left the room immediately. Poirot, meanwhile, was on his knees by the small writing-table. He seemed less interested in the body than in the carpet. I watched him as he carefully picked up a tiny sliver of something and placed it in an envelope.
“What is it, Poirot?” I whispered.
“A small fragment of dried mud, Hastings. Very dry, very grey. It did not come from a London street to-day.”

The Inspector, having completed his preliminary survey, turned to Graves. “You say these two men arrived at eight o’clock? And you left at eight-thirty? Was the dinner over then?” “No, sir, they were just starting on the second course—the fish. I had only just brought it down from the lift.” Poirot interposed a question. “And when you left, was the Count in good spirits?” “He seemed a bit tense, sir, but he was playing the host well enough.” Poirot nodded thoughtfully, his eyes wandering back to the table where the three coffee cups stood in their silent testimony.

The inspector was highly satisfied. “A very clear case,” he remarked. “This Signor Ascanio and his friend come here to squeeze the Count. The Count refuses. They get violent, one of them picks up that image there, and cracks him over the head with it. Then they clear out. We should have them behind bars before morning.” Poirot murmured something to himself, but he did not openly disagree. Instead, he turned his attention back to Graves, who stood by the door, his face a mask of respectful grief, and began to question him once more about the Count’s habits and the exact events of the preceding morning.

The inspector, a brisk man of the name of Miller, was already busy with his notebook. “We must lay our hands on this Signor Ascanio at once,” he remarked. “Graves, did your master leave any address or a card of this gentleman?” The valet hesitated, then his eyes brightened. “Now you mention it, sir, I saw the Count placing a card in the small drawer of the writing-table after the gentlemen left yesterday morning.” The inspector moved quickly to the desk, and after a moment’s search, produced a visiting card. “Signor Paolo Ascanio,” he read aloud. “Hotel Lucania, Soho. That simplifies matters considerably. We shall see what the gentleman has to say for himself.”

The Inspector was busy taking notes. “Ascanio,” he muttered. “We must find this Signor Ascanio. Did he leave no address, Graves?”
“None, sir. But he spoke with a very marked Italian accent. The younger gentleman, however, spoke English like an Englishman.”
Poirot, who had been wandering round the room, now joined us. “Tell me, Graves,” he said, “did your master often have guests to dinner?”
“Very seldom, sir.”
“And did he always order the same menu?”
Graves looked puzzled. “I—I really couldn’t say, sir. He changed it from time to time.”
“But he was a man of habit, was he not? A man of method?”
“In some things, yes, sir.”
Poirot nodded thoughtfully and turned his attention back to the dining table, his eyes resting once more on the three coffee cups.

“Well,” said the inspector, refastening his notebook. “The case
seems clear enough. The only difficulty will be to lay our hands
on this Signor Ascanio. I suppose his address is not in the dead
man’s pocket-book by any chance?”

As Poirot had said, the late Foscatini was an orderly man. Neatly
written in small, precise handwriting was the inscription, “Signor
Paolo Ascanio, Grosvenor Hotel.”

The inspector busied himself with the telephone, then turned to us
with a grin.

“The gentleman’s there, all right. He came in at half-past nine,
and is now in his room.”

Poirot did not say a word. He was looking at the dinner-table.

“What is it, Monsieur?” asked the inspector.

“I was wondering,” said Poirot, “if the murderer, after killing
his victim, could have sat down and finished his dinner?”

“Not likely,” said the inspector, with a shudder.

“It would certainly have been a most unusual thing,” agreed
Poirot. “And yet, you see, there are only three coffee-cups on the
table, and they have all been drained.”

“The third person being the dead man,” I put in.

“Precisely,” said Poirot. “And yet there were four people in the
room—Count Foscatini and his three guests.”

“Three guests?” I cried.

“The two who came to dinner, and the one who came later,” said
Poirot. “Don’t you see, the telephone call was at 8.47. The
manager tells us that the three gentlemen were dining together at
eight. Therefore at 8.47 there must have been four people in the
room.”

“Unless,” I suggested, “one of the guests committed the murder
and then fled.”

“In that case,” said Poirot, “why should the third guest be
wanting to telephone for help? He must have been an accomplice.”

“Wait a minute,” said the inspector. “There’s another possibility.
Suppose the two guests were the murderers, and that there was no
third guest?”

“In that case,” said Poirot, “why should Count Foscatini telephone
for help?”

“Because he wasn’t dead yet,” said the inspector.

“But the blow on the head would have rendered him unconscious at
once,” I objected.

“Suppose,” said Poirot, “that it was not the Count who telephoned?”

“But Miss Rider said it was the Count’s voice,” I cried.

“She had only heard it once before,” Poirot reminded me. “And in
any case, it was a very faint whisper.”

“Then you think—?”

“I think,” said Poirot, “that we should go and see Signor Ascanio.”

The inspector agreed, and we all drove off to the Grosvenor Hotel.
Signor Ascanio was in his room. He was a tall, dark man with a
somewhat sinister expression. He seemed surprised at our visit,
but he was quite ready to answer our questions.

He admitted that he and his friend had dined with Count Foscatini
that evening. They had discussed a certain matter of business, but
it had been quite an amicable discussion. They had left the flat
at half-past eight.

“And where did you go then?” asked the inspector.

“We went for a walk in the park,” said Ascanio. “My friend is very
fond of walking. Then we came back here.”

“And your friend—where is he now?”

“He is in his room. He was tired and went to bed at once.”

“I should like to see him,” said the inspector.

Ascanio led the way to the next room. The young man was in bed and
appeared to be asleep. The inspector woke him and questioned him.
His story was the same as Ascanio’s.

“Well,” said the inspector, when we were back in the hall, “it
seems a bit thin, but we can’t do anything more to-night. I shall
have them watched, of course.”

“_Une petite question_, Signor Ascanio,” said Poirot. “Did you
enjoy your dinner this evening?”

Ascanio looked surprised.

“The dinner? Oh, yes, it was very good.”

“The rice soufflé, in particular, was it not excellent?”

“I do not remember any rice soufflé,” said Ascanio. “We had some
kind of savoury to finish with.”

“Ah!” said Poirot. “That is very interesting.”

As we drove back to our rooms, Poirot was very silent. I knew the
signs, and did not disturb him.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, as we sat in our comfortable chairs, “what
do you think of it all?”

“I think, Hastings, that it is a very interesting case. A very
interesting case indeed.”

“You think Ascanio is the murderer?”

“I do not think so, Hastings. No, I do not think so.”

“Then who—?”

“_Attendez, mon ami_. Let us look at the facts. We have a man
murdered at 8.47. We have two guests who leave at 8.30. We have a
telephone call at 8.47 from a man who says he is being murdered.
We have three coffee-cups on the table. And we have a rice soufflé
of which a fair amount is left.”

“What has the rice soufflé to do with it?” I asked.

“Everything, my friend. Everything. But now I will tell you
something that is more important still. When I was in the kitchen,
I looked at the plates that had come up from Flat II. There were
three sets of plates—soup, fish, and meat. But there was only
_one_ dessert plate.”

“Only one?” I cried.

“Only one,” said Poirot. “And yet there were three people at
dinner. What do you make of that, Hastings?”

“I don’t know,” I confessed. “It’s very strange.”

“It is more than strange,” said Poirot. “It is significant. And
there is another thing. Did you notice the coffee-cups? There were
three of them. Two were black, and one had milk in it. Now,
Signor Ascanio says they had no rice soufflé, but a savoury. But
the order from the kitchen was for a rice soufflé. And the man in
the kitchen said the plates were all soiled, and the dishes empty—
except for the rice soufflé.”

“Then Ascanio was lying,” I said.

“Perhaps,” said Poirot. “But why should he lie about a rice
soufflé? It seems such a trivial thing.”

“And what about the coffee-cups?” I asked.

“Ah, the coffee-cups! That is the most significant thing of all.
Two black, and one with milk. Now, who takes milk in their
coffee, Hastings?”

“Lots of people,” I said.

“True. But does a man like Count Foscatini take milk in his
coffee? I think not. And do two Italians like Ascanio and his
friend take milk in their coffee? I think not. They would take it
black, as is the custom in their country.”

“Then who took the milk?” I asked.

“That is the question, Hastings. That is the question.”

Poirot was silent for a moment, then he said:

“I think, Hastings, that we will pay another visit to Regent’s
Court to-morrow morning. There are one or two things I should like
to check.”

The next morning we were back at the flat. The inspector was there,
and he looked rather discouraged.

“No luck, Monsieur Poirot,” he said. “I’ve been through all the
Count’s papers, but there’s nothing to show why anyone should want
to kill him. He seems to have been a most respectable man.”

“And Signor Ascanio?” asked Poirot.

“I’ve had a report from the hotel. He and his friend were there
all night. They didn’t leave until this morning, and then they
went to the Italian Embassy.”

“Ah!” said Poirot. “That is interesting.”

He began to walk about the room, looking at everything with his
quick, bird-like eyes. Suddenly he stopped in front of the
writing-table.

“This clock,” he said, “it was swept off the table, you say, at
8.47?”

“Yes,” said the inspector. “The glass is broken, and the hands are
stopped at that hour.”

Poirot picked up the clock and looked at it closely.

“It is a very good clock,” he said. “A very good clock indeed. It
is a pity it is broken.”

He set it down and turned to the window.

“The curtains were drawn, I suppose, when the murder was
committed?”

“Yes,” said the inspector. “The valet says he drew them before he
went out.”

Poirot nodded. He went over to the sideboard and looked at the
decanter of port.

“Half-full,” he remarked. “And three glasses. They all took port,
then.”

“Yes,” said the inspector. “The glasses were all soiled.”

Poirot turned to the valet, who was standing by the door.

“Tell me, Graves,” he said, “did your master often have guests to
dinner?”

“Not very often, sir.”

“And did he always have the same dinner?”

“Oh, no, sir. He was very fond of variety.”

“I see. And did he always have port after dinner?”

“Yes, sir. He was very fond of his port.”

“And did he always have coffee?”

“Yes, sir.”

“And did he always take it black?”

“Yes, sir. He never took milk.”

“I thought as much,” said Poirot. “And what about his guests? Did
they take milk?”

“I couldn’t say, sir, I’m sure. I didn’t notice.”

“I see. Well, thank you, Graves. That will be all for the
present.”

The valet left the room, and Poirot turned to the inspector.

“I think, Inspector,” he said, “that I can tell you who killed
Count Foscatini.”

“You can?” cried the inspector. “Who was it?”

“It was a man who takes milk in his coffee,” said Poirot.

The inspector looked disappointed.

“That doesn’t help much,” he said. “There must be thousands of
men who take milk in their coffee.”

“True,” said Poirot. “But there are not many who would kill a
Count for it.”

He smiled at the inspector’s bewildered face.

“Come, Hastings,” he said. “We have much to do.”

As we left the flat, I asked Poirot what he meant.

“It is very simple, Hastings. The milk in the coffee is the key to
the whole mystery. But we must find the man who took it.”

“But how?” I asked.

“By a little process of elimination, my friend. A little process
of elimination.”

We spent the rest of the morning visiting various people who had
known Count Foscatini. But we didn't seem to be getting any
nearer to the truth. Everyone spoke highly of the Count, and no
one could suggest a motive for his murder.

It was late in the afternoon when we returned to our rooms. We
found a message waiting for us from the inspector.

“I’ve found something, Monsieur Poirot,” it said. “Come to the
station at once.”

When we arrived, the inspector was looking very pleased with
himself.

“I’ve found the weapon,” he said. “It was in a dustbin in a small
alleyway not far from Regent’s Court. It’s a heavy brass
candlestick, and it’s covered with blood.”

“A brass candlestick?” said Poirot. “But I thought the weapon was
a marble statuette?”

“So did we,” said the inspector. “But we found this candlestick,
and it fits the wound perfectly. The statuette must have been a
blind.”

“A blind?” said Poirot. “That is very interesting.”

He looked at the candlestick for a moment, then he said:

“And have you found the man who used it?”

“Not yet,” said the inspector. “But we’re looking for him.”

“I think I can help you there,” said Poirot. “If you will come
with me, I think I can show you the murderer.”

The inspector looked surprised, but he followed Poirot out of the
station. We drove to a small house in a quiet street in Chelsea.
Poirot rang the bell, and a woman answered the door.

“Is Mr. Graves at home?” asked Poirot.

“Yes, sir,” said the woman. “He’s in the sitting-room.”

We followed her into the room. Graves was sitting in an armchair,
reading a newspaper. He looked up as we entered, and his face
turned pale.

“What is the meaning of this?” he asked.

“It means, Mr. Graves,” said Poirot, “that the game is up. We
know that you killed Count Foscatini.”

Graves sprang to his feet.

“It’s a lie!” he cried. “I didn’t do it!”

“It is no lie,” said Poirot. “I have the proof.”

He turned to the inspector.

“If you will search Mr. Graves’s room, Inspector, I think you will
find a suit of clothes with bloodstains on it. And you will also
find a small bottle of milk.”

The inspector went out of the room, and returned a few minutes
later with a suit of clothes and a bottle of milk.

“You were right, Monsieur Poirot,” he said. “Here they are.”

Graves sank back into his chair, his face buried in his hands.

“I didn't mean to do it,” he sobbed. “It was an accident.”

“An accident?” said Poirot. “To hit a man on the head with a
heavy candlestick is not an accident.”

“He was going to dismiss me,” said Graves. “I had been with him
for ten years, and he was going to turn me out without a penny. I
couldn't help it. I just lost my temper.”

“And the telephone call?” asked Poirot. “And the coffee-cups?
And the rice soufflé?”

“It was all a plan,” said Graves. “I wanted to make it look as if
someone else had done it. I knew about Signor Ascanio and his
friend, so I thought I would use them as a cover. I made the
telephone call myself, pretending to be the Count. And I set the
table for three, and put the coffee-cups out. I even ate some of
the dinner myself, to make it look as if three people had been
dining there.”

“But you made one mistake,” said Poirot. “You took milk in your
coffee.”

Graves looked at him in surprise.

“How did you know that?” he asked.

“Because, as I told the inspector, there were three coffee-cups on
the table, and one of them had milk in it. And I knew that neither
the Count nor his Italian guests would take milk in their coffee.
So it had to be someone else. And who else could it be but you?”

Graves didn't say another word. He was led away by the inspector,
and we never saw him again.

As we walked back to our rooms, I said to Poirot:

“That was a brilliant piece of deduction, Poirot. I would never
have thought of the milk in the coffee.”

“It was simple, Hastings. Quite simple. But it just goes to show
that it is the little things that matter. The little things are
always the most important.”

And with that, we went home to our dinner.
