“Signor Ascanio is still at the hotel. He is at this moment being
interrogated by our local inspector. We’ll go down there at once.”

The inspector’s face as he replaced the receiver was anything
but jubilant.

“He’s got an alibi,” he said, shortly. “At least he’s got an alibi
for the time of the telephone call—the time of the murder. He was
sitting in the restaurant of the hotel from eight o’clock until
ten. The manager and the waiter can both testify to the fact.
And his companion—the younger man—was with him.”

Poirot’s eyes narrowed.

“A very solid alibi,” he murmured. “It would seem that our Signor
Ascanio was not the murderer, then.”

“Then who was?” I cried. “The valet, Graves?”

“He also has an alibi,” the inspector reminded me. “He was at the
music hall from 8.45 onwards. His friend will swear to that.”

“Then,” I said, “it must have been some third party.”

“But who?” asked the inspector. “The lift man saw no one else
go up or down.”

Poirot, who had been listening with a far-away look in his eyes,
now spoke.

“Let us go back to the flat,” he suggested. “There is something
there that I wish to see again.”

“What is it?” I asked.

“The dinner table,” said Poirot. “I have a fancy to look at those
coffee cups once more.”

“That’s it,” he said, in a satisfied tone. “They tell me he’s there
all right—has been there since Monday. He’s out now, but I’ve
asked them to let me know as soon as he returns. I’ll be off now
and see if I can’t get hold of him.”

We accompanied him to the lift, where Poirot, after a few words of
general conversation, took his leave.

I noticed that he looked very thoughtful as we walked back
towards our rooms. I waited for him to speak. He did not do so
until we were once more in our own sitting-room.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of it all?” he asked then.

“A fairly simple case, I should imagine,” I replied. “The motive
was evidently some financial secret, and the murderer is Ascanio.
The only point that puzzles me is why he should leave his address
behind him like that.”

“Precisely,” said Poirot, “a very interesting point. And there are
others.”

“What others?”

“The coffee,” he replied, with a little smile. “It was very
instructive, that coffee.”

I did not see it. I said so.

“Wait,” he said, “and see what our friend Japp has to say about it.
He will be round in the morning, I expect.”

True to Poirot’s prediction, Japp arrived early the next morning.
He looked rather depressed, and I gathered that things had not gone
as smoothly as he had expected.

“Well, Japp,” said Poirot, “any news?”

“I’ve seen Ascanio,” replied the inspector, “and a more slippery
customer I’ve never come across. He’s an Italian, of course, but
he speaks English like a native. He admits having dined with
Foscatini last night, but he says that he and his friend left
exactly at half-past eight.”

“And their reason for leaving so early?”

“Ascanio says they had an appointment elsewhere at 8.45. He won’t
say where, or with whom. He denies that there was any quarrel,
and he says he knows nothing of any financial secret.”

“And the other man?”

“Ascanio won’t give his name. He says he was just a friend. I don’t
believe a word of it, of course, but I can’t prove anything—yet.”

“What about the weapon?” I asked. “Were there any finger-prints on
it?”

“None at all,” replied Japp. “It had been carefully wiped.”

Poirot smiled.

“I told you he was a man of method,” he remarked.

“Who? The murderer?”

“No, the man who wiped the statuette.”

Japp looked puzzled.

“But they’re the same, aren’t they?”

“Not necessarily,” replied Poirot, with a twinkle in his eyes.

He then proceeded to tell Japp of our visit to the kitchens the
night before, and of the information we had gained there.

“I don’t see what that’s got to do with it,” said Japp, when he
had finished. “But you always were one for detail, Poirot. Now,
I’ve got another piece of news for you. We’ve found the taxi-man
who drove Ascanio and his friend away from Regent’s Court. He
picked them up just outside at 8.35, and he dropped them at the
corner of Albemarle Street at 8.45.”

“That seems to bear out Ascanio’s story,” I remarked.

“It does,” admitted Japp, “but it doesn't prove it. They might have
come back, you know.”

“True,” said Poirot. “And now, Japp, I have a little suggestion to
make to you. I want you to find out for me if any of the other
tenants in Regent’s Court heard the sound of a struggle or a fall
about 8.45 last night.”

“I’ve already done that,” replied Japp. “No one heard anything.
But then, the walls are very thick, and Foscatini’s dining-room is
at the back of the building.”

“Quite so,” said Poirot. “And now there is one more thing. I want
you to find out for me the exact time that Graves left the flat.”

“He said 8.30,” replied Japp.

“I know he did, but I want you to make sure. Ask the lift-man.”

Japp looked at him curiously.

“You’ve got some idea in your head, Poirot. What is it?”

“I will tell you when you have got the information I want,” replied
Poirot, with a smile.

When Japp had gone, I turned to Poirot.

“What is this idea of yours?” I asked.

“It is very simple, Hastings. I am interested in the menu of the
dinner.”

“The menu? But what can that have to do with it?”

“A great deal, my friend. A great deal. Consider. Three men sit
down to dinner. They eat soup, fish, a main course, and a sweet.
And yet, when we arrive, there are only three coffee-cups on the
table, and the dessert plates are untouched.”

“I don’t see anything strange in that,” I said. “They probably
didn't want any dessert.”

“Perhaps not. But why only three coffee-cups? If there were three
men at dinner, and they all had coffee, there should be three
cups. But if one of them did not have coffee, there would only be
two. And yet there were three.”

“I don’t follow you,” I said, feeling rather confused.

“It is very simple, Hastings. If Ascanio and his friend left at
8.30, they could not have had coffee. And yet there were three
coffee-cups on the table. Who, then, drank the coffee?”

“The murderer?” I suggested.

“Perhaps. But why should the murderer stop to have coffee after he
had committed a brutal crime? It does not seem very likely, does
it?”

“Then who was it?”

“That is what I mean to find out,” replied Poirot.

The rest of the morning passed slowly. Poirot seemed to be in a
state of suppressed excitement, and he wandered about the room,
muttering to himself in French. At last, about two o’clock, Japp
returned.

“Well?” said Poirot, eagerly.

“I’ve got the information you wanted,” replied Japp. “The lift-man
says he saw Graves leave the building at 8.25. He remembers it
distinctly because he noticed the time on the hall clock.”

“Ah!” said Poirot, with a sigh of satisfaction. “That is very
interesting. Very interesting indeed. And now, Japp, I think I
can tell you who killed Count Foscatini.”

“Who was it?” we both asked in one breath.

“It was a man of method,” replied Poirot, with a smile. “A man who
thought of everything—except one little thing.”

“And what was that?” asked Japp.

“The appetite of Count Foscatini,” replied Poirot.

He then proceeded to explain his theory.

“Consider the facts,” he said. “Three men sit down to dinner at
eight o’clock. They have four courses. Now, how long does it take
to eat a four-course dinner? At least an hour, I should say. And
yet, at 8.30, Ascanio and his friend are seen leaving the
building. That means they could not have had more than two courses
at the most. And yet, when we arrived at the flat, all the dishes
were empty, and the plates had been sent up to the kitchen.”

“But the man in the kitchen said they had all the courses,”
objected Japp.

“Precisely,” said Poirot. “And that is where the man of method made
his mistake. He wanted it to appear that the dinner had been
eaten, so he soiled the plates and emptied the dishes himself.
But he forgot one thing. He forgot that three men cannot eat four
courses in half an hour.”

“Then you mean that Ascanio and his friend had nothing to do with
it?” I asked.

“I do not say that. But I do say that they did not kill Count
Foscatini. He was alive when they left the flat.”

“Then who killed him?” asked Japp.

“The man who was in the flat after they left,” replied Poirot. “The
man who had plenty of time to eat the dinner—or at least to make
it appear that it had been eaten. The man who then telephoned to
Dr. Hawker, pretending to be the dying Count, and then struck the
Count down from behind.”

“But who was this man?” asked Japp.

“There is only one man who could have done it,” replied Poirot.
“The man who had a key to the flat, and who knew that the Count
would be alone. The man who had been listening to the conversation
the day before, and knew all about Signor Ascanio’s visit.”

“You mean—Graves?” said Japp, in astonishment.

“I mean Graves,” replied Poirot. “He did not go to the music hall
at 8.30. He only pretended to. He came back to the flat, killed
his master, and then went out again. He thought he had covered
his tracks perfectly, but he forgot that a man’s appetite is not
so easily faked.”

“But what about the telephone call?” I asked. “Miss Rider said she
heard a voice crying for help.”

“It was Graves,” replied Poirot. “He is a good actor, and he knew
how to imitate his master’s voice. He even managed to get the name
‘Foscatini’ into the conversation, so that there would be no doubt
as to who was speaking.”

“But why should he do it?” asked Japp.

“For the same reason that many men commit murder,” replied Poirot.
“Money. He knew that the Count had a large sum of money in the
flat—the money that Ascanio had brought him. He killed him to
get possession of it.”

“And the coffee?” I asked. “What about the three coffee-cups?”

“That was another of Graves’s mistakes,” replied Poirot. “He
wanted to make it appear that the three men had finished their
dinner and were having coffee together. So he prepared three cups
of coffee. But he forgot that he himself had been told to go out
before the coffee was served. If he had been a truly clever man,
he would only have prepared two cups.”

“Well,” said Japp, “it seems a very plausible theory. I’ll go and
have a talk with Mr. Graves.”

A few hours later, Japp returned with the news that Graves had
confessed. He had indeed killed his master for the money, and had
then tried to throw the blame on Ascanio.

“It was a very clever plot,” said Japp, “but he hadn't reckoned on
Monsieur Poirot.”

Poirot smiled.

“It is the little things that matter, Japp,” he said. “The little
things that no one else notices. To a man of method, they are
the most important of all.”

“He’s there, all right. They’ll send him round at once. If he
doesn’t come, he’ll be fetched.”

A few minutes later we were all introduced to the mysterious
Signor Ascanio. I was surprised when I saw him. He was a tall,
well-built man, with a slight black moustache and a quiet,
determined manner. He did not seem to be particularly perturbed by
the suddenness of the inspector’s summons.

“I was to have seen Count Foscatini to-morrow morning,” he remarked,
“and I understood from him that he was leaving London to-morrow
afternoon.”

The inspector’s reply was a direct question.

“Will you tell me where you were this evening, between the hours
of 8.30 and 9?”

The Italian hesitated for a moment, then answered quietly:

“I was at the hotel.”

“Indeed! Can you prove that?”

“Certainly. I had a small dinner-party there this evening. We
stayed in the dining-room until nearly 9 o’clock.”

“And since then?”

“I have been in my room.”

The inspector looked at him with a meaning smile.

“I must inform you, Signor Ascanio, that Count Foscatini was
murdered this evening at 8.47, and that your presence at the
Regent’s Court flats has been deposed to by his servant.”

Signor Ascanio’s face remained impassive.

“Indeed! I spent the whole evening at the Grosvenor Hotel. As
regards my visit to Count Foscatini, I was there yesterday
morning, certainly, but I did not go there this evening. The
servant must be mistaken.”

The inspector turned to Graves.

“Well, Graves, what do you say to that?”

“I say that this is the gentleman who called on my master
yesterday morning, and that he and the other gentleman arrived
at eight o’clock this evening for dinner.”

Signor Ascanio shook his head.

“I am sorry,” he said, “but I was at the Grosvenor Hotel all the
evening.”

The inspector’s face began to look very stern indeed.

“You realize that this is a very serious matter, Signor Ascanio?
I must ask you to accompany me to the station.”

Ascanio bowed.

“I am at your service.”

As the door closed behind them, Poirot turned to me.

“What do you think of it, Hastings?”

“Well,” I said, “it seems a pretty clear case. But what was the
motive? Blackmail?”

Poirot shook his head.

“No, no, _mon ami_, not blackmail. I suspect it was something
much more serious than that.”

“Then what do you think it was?”

“I think,” said Poirot, “that we have here a very pretty little
problem.”

He walked to the window and looked out.

“A very pretty little problem indeed,” he repeated. “I wonder—I
wonder——”

He fell into a fit of abstraction. At last he turned to me.

“Hastings,” he said, “you have a good memory. Tell me, what was
the menu of the dinner that Count Foscatini ordered?”

“Soup julienne, filet de sole normande, tournedos of beef, and
a rice soufflé,” I replied promptly.

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “A very good dinner—a very good dinner
indeed. And yet—and yet——”

He stopped.

“And yet what?” I asked.

“And yet,” said Poirot, “it was a very strange dinner for three
men to have eaten.”

“Why?” I asked.

“Because,” said Poirot, “there was no mention of a salad.”

I stared at him.

“A salad!” I exclaimed. “But what has a salad to do with it?”

“A great deal, _mon ami_. A great deal. A salad is a very
important part of a dinner. And yet, in the menu that Count
Foscatini ordered, there was no mention of a salad.”

“But,” I protested, “many people do not care for salad.”

“That is true,” said Poirot. “That is true. But Count Foscatini
was an Italian. And Italians always have a salad with their
dinner.”

He turned back to the window.

“A very pretty little problem,” he murmured. “A very pretty
little problem indeed.”

“Well, he’s there all right! He says he’s only just returned from
the theatre. They’re sending a couple of men down there now to
invite him to come here and help us with our inquiries. I must say
I don’t think much of his head-piece to leave his name and address
around like that.”

Poirot’s eyes had a far-away look in them as he replied:

“The case—as you say—is very simple. Only I must tell you that I
do not find it as simple as it looks.”

“Why, what do you mean?”

“It is what I have been looking for—that mistake I spoke of.”

“The clock, you mean?”

“Not the clock,” replied Poirot. “But we shall see. In the
meantime, let us see this Signor Ascanio when he arrives.”

Wait—what of the telephone call? I asked. If the Count was struck from behind, how did he have the strength to reach the phone and name his location? And why say "Foscatine" instead of his own name? 

Poirot tilted his head. "A dying man's last effort is often strange, Hastings. But perhaps he was not naming himself. Perhaps he was naming his nemesis. Or perhaps... he was naming a dish."

"A dish?" I cried. "The rice soufflé?"

"We shall see," Poirot repeated, his eyes twinkling with that cat-like green light that always presaged a discovery.

“Just in time. Our fine gentleman was off to catch the boat train
to the Continong. Well, gentlemen, that’s about all we can do here.
It’s a bad business, but straightforward enough. One of these
Italian vendetta things, as likely as not.”

Thus airily dismissed, we found our way downstairs. Dr. Hawker was
full of excitement.

“Like the beginning of a novel, eh? Real exciting stuff. Wouldn’t
believe it if you read about it.”

Poirot did not speak. He was very thoughtful. All the evening he
had hardly opened his lips.

“What says the master detective, eh?” asked Hawker, clapping him
on the back. “Nothing to work your grey cells over this time.”

“You think not?”

“What could there be?”

“Well, for example, there is the window.”

“The window? But it was fastened. Nobody could have got out or in
that way. I noticed it specially.”

“And why were you able to notice it?”

The doctor looked puzzled. Poirot hastened to explain.

“It is to the curtains I refer. They were not drawn. A little odd,
that. And then there was the coffee. It was very black coffee.”

“Well, what of it?”

“Very black,” repeated Poirot. “In conjunction with that let us
remember that very little of the rice soufflé was eaten, and we
get—what?”

“Moonshine,” laughed the doctor. “You’re pulling my leg.”

“Never do I pull the leg. Hastings here knows that I am perfectly
serious.”

The next morning, Inspector Japp arrived early to provide us with the latest developments. He was in high spirits, convinced that the mystery was as good as solved. "We’ve got him, Poirot!" he announced. "Signor Ascanio was picked up at the Grosvenor Hotel just as he was preparing to leave for the continent. He’s a cool customer, I’ll grant you that. Admits to being at the flat for dinner, but swears he left by half-past eight and that the Count was alive and well then. Naturally, he can’t produce a witness to prove it. Graves's story holds water perfectly, and the timing of that phone call to Dr. Hawker's house cinches it. At 8.47, the Count was gasping his last, and Ascanio was the only man who could have been there."

On the following morning, Inspector Japp dropped in to see us, looking
uncommonly pleased with himself. He informed us that Signor Ascanio
had been apprehended at Victoria Station just as he was about to
leave the country. Despite the gravity of the charge, the Italian
remained obstinately silent, refusing to provide any explanation for
his presence at the flat or his hurried departure. Japp was
supremely confident, but Poirot’s brow remained clouded with
uncertainty. He began to pace the room, his eyes fixed on the
ceiling as he muttered something about the digestive powers of
different nationalities.

The Inspector’s prediction was verified. Signor Ascanio was discovered at the Grosvenor Hotel, just as he was on the point of departure. He was a man of middle age, with a thin, aristocratic face and an air of quiet self-possession that was not easily shaken. He admitted without hesitation that he had dined with Count Foscatini, but he denied any knowledge of the tragedy. He and his companion, he stated, had left the flat at half-past eight, at which time the Count was alive and well. As to the nature of their conversation, he was less forthcoming, asserting that it concerned private matters of a financial character which he did not feel called upon to reveal to the police.

The following morning found us at Scotland Yard, where Inspector Japp was looking particularly pleased with himself. He had intercepted Signor Ascanio at the Grosvenor Hotel just as the Italian was preparing to leave for the continent. The man was now in custody, though he maintained an air of haughty indifference to the charges. He admitted to having dined with Count Foscatini, but asserted that he and his young companion had taken their leave at half-past eight, at which time the Count was perfectly well. He flatly refused to divulge the nature of the business discussed, characterizing it as a private matter of a political character. Japp, however, remained unconvinced, pointing out the suspicious timing of the telephone call and the physical evidence at the scene.

The Grosvenor Hotel proved to be a scene of some activity. We arrived just as the inspector was emerging from the lift, accompanied by a tall, dark man of aristocratic bearing who looked both indignant and alarmed. This, it appeared, was Signor Paolo Ascanio. He was protesting volubly in Italian, but the inspector was stolidly indifferent to his outbursts. Poirot stepped forward, his eyes twinkling with a curious light as he surveyed the prisoner, who was currently being ushered into a private room for questioning. Following in their wake, we were permitted to be present at the interview.

“I don’t know what you are getting at, all the same,” I confessed.
“You don’t suspect the manservant, do you? He might have been in
with the gang, and put some dope in the coffee. I suppose they’ll
test his alibi?”

“Without doubt, my friend; but it is the alibi of Signor Ascanio
that interests me.”

“You think he has an alibi?”

“That is just what worries me. I have no doubt that we shall soon
be enlightened on that point.”

The _Daily Newsmonger_ enabled us to become conversant with
succeeding events.

The account of the murder of Count Foscatini was a sensation of the
first water. It appeared that Signor Ascanio was at the Grosvenor
Hotel, but denied any knowledge of the crime. He had visited Count
Foscatini on the evening of the murder, he admitted, but had left
early—about half-past eight. His friend, a young man whom he called
Andrea, had been with him. They had had a business talk with the
Count, and had then left. He denied that there had been any
threats or anything of an unpleasant nature. He had a perfectly
valid alibi, as it appeared. He had gone straight from Regent’s
Court to the Italian Embassy, and from there he had gone to a
well-known restaurant where he had been seen by several people.

The _Daily Newsmonger_ went on to state that the police were
searching for the young man Andrea.

The next development came two days later. Poirot had been more than
usually silent, but he had not been idle. He had had a long
interview with Inspector Japp, and had spent some time in the
Regent’s Court kitchen.

“Hastings,” he said to me, “we must go and see Dr. Hawker. He is
one of our best friends, and I should like to have a talk with
him.”

We found the doctor at home. He was as cheery as ever.

“Well, have you solved the mystery?” he asked. “The police seem to
be in a bit of a fog. This Ascanio fellow has a first-class alibi,
it seems. They can’t find the young man Andrea, either. He seems to
have vanished into thin air.”

“Is that so?” said Poirot. “I think I have a little light to throw
on the matter myself.”

The doctor’s face fell.

“You don’t say so! I was hoping it was going to be one of those
mysteries that are never solved. More romantic, you know.”

“Not for the police,” Poirot said with a smile. “But before we get
to the solution, I want to ask you a few questions, doctor. You
remember that evening when you were called away to Regent’s Court?”

“Perfectly.”

“And you remember the telephone call that your housekeeper, Miss
Rider, received?”

“Of course. It was that which started the whole thing.”

“Exactly. Now, Miss Rider said the voice was a ‘terrible’ one. What
did she mean by that, do you think?”

“Well, I suppose she meant it was a dying man’s voice—gasping and
faint.”

“Perhaps. And then there is the word ‘Foscatine.’ Miss Rider thought
it was ‘Foscatini,’ but she wasn’t sure. It sounded like ‘Foscatine.’
Does that suggest anything to you?”

“Nothing whatever.”

“It suggests a good deal to me,” Poirot said. “But let us go on to
the flat. You remember the dinner table?”

“Of course.”

“The three coffee cups, the three dessert plates—untouched—the port
decanter half full. It all seemed very natural, did it not?”

“Quite.”

“And yet there was one thing that was not natural. You remember I
said I was looking for a mistake? Well, I found it.”

“What was it?”

“The coffee. It was very black, as I said. Now, why should it be
so black?”

“I suppose because the Count liked it like that.”

“Perhaps. But there is another reason. And then there is the rice
soufflé. You remember there was a good deal of it left?”

“Yes, I remember.”

“Well, that is also a point of importance. And now, doctor, I will
ask you one more question. Do you happen to have a patient named
Signor Ascanio?”

The doctor’s face changed. He looked at Poirot with a new
expression in his eyes.

“Signor Ascanio? No. Why do you ask?”

“Because I think you have. Or rather, you have had. He is not a
patient of yours now, I believe.”

The doctor did not answer for a moment. Then he said:

“I don’t know what you are talking about.”

“I think you do,” Poirot said quietly. “And I think you also know
what has become of the young man Andrea.”

The doctor stood up. He was very pale.

“I think you had better go,” he said. “I have nothing more to say
to you.”

“As you please,” Poirot said. “But before I go, I will tell you one
thing. I know who killed Count Foscatini.”

“Who was it?”

“It was—but no, I will not tell you now. I will tell you when I
have all the proofs in my hand. Good-bye, doctor.”

We walked back to our rooms in silence. I was completely bewildered.
What did it all mean? Who was the murderer? And what had Dr. Hawker
to do with it?

I asked Poirot, but he only shook his head.

“Patience, my friend. All will be revealed in good time. In the
meantime, I have a little business to attend to.”

He went out, and did not return until late that evening. He looked
weary but satisfied.

“I have seen Inspector Japp,” he said. “And I think we are nearing
the end.”

“But who is the murderer?” I cried.

“To-morrow, Hastings. To-morrow you shall know everything.”

The next morning, Poirot received a letter. He read it with a smile.

“From our friend Japp,” he said. “He has made an arrest.”

“Who?”

“Signor Ascanio.”

“Then he did it after all!”

“Not so fast, my friend. Not so fast. We must see what Japp has to
say.”

We went to Scotland Yard, and found Japp in his room. He looked
very pleased with himself.

“Well, we’ve got him,” he said. “Ascanio. We found him at a small
hotel in Soho. He tried to get away, but we were too quick for him.
And we’ve found the young man Andrea, too. He was with him.”

“And what does Ascanio say?” Poirot asked.

“Denies everything, of course. Says he knows nothing about the
murder. But we’ve got enough evidence to hang him. The valet, Graves,
has identified him as the man who called on the Count the day before
the murder. And we’ve found the weapon—the statuette—in his
lodgings.”

“In his lodgings?” Poirot repeated. “That is very interesting. And
the young man Andrea? What does he say?”

“Nothing. He’s as dumb as an oyster. But we’ll get it out of him.”

“I think not,” Poirot said. “I think you will find that the young
man Andrea has nothing to say because he knows nothing.”

Japp stared at him.

“What do you mean?”

“I mean,” Poirot said, “that the young man Andrea is not the person
you think he is. And I mean also that Signor Ascanio did not kill
Count Foscatini.”

“Then who did?” Japp cried.

“I will tell you,” Poirot said. “But first, I must ask you to come
with me to Regent’s Court. I have a little experiment to make.”

We went to Regent’s Court, and Poirot led the way to Flat II. The
place was still under police supervision, but Japp’s presence
gained us admittance.

Poirot went straight to the dining-room. He stood by the table and
looked round.

“Now,” he said, “I want you to imagine the scene on the night of
the murder. The three men are sitting here at dinner. They have
finished their meal, and are drinking their port and coffee.
Suddenly, one of them—the murderer—rises, goes to the writing-table,
takes up the statuette, and strikes the Count down from behind. Then
he goes to the telephone, calls up Dr. Hawker’s house, and speaks.
After that, he hangs up the receiver, leaves the flat, and goes
away. Is that not so?”

“Yes,” Japp said. “That is what must have happened.”

“And who was the man who did all this?” Poirot asked. “Was it
Ascanio? Or was it the young man Andrea? Or was it someone else?”

“It must have been Ascanio,” Japp said. “The valet saw him.”

“The valet saw him the day before,” Poirot corrected. “He did not
see him on the night of the murder. Remember, he was told he could
have the evening off. He left at half-past eight.”

“But the lift man saw them come in.”

“He saw two men come in. He did not say they were Ascanio and
Andrea. He said they were ‘foreign gentlemen.’ And remember, he did
not see them leave.”

“Then who were they?” Japp asked.

“I will tell you,” Poirot said. “They were—but no, let us first
look at the evidence of the table. You remember the coffee? It was
very black. Why? Because it was not coffee at all. It was—charcoal!”

“Charcoal!” I cried.

“Yes. And the rice soufflé? Why was so much of it left? Because it
was not rice soufflé. It was—well, I will not say what it was, but
it was something that no one would want to eat much of. And the port?
It was not port. It was red ink!”

“Red ink!” Japp gasped. “What are you talking about?”

“I am talking about the fact that no dinner was eaten in this room
that night,” Poirot said. “The whole thing was a comedy—a piece of
acting. The three men were not dining together. There was only one
man here—the murderer.”

“But the lift man saw two men come in!” Japp cried.

“He saw two men come in, yes. But he did not see them go into this
flat. They may have gone into another flat, or they may have gone
out again immediately. The murderer was already here. He was the
only person in the flat.”

“But who was he?” I asked.

“He was the man who had the best opportunity to commit the crime,”
Poirot said. “The man who knew the flat, and who knew the Count’s
habits. The man who could come and go as he pleased without being
suspected. The man who—but here he is!”

The door opened, and a man came into the room. It was Graves, the
valet. He looked at us in surprise.

“I beg your pardon, gentlemen,” he said. “I didn’t know anyone was
here. I came to get some of my things.”

“Stay a moment, Mr. Graves,” Poirot said. “I have a few words to
say to you. You are the man who killed Count Foscatini.”

The man turned pale. He looked at Poirot with terror in his eyes.

“I? What do you mean? I was at the music hall.”

“You were not at the music hall,” Poirot said. “You were here. You
killed the Count, and then you set the stage for the comedy of the
dinner party. You soiled the plates, you poured the red ink into
the glasses, you put the charcoal into the coffee cups. Then you
went to the telephone and called Dr. Hawker’s house. You spoke in
a ‘terrible’ voice—a voice that you hoped would be mistaken for the
Count’s. You said ‘Help—Doctor—help. They’ve killed me!’ And then
you said the word ‘Foscatine.’ You hoped that would be taken for
the Count’s name. But it was not. It was the name of a—disinfectant!”

“A disinfectant!” I cried.

“Yes. A disinfectant that is used in this building. You had been
using it that afternoon, and the name was in your mind. It was a
little mistake—one of those little mistakes that the murderer
always makes.”

Graves did not speak. He stood as though turned to stone.

“And the weapon?” Poirot went on. “You did not leave it in Ascanio’s
lodgings. You put it there later, after you had seen him and his
friend Andrea. You knew they had visited the Count the day before,
and you saw your chance to fasten the crime on them. You followed
them, found out where they were staying, and planted the weapon.
It was a clever plan, but it failed.”

Graves suddenly made a dash for the door, but Japp was too quick
for him. In a moment he was handcuffed and led away.

“Well,” I said, when we were alone. “That was a most extraordinary
case. But tell me, Poirot, what made you suspect Graves?”

“The coffee, my friend. The coffee. It was too black. And the rice
soufflé. And the port. They were all wrong. And then there was the
window. The curtains were not drawn. Now, a man like Count Foscatini
would never dine with the curtains open. It was a small point, but
it was significant. And finally, there was the telephone call.
Why should a dying man call his doctor? He would call the police.
But the murderer called the doctor because he wanted someone to
come at once and find the body—and he wanted someone who would be
easily deceived by the comedy he had prepared.”

“And what about Dr. Hawker?” I asked. “Why did you suspect him?”

“I did not suspect him,” Poirot said with a smile. “I only wanted
to see how he would react to my questions. He is a good man, but
he is a little—what you call—romantic. He liked the idea of a
mysterious crime, and he was a little disappointed when I solved it.”

“And the young man Andrea?”

“He was just a young man who was with Ascanio. He had nothing to do
with the crime. He is probably back in Italy by now.”

“Well,” I said. “It was a most remarkable case.”

“Yes,” Poirot said. “It was a case of—how shall I say?—theatre.
The murderer was an actor, and he played his part well. But he
forgot one thing.”

“What was that?”

“He forgot that Hercule Poirot is also—something of an actor!”

And with a little bow, Poirot led the way out of the room.

Signor Ascanio had been arrested and, in spite of his protests,
was kept in custody. He appeared to have a most complete alibi.
For some unknown reason, he had gone to a house in Hammersmith
between 8.30 and 10.30, and the occupants of the house could swear
most positively to his being there. On the other hand, the waiter
at Regent’s Court was certain that he was the same man who had
dined there.

Poirot was immensely interested. He spent most of his time reading
the reports of the trial. One evening he went out, and was gone
nearly three hours. He returned with a twinkle in his eye and a
mysterious smile on his face.

“I have seen him!” he announced.

“Signor Ascanio?”

“Exactly. Also I have seen the house in Hammersmith.”

“And what do you think of it all?”

“_Mon ami_,” said Poirot, “I am inclined to think that the alibi
is a good one. It is a very good one. It is almost too good.”

I stared.

“And now,” said Poirot, “I have a little business for you. I want
you to find out for me if Dr. Hawker’s housekeeper, Miss Rider,
is an habitual frequenter of the cinema.”

“The cinema?” I asked in amazement.

“Precisely.”

I was beginning to feel that I should never understand my friend.
However, I did as he requested, and was soon able to inform him
that Miss Rider was indeed a devotee of the ‘movies,’ and went at
least twice a week.

“Ah!” said Poirot. “And did she go on the night of the murder?”

“As it happens, she did. She went to the first performance, and
came home about nine o’clock.”

“Splendid!” said Poirot. “Now we are getting on.”

“But I don’t see what the cinema has to do with it.”

“You will see in time, my friend. It is all a matter of method.
Method and the little grey cells.”

A few days later the police were forced to release Signor Ascanio,
the evidence against him being insufficient. The case against his
young companion also fell through.

The murder of Count Foscatini became one of the ‘unsolved
mysteries’ of the season.

Poirot, however, did not seem at all perturbed. He was, on the
contrary, in a very good humour. He spent his time humming little
French songs and rearranging his bookshelves.

“Well,” I said one morning, “I suppose you have given up the
Foscatini case?”

“On the contrary, I have just finished it.”

“Finished it?”

“Precisely. I know now who killed Count Foscatini.”

“You do? Then why don’t you tell the police?”

“Because, my friend, I have no proof. At least, no proof that
would satisfy a jury. But I can tell _you_.”

“Who was it?” I asked eagerly.

“It was——” Poirot paused. “But first let us go over the facts.”

Ascanio was arrested at the hotel, but his explanation was a
simple one. He admitted that he had been to Count Foscatini’s
flat. He had been there about eight-thirty. He had had a long talk
with the Count, and then had left him to go to the Grosvenor Hotel.
He had seen the Count alive and well at the time of his departure.
No, he knew nothing about any other person being there.

As to what the business had been that had taken him there, he
refused to say. It was a private matter, he declared.

The evidence of the lift man corroborated this. He had taken
Ascanio up to the second floor at half-past eight, and had seen
him go into Flat II. He had also seen him come out about five
minutes later.

“If the lift man is right,” I remarked to Poirot, “Ascanio is
cleared. He couldn’t have committed the murder between 8.30 and
8.35.”

“Precisely,” said Poirot. “And if he is right, why was the dinner
order given for three? And why were there three chairs pushed
back?”

I could see no explanation of these facts.

“Was there anyone else in the flat besides the Count and his
guests?” I asked.

“Apparently not. Graves was out, as he says. And there was no
one else.”

“Then it must have been the other man who was with Ascanio,” I
suggested.

“Who was he? Ascanio says he was alone. The lift man says the same.
Who was the second man Graves spoke of? And what has become of him?
He seems to have vanished into thin air.”

“That is the point,” said Poirot. “He has vanished. And why?”

I could not say.

“Let us go and see the flat,” suggested Poirot. “I have an idea
that we may find something there.”

We found the inspector in charge of the flat. He was quite willing
to let us look round.

“Nothing new has turned up,” he told us. “The fingerprints on the
statuette were the Count’s own. He must have been using it as a
paper-weight. No others. Ascanio’s alibi seems to hold water all
right. The lift man is positive as to the time. 8.30 to 8.35.”

“What about Graves?” asked Poirot.

“His alibi is all right, too. He was at the Metropolitan Music Hall
from nine o’clock till eleven. He was seen there by several people
who knew him. So that’s that.”

Poirot wandered round the room. He seemed particularly interested
in the dining-table. He looked at the three coffee-cups again,
and then at the fruit-dish. There were three dessert-plates, as
I have said, and on each of them was a little heap of fruit skins.

“Two of them had oranges,” remarked Poirot, “and one had a pear.
The Count, I think, had the pear.”

“How do you know that?” I asked.

“Because the knife used for it has a slight stain of juice on it.
The other two were fruit-knives, and they have only the stain of
the orange juice.”

“Well, what of it?”

“Nothing much. Only it shows that three people _did_ dine here.”

“Then who was the third person?”

“That is what we have to find out,” said Poirot.

He went into the kitchen. The service lift was still there, and
the small telephone beside it. Poirot looked at it for some
moments in silence. Then he turned to the inspector.

“I should like to see Graves again,” he said.

The man was fetched. He looked pale and anxious.

“I want to ask you a few more questions, Graves,” said Poirot.
“About the dinner that was served that night. You say it was
ordered for three?”

“Yes, sir. The Count told me so himself.”

“And you served it?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Now, think carefully. Did you see the three people sitting at the
table?”

Graves hesitated.

“Well, no, sir, not exactly. You see, the Count told me I could go
as soon as I had put the port on the table. I didn’t actually see
them sitting down.”

“But you saw the three places laid?”

“Oh, yes, sir.”

“And you saw the three guests?”

“I saw Signor Ascanio and the other gentleman in the lounge before
they went in to dinner.”

“And what was the other gentleman like?”

“He was a young man, sir. Very well dressed. I didn’t notice him
particularly.”

“I see. Now, one more question. When you went out at 8.30, did you
see Signor Ascanio?”

“No, sir. He must have gone by then.”

“I see,” said Poirot again.

He dismissed the man and turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of it?”

“It’s a muddle,” I said. “I can’t make head or tail of it.”

“It is not a muddle,” said Poirot. “It is very simple—if you look
at it the right way.”

“And what is the right way?”

“The way of the rice soufflé,” said Poirot, with a smile.

I looked at him in despair. He was always like this when he had
a clue. He would never tell me what it was.

“Let us go back to our rooms,” he said. “I have much to think
about.”

As we walked along, Poirot was very silent. I knew he was working
out some problem in his mind. Suddenly he stopped and looked at
me.

“Hastings,” he said, “what was the first thing that struck you
when we entered that room?”

“The dead body, of course,” I said.

“No, no. I mean before that. When we were in the lounge.”

“I don’t know. I didn’t notice anything particular.”

“Didn’t you notice the smell?”

“The smell?”

“Yes. The smell of cooking. It was very strong.”

“Well, I suppose it would be. They had just had dinner.”

“Exactly. They had just had dinner. And yet the window was open.”

“Was it?”

“Yes. I noticed it at once. And that is why I asked the doctor
about the curtains. If the window was open, the curtains should
have been drawn to keep out the draught. But they were not. Why?”

“I don’t know,” I said.

“Because someone wanted the smell of cooking to get out of the
room as quickly as possible,” said Poirot.

“But why?”

“That is what I am going to find out,” said Poirot.

He was silent again for some time. Then he spoke again.

“There is one more thing, Hastings. Do you remember the telephone
call?”

“Of course.”

“Miss Rider said the voice was very faint. It ‘tailed away,’ she
said. And the word she heard was ‘Foscatini’—or something like
it. Now, why should a man who is dying give his own name? He would
know that the doctor would know who was speaking.”

“Perhaps he was afraid the doctor wouldn’t recognize his voice,”
I suggested.

“Perhaps. But there is another possibility. Suppose it wasn’t
Count Foscatini who was speaking?”

“Then who was it?”

“That is what I am going to find out,” said Poirot again.

We had reached our rooms by now. Poirot went straight to the
telephone and called up Inspector Japp.

“Is that you, Japp? . . . Yes, Poirot speaking. . . . Look here,
I want you to do something for me. . . . No, it’s about the
Foscatini case. . . . I want you to find out if anyone else
besides Graves had a key to the flat. . . . Yes, that’s it. . . .
And find out where Miss Rider was between eight and nine o’clock
that night. . . . Yes, I know she was at the doctor’s, but find out
if she went out at all. . . . Right. . . . Goodbye.”

He hung up the receiver and turned to me.

“And now, Hastings, we will have a little dinner. I feel that I
have earned it.”

I was still as much in the dark as ever, but I knew it was no use
asking Poirot any more questions. He would tell me in his own good
time.

The next morning Poirot was up early. He had already received a
report from Japp.

“Well?” I asked.

“Miss Rider did not leave the house after eight o’clock,” he told
me. “So that is one possibility eliminated. As for the key, it
seems that Graves was the only person who had one, besides the
Count himself. But there is one other thing. The manager of the
flats says that a new maid was engaged about a week ago. Her name
is Annie, and she has the key of all the flats on that floor.”

“Do you suspect her?” I asked.

“We shall see,” said Poirot. “I think we will go and have a little
talk with Annie.”

We found Annie in the kitchen of the flats. She was a pleasant-faced
young woman, and seemed quite ready to talk.

“Yes, sir,” she said, in answer to Poirot’s questions. “I have the
key of all the flats on the second floor. It’s my business to go
in and do the cleaning and so on.”

“And were you in Flat II on the night of the murder?”

“No, sir. I’d finished my work there in the morning. I didn’t go
near it again.”

“Did you see anyone going in or out of the flat that evening?”

“No, sir. I was busy in the kitchens most of the time.”

“I see. And you didn’t lend your key to anyone?”

“Oh, no, sir!”

“Are you sure?”

“Quite sure, sir.”

Poirot looked at her keenly for a moment.

“I think you are telling me the truth, Annie,” he said. “But tell
me, have you lost your key at any time?”

The girl started.

“How did you know that, sir? Yes, I did lose it—just for a few
hours. It was the day before the murder. I must have dropped it
somewhere. But I found it again the next morning. It was lying on
the floor in the hall.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “Thank you, Annie. That is all I wanted to
know.”

As we left the kitchen, Poirot turned to me with a smile.

“You see, Hastings? The plot thickens. Someone had that key for a
few hours. Long enough to have a duplicate made.”

“But who?” I asked.

“That is what we are going to find out,” said Poirot.

He was silent for a moment, then he said:

“I think we will go and see Dr. Hawker.”

We found the doctor in his surgery. He seemed surprised to see us.

“Well, Poirot,” he said. “Any news?”

“A little,” said Poirot. “I want to ask you a question, doctor.
When Miss Rider came to our rooms that night, she said she had
received a telephone call from Count Foscatini. Now, tell me, did
she seem very much upset?”

“She was absolutely terrified,” said the doctor. “I’ve never seen
her like it before. She’s a very calm, sensible woman as a rule.”

“I see. And did she tell you exactly what the voice said?”

“She said it was a man’s voice, and that it said, ‘Help—doctor—
help. They’ve killed me!’ And then it said something like
‘Foscatine—Regent’s Court.’”

“I see. Now, doctor, I want you to tell me something else. Did
you notice anything unusual about Miss Rider lately?”

The doctor looked thoughtful.

“Well, now you mention it, she has been a bit nervous and jumpy
lately. I put it down to the heat. It’s been very trying, hasn’t
it?”

“Very,” agreed Poirot.

He was silent for a moment, then he said:

“Thank you, doctor. That is all I wanted to know.”

As we left the surgery, Poirot turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think now?”

“I don’t know what to think,” I said. “It seems more of a muddle
than ever.”

“On the contrary,” said Poirot. “It is becoming very clear. There
is only one more thing to do, and then I think I shall be able to
tell you the whole story.”

“And what is that?”

“I am going to have a little talk with Signor Ascanio.”

We found Ascanio at the Grosvenor Hotel. He was a tall, dark man,
with a rather sinister expression. He didn’t seem at all pleased
to see us.

“I have already told the police all I know,” he said. “I have
nothing more to say.”

“But I have something to say to you,” said Poirot. “I know why
you went to see Count Foscatini that night.”

Ascanio started.

“What do you mean?”

“You went there to blackmail him,” said Poirot.

Ascanio turned pale.

“It’s a lie!” he cried.

“Is it? I don’t think so. I think you knew something about the
Count’s past—something that he didn’t want anyone else to know.
And you were making him pay for your silence.”

Ascanio was silent for a moment. Then he said:

“Even if that were true, it doesn’t prove that I killed him.”

“No,” said Poirot. “But it gives you a motive. And you were there
that night.”

“I’ve already explained that. I was only there for five minutes.
The lift man will tell you that.”

“I know what the lift man says,” said Poirot. “But I also know
something else. I know that you were not alone when you went to
the flat.”

Ascanio stared at him.

“What do you mean?”

“I mean that there was someone else with you. A young man. Very
well dressed. Graves saw him.”

Ascanio laughed.

“Graves is mistaken. I was alone.”

“Then who was the young man?”

“There was no young man.”

Poirot looked at him for a moment in silence. Then he said:

“Very well, Signor Ascanio. If you won’t tell me the truth now,
you will have to tell it to the police later.”

As we left the hotel, Poirot turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, the case is complete. I know who killed Count
Foscatini.”

“Who?” I asked eagerly.

“Wait a little, my friend. I have one more thing to do. I must
see Dr. Hawker again.”

We found the doctor still in his surgery.

“Well, Poirot,” he said. “Found out who did it?”

“Yes,” said Poirot. “I have.”

The doctor looked surprised.

“Who was it?”

“It was you, doctor,” said Poirot.

I gasped. The doctor turned pale.

“Me? You’re joking!”

“I never joke about murder,” said Poirot. “You killed Count
Foscatini, and you used Miss Rider to help you.”

“This is absurd!” cried the doctor. “How could I have killed him?
I was with you and Hastings all the evening.”

“Not all the evening,” said Poirot. “You went out for a few
minutes—to see a patient, you said. And it was during those few
minutes that you killed the Count.”

“But the telephone call! Miss Rider received it while I was with
you!”

“The telephone call was a fake,” said Poirot. “Miss Rider was in
it with you. She pretended to receive a call from the Count, but
it was really you calling from another room.”

“But the lift man! He saw Ascanio go into the flat at 8.30!”

“Yes, and he saw him come out at 8.35. That was all part of your
plan. You knew Ascanio was going to see the Count that night, and
you timed your murder to coincide with his visit.”

“But the dinner! The dinner for three!”

“There was no dinner for three,” said Poirot. “The Count dined
alone. You and Miss Rider went to the flat later, and you made
it look as if three people had dined there. You even ate some of
the food yourself!”

“But why? Why should I kill the Count?”

“Because he was blackmailing you,” said Poirot. “He knew something
about your past—something that would have ruined your career. And
so you decided to kill him.”

The doctor was silent for a moment. Then he suddenly pulled a
revolver from his pocket.

“You’re too clever, Poirot!” he cried. “But you won’t live to tell
anyone!”

Before he could fire, I had sprung upon him and wrestled the gun
from his hand.

“Well done, Hastings!” said Poirot. “And now, I think we had
better send for the police.”

As we waited for the police to arrive, Poirot explained the whole
thing to me.

“It was the rice soufflé that gave me the first clue,” he said.
“The man in the kitchen said that most of it was left. Now, if
three people had been dining, they would have eaten more of it.
And then there was the coffee. It was very black—because it had
been standing for a long time. And the window being open—to get
rid of the smell of the dinner that had been eaten hours before.”

“But how did you know about the blackmail?” I asked.

“I didn’t—until I saw Ascanio. He was blackmailing the Count,
but the Count was also blackmailing the doctor. It was a vicious
circle, you see.”

“And Miss Rider?”

“She was in love with the doctor, and she was willing to do
anything to help him. She even stole the key from Annie so that
they could get into the flat.”

“It’s a strange case,” I said.

“Yes,” agreed Poirot. “But, as I always say, the little grey
cells—they never fail!”

The police had arrested Signor Ascanio as he was about to step
into the Continental boat train. A search of his person had
disclosed a large sum in English bank-notes, and he was at once
confronted with Graves, the valet-butler. Graves identified him
as the elder of the two men who had visited his master on the
previous day and on the night of the murder. But he refused to
answer any questions and maintained an air of haughty indifference.

The discovery of a small but significant fact tended still more to
implicate him. His alibi for the time of the murder was a very
slender one. He claimed to have been walking in the park, but
there were no witnesses to prove it.

The police were jubilant. But Poirot remained strangely silent.
He was thinking deeply, and for two days he refused to discuss the
case with me.

On the third day we received a visitor. It was none other than
Japp, of Scotland Yard. He looked more like a ferret than ever,
and there was a gleam of triumph in his eye.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” he said, as he seated himself. “I’ve got
some news for you. It’s a bit of a surprise, I can tell you.”

“Indeed?” said Poirot, with a smile. “What is it?”

“It’s about that Signor Ascanio. He’s got an alibi after all. A
perfectly good alibi. It seems that at 8.45—just two minutes
before the murder was committed—he was at the Italian Embassy.
He’d gone there to see the Ambassador on some important business,
and he was there for over half an hour. The Ambassador himself
vouchsafes for him.”

“Aha!” said Poirot. “That is very interesting.”

“It’s more than interesting,” said Japp. “It’s a regular floorer.
We can’t possibly charge him now. And yet Graves is positive he’s
the man. What do you make of it?”

Poirot reflected for a moment.

“I should like to see this Graves again,” he said at last. “Could
you arrange for him to come here?”

“Certainly. I’ll send him round this afternoon.”

When Graves arrived he was as self-assured as ever. He repeated
his story with a great deal of detail, and was quite certain of
his identification of Ascanio.

“You are quite sure,” said Poirot, “that it was Signor Ascanio who
visited your master on the night of the murder?”

“Positive, sir. I saw him as plain as I see you now.”

“And you are also sure that he was one of the two men who dined
with the Count?”

“Yes, sir. I waited on them myself.”

Poirot nodded.

“Thank you, Graves. That will do.”

When the man had gone Poirot turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of it?”

“It’s a mystery,” I said. “If Ascanio was at the Embassy, he
couldn’t have been at Regent’s Court. And yet Graves is positive.
Someone must be lying.”

“Not necessarily,” said Poirot. “It is possible that they are both
telling the truth—as they see it.”

“But how can that be?”

“That is what we have to find out. And I think I see a way. We must
pay another visit to Regent’s Court.”

We found the flat just as we had left it. The police had finished
their work, and the body had been removed. Poirot went straight
to the dining-room and began to examine the table again.

“See here, Hastings,” he said, pointing to the coffee-cups. “What
do you notice about them?”

“Nothing in particular,” I said. “They’re just ordinary
coffee-cups.”

“But look at the remains of the coffee. In two of them it is quite
black. In the third it has been mixed with milk.”

“Well, what of that? Some people like milk in their coffee, and
some don’t.”

“True. But look at this.” He pointed to a small stain on the
tablecloth near one of the cups. “That is a milk stain. And yet
the cup nearest to it contains black coffee.”

“Perhaps someone spilled a little milk,” I suggested.

“Perhaps. But there is something else. Look at these dessert
plates. They are all quite clean. Not a fruit stain or a crumb
on any of them.”

“Well, they didn’t have any dessert. The murderer probably
interrupted them before they got that far.”

“But they had their coffee and port. That usually comes after the
dessert, does it not?”

“I suppose it does. But they might have changed the order of
things.”

“Perhaps. But there is another thing that strikes me as being very
singular. Do you remember what the man in the kitchen told us? He
said that the plates and dishes were all soiled, and the dishes
empty—with the exception of the rice soufflé. Now, if three people
dined here, there should be three sets of soiled plates and dishes.
But when we looked into the kitchen, I saw only two sets.”

“Only two? But the man said three.”

“He said the order was for three. He didn’t say he had seen three
people eating. He only saw the plates when they were sent up in
the lift.”

“Then you think only two people dined here?”

“I am sure of it. And I think I can tell you who they were.”

“Who?”

“Count Foscatini and—his murderer.”

“But what about the third person? And what about Ascanio?”

“Ascanio was never here. He was at the Embassy, as he said. The
man who came here and dined with the Count was someone else—someone
who was carefully disguised to look like Ascanio.”

“But why? What was the object?”

“To provide an alibi for the murderer, of course. If Ascanio was
suspected, he could prove that he was elsewhere at the time. And
as he was the only person who had a motive for the murder, the
police would be completely baffled.”

“But who was the murderer?”

“That is what we are going to find out now. And I think our friend
Graves can help us.”

He rang the bell for the valet. When Graves appeared, Poirot
looked at him keenly.

“Graves,” he said, “I want you to tell me the truth. Who was the
man who dined with the Count on the night of the murder?”

Graves looked startled.

“Why, Signor Ascanio, sir. I’ve told you that already.”

“I know you have. But I also know that it was not Signor Ascanio.
Signor Ascanio was at the Italian Embassy at that time.”

Graves turned pale.

“I—I don’t know what you mean, sir.”

“I think you do. You were the one who admitted the two men to the
flat, were you not?”

“Yes, sir.”

“And you were the one who served the dinner?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Then you must have known that there were only two people at the
table.”

Graves hesitated.

“Well, sir, now you mention it, I believe there were only two. I
suppose the other gentleman must have gone away early.”

“He didn’t go away early. He was never here. You lied to the police,
Graves. Why did you do it?”

“I—I was afraid, sir. I didn’t want to get mixed up in it.”

“A very poor excuse. And now I will tell you what really happened.
The man who dined with the Count was the murderer. He came here
disguised as Ascanio, and he had an accomplice who was also
disguised. They knew that Ascanio would be at the Embassy, and
they planned the whole thing so as to throw suspicion on him.”

“But who were they, sir?”

“That is what I am going to tell you. One of them was a man named
Graves.”

Graves gave a cry of terror and turned to flee, but Poirot was too
quick for him. He seized him by the arm and held him fast.

“No, you don’t, my friend. You’re not going to get away as easily
as that. You were the one who struck the blow that killed Count
Foscatini. And your accomplice was—Miss Rider!”

I gasped in astonishment. Miss Rider! The quiet, middle-aged
housekeeper! It seemed incredible.

“Yes,” said Poirot, “Miss Rider. She was the one who made the
telephone call from the doctor’s house. She knew that the doctor
was with us, and she knew that his housekeeper would be at home.
She simply went to the telephone and told her story, and then
hurried back to the flat to help you with your grisly work.”

“But how did you know?” I asked.

“It was the coffee that gave them away,” said Poirot. “You see,
there were three cups on the table, but only two of them had been
used. The third one was quite clean, but it had been filled with
black coffee to make it look as if someone had been drinking from
it. But the person who did it made a mistake. They spilled a
little milk on the table, and then, realized their mistake, they
filled the cup with black coffee instead of coffee and milk. It
was a small thing, but it was enough to show me that the whole
scene had been carefully prepared.”

“And what about the rice soufflé?” I asked.

“That was another mistake,” said Poirot. “The murderer knew that
the Count was fond of rice soufflé, so he ordered it for three.
But as there were only two of them eating, they couldn’t finish
it. That is why there was so much left.”

“But why did they do it?” I asked.

“For money, of course. Graves knew that the Count had a large sum
of money in the flat, and he and Miss Rider planned to rob and
murder him. They used Ascanio as a scapegoat, knowing that his
quarrel with the Count would make him a likely suspect.”

Graves made a full confession, and he and Miss Rider were duly
brought to justice. It was one of Poirot’s most brilliant cases,
and it showed once again that even the most carefully planned
crime can be foiled by a single small mistake.

Ascanio had been arrested, and his statement was an interesting
one. He had, he said, been at the hotel all the evening. He had
never set foot in the flat that night. He had had a dinner
engagement, which he had cancelled by telephone. The police had
found it was true. But, unfortunately for Signor Ascanio, the hotel
people could only swear to his presence there until seven-thirty.
After that, no one had seen him. Then there was the weapon. A
silver statuette, with a heavy marble base. His finger-prints
were found on it.

Ascanio, when confronted with this, merely shrugged his shoulders.
He had, he said, looked at the statuette on the previous day.

“An unlikely story,” commented the inspector.

The trial was a short one. Ascanio was found guilty and sentenced
to death.

Poirot followed the proceedings with the closest attention. He
shook his head several times.

“The evidence is too complete,” he said. “Too perfect. It is the
one thing that makes me suspicious.”

“You think he didn’t do it?” I asked.

“I am almost sure of it.”

“Then who did? One of the other guests?”

“There were no other guests, Hastings.”

“No other guests! But the table was laid for three.”

“Precisely. That is just what I am thinking about.”

I looked at him in surprise.

“You mean that only one guest came?”

“I mean that _no_ guest came.”

“But the lift man saw them!”

“He saw two men, but he did not see their faces. They were muffled
up in overcoats.”

“And the dinner? The four courses?”

“My friend, have you ever tried to eat a dinner for three? It is
not an easy task. That is why I was so interested in the rice
soufflé. It was the only dish of which any remained.”

“But the coffee? The three cups?”

“Ah, the coffee! That is the most interesting point of all. One
cup was with milk. Now, an Italian never takes milk in his coffee
after dinner. It is a French or English custom. That was the
mistake I was looking for. The murderer was not an Italian.”

“Then who was he?”

“I think,” said Poirot, “that we will have a little talk with
Dr. Hawker.”

I stared at him in amazement.

“Dr. Hawker! You don’t mean that _he_ is the murderer?”

“I mean that he can tell us something—if he will.”

But the doctor, when we saw him, was not at all communicative. He
seemed, indeed, to be in a state of great nervous tension.

“I have nothing to say,” he said. “Nothing at all. The man has
been convicted, and there’s an end of it.”

“Not quite an end, I think,” said Poirot. “There is still the
question of the telephone call.”

“The telephone call? What about it?”

“It was a very remarkable call, was it not? A man who is at the
point of death does not usually think of telephoning to his doctor.
He has other things to think about.”

“He might have done it,” said the doctor. “It’s possible.”

“Possible, but not likely. And then there is the question of the
statuette. Why should Ascanio leave his finger-prints on it? He
would have been more careful than that.”

“The man was a fool,” said the doctor.

“On the contrary, he was a very clever man. So clever that he
almost succeeded in outwitting the police.”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean,” said Poirot, “that the whole thing was a plant. Ascanio
was never in the flat that night. The two men who were seen to
enter were not Ascanio and his friend. They were two other people.”

“Who were they?”

“I think,” said Poirot, “that one of them was the man Graves.”

“Graves! But he had an alibi.”

“A very good alibi. He was at the music-hall. But he did not go
there until half-past eight. That gave him plenty of time.”

“Time for what?”

“Time to kill his master, and to set the stage for the murder.”

“But the telephone call? Miss Rider heard the voice.”

“She heard _a_ voice. She did not know whose it was. She assumed
it was Count Foscatini’s because he mentioned his name and address.”

“But why should Graves kill him?”

“Because he had discovered a secret. Count Foscatini was not a
Count at all. He was a common blackmailer. He had been blackmailing
Signor Ascanio for years. Graves found it out, and he decided to
do a little blackmailing on his own account. But the Count was
not an easy person to blackmail. He threatened to go to the police.
So Graves killed him.”

“And the other man? The one who went into the flat with him?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is where the doctor comes in.”

He turned to Hawker.

“Am I not right, monsieur? You were the second man.”

The doctor’s face went white.

“It’s a lie!” he gasped. “A lie!”

“Is it? We shall see. You were in debt, Dr. Hawker. You had lost
money on the Turf. Graves knew it. He offered you a way out. All
you had to do was to go to the flat with him, and to help him
to arrange the scene. You were to be the witness who would prove
that the murder had been committed by Ascanio.”

“It’s not true!” cried the doctor. “I tell you it’s not true!”

“Then how do you explain the coffee?” asked Poirot. “The coffee
with milk? You are an Englishman, Dr. Hawker. You take milk in
your coffee. You forgot that an Italian would not do so. It was
a little mistake, but it was enough.”

The doctor buried his face in his hands.

“God help me!” he groaned. “It’s true. Every word of it is true.”

“I thought so,” said Poirot. “And now, if you will be so good as
to come with me to Scotland Yard, we will see what can be done for
Signor Ascanio.”

As we walked away from the doctor’s house, I turned to Poirot.

“How did you know?” I asked. “What made you suspect him?”

“It was the rice soufflé, my friend. A man who is about to be
murdered does not eat a whole rice soufflé. It is not natural.
And then there was the telephone call. As I told the doctor, it
was too convenient. It was intended to fix the time of the murder,
and to provide an excuse for our visit to the flat. It was all
very cleverly arranged, but the murderer made one mistake—he
forgot the coffee.”

“And Graves?” I asked. “What will happen to him?”

“He will be arrested, of course. He is the real culprit. The doctor
was only his tool. A weak man, but not a murderer.”

“And Signor Ascanio?”

“He will be released. He has been very lucky. If it had not been
for the rice soufflé, he would certainly have been hanged.”

“It is a wonderful thing, the mind,” I remarked.

“It is the only thing that matters,” said Poirot. “The little grey
cells, Hastings—the little grey cells!”

Signor Ascanio was arrested and charged with the murder of Count
Foscatini. When arrested, he denied knowing the Count, and declared
he had never been near Regent’s Court either on the evening of the
crime or on the previous morning. The younger man had disappeared
entirely. Signor Ascanio had arrived alone at the Grosvenor Hotel
from the Continent two days before the murder. All efforts to trace
the second man failed.

But the sensation was yet to come. On the Monday morning, when
Signor Ascanio was brought before the magistrate, he was discharged.
The police withdrew the charge. He was able to prove an
incontestable alibi. Between eight and nine o’clock on the night
of the murder he had been at the Italian Embassy. The first
secretary and two other officials at the Embassy bore witness to
the fact. At 8.45 he had been in the middle of a conversation with
the Ambassador himself.

The case against him collapsed. The police were at their wits’
end. The theory of the Italian vendetta was still the only one
they had to work on. Signor Ascanio admitted that he was a
compatriot of the dead man, but beyond that he would say nothing.
He refused to state the nature of his business with the Count, or
the name of the young man who had accompanied him on his first
visit. He denied having visited the Count on the second evening.

The mystery seemed to be deeper than ever. Japp, who had been put
in charge of the case, came to see us. He was a small, sharp,
ferret-faced man, and a great friend of Poirot’s.

“I’m fairly up against it this time,” he confessed. “There’s
no doubt the fellow’s in it up to his neck. That alibi’s a bit
too thick. And yet—well, you can’t get over the Ambassador. He’s
a man of the highest character.”

“It is a very pretty problem,” said Poirot. “I have been thinking
about it. There is one person I should very much like to see.”

“Who’s that? Ascanio?”

“No. The valet, Graves.”

“Well, you can see him. He’s staying at a small hotel in the
neighbourhood. I’ll give you the address.”

“I’m going to see him this afternoon,” I said. “I’m on my way there
now. Come with me if you like.”

“I’ll come,” said Poirot. “I’m interested in that man.”

We found Graves in a small room on the second floor of a somewhat
shabby hotel. He seemed a good deal surprised to see us.

“I didn’t expect to see you again, gentlemen,” he said. “I hope
there’s nothing wrong?”

“Nothing at all,” said Poirot. “I just wanted to ask you one or
two questions.”

“Certainly, sir. Anything I can do to help.”

“You told us that on the night of the murder you went to the
Metropolitan Music Hall?”

“Yes, sir.”

“What time did you get there?”

“About nine o’clock, sir.”

“And you stayed there until when?”

“Until the end—about half-past eleven.”

“Did you see anyone you knew there?”

“No, sir.”

“You didn’t happen to see Dr. Hawker there?”

“Dr. Hawker? No, sir.”

“I thought you might have. He was there that evening.”

“Was he? I didn’t see him.”

“One other thing. You said that the two men who called on the Count
the morning before the murder were Italians. How did you know?”

“They spoke Italian, sir.”

“Do you understand Italian?”

“No, sir.”

“Then how do you know they were speaking Italian?”

The man hesitated for a moment.

“I’ve heard it spoken before, sir. It’s got a sort of sound of its
own.”

“I see. And you’re sure they were the same two men who came the
next evening?”

“Oh, yes, sir. I recognized them at once.”

“Thank you. That’s all I wanted to know.”

As we went down the stairs, I asked Poirot what he had gained from
the interview.

“Not much, Hastings. But enough to confirm my suspicions.”

“Suspicions? You suspect Graves?”

“I have my ideas, my friend. But we must have proof. And for that
we must go to the Italian Embassy.”

We were lucky enough to get an interview with the first secretary.
He was a very polite and charming young man.

“Signor Ascanio? Yes, he was here on the night you mention. He
arrived about eight o’clock and stayed until nearly half-past
nine.”

“You are quite sure of the time?”

“Oh, yes. I remember it perfectly. We had a long talk on several
matters of importance.”

“And was he alone?”

“Quite alone.”

“He did not have a young man with him?”

“No. He was quite alone.”

“Thank you. That is what I wanted to know.”

As we walked away, Poirot turned to me.

“You see, Hastings? The plot thickens. According to Graves, two men
visited the Count that evening. According to the Embassy, Signor
Ascanio was there alone. One of them is lying. Which?”

“It must be Graves,” I said. “The Embassy officials have no reason
to lie.”

“Exactly. And yet—why should Graves lie? What had he to gain by
it? If he were the murderer, why should he invent two mysterious
Italians? It would only make things more difficult for him.”

“Perhaps he wanted to throw the blame on someone else.”

“Then why choose someone like Ascanio, who could so easily prove
an alibi? No, Hastings, there is something here that we do not
understand. Something very deep and very clever.”

“What are you going to do now?”

“I am going to have a little talk with my friend Japp. And then—well,
then we shall see.”

The next morning Poirot was early astir. He spent some time at the
telephone, and then announced that he was going out.

“I have some business to attend to,” he said. “I may be late for
lunch.”

He did not return until nearly three o'clock. He looked tired but
triumphant.

“Well?” I asked. “Have you found out anything?”

“Everything, my friend. The case is complete.”

“Who is the murderer?”

“I will tell you that presently. First I must see Dr. Hawker.”

“Dr. Hawker? What has he to do with it?”

“More than you think, Hastings. Much more than you think.”

We found the doctor in his surgery. He seemed a good deal
surprised to see us.

“Hullo, Poirot! What’s the news? Found the murderer yet?”

“I believe so, doctor. But I want your help.”

“My help? Anything I can do, of course. What is it?”

“I want you to tell me exactly what happened on the night of the
murder. From the moment Miss Rider came into the room.”

“But I’ve told you all that already.”

“I know. But I want you to tell me again. Every little detail.”

The doctor looked a bit puzzled, but he did as he was asked. He
described the arrival of Miss Rider, the telephone message, the
drive to Regent’s Court, the discovery of the body.

“And you’re quite sure about the time?”

“Oh, yes. It was just about a quarter to nine when the telephone
rang.”

“And you went straight to the flat?”

“Yes. We got there about nine o’clock.”

“And the body was still warm?”

“Yes. He couldn’t have been dead more than ten or fifteen minutes.”

“I see. And you’re sure he died from the blow on the head?”

“Oh, yes. There was no doubt about that.”

“Thank you, doctor. That’s all I wanted to know.”

As we left the surgery, Poirot turned to me.

“You see, Hastings? It is all very clear now.”

“It may be clear to you,” I said, “but it’s as dark as night to
me. Who is the murderer?”

“Wait a little, my friend. All will be revealed in good time.
Tonight I have invited a few friends to our rooms. Dr. Hawker,
Miss Rider, Mr. Graves, and Signor Ascanio. We shall then have the
pleasure of hearing the truth.”

I was full of excitement as the evening approached. What was the
truth? Who was the murderer? And how had Poirot found out?

At eight o’clock our guests arrived. Dr. Hawker and Miss Rider
came first, then Graves, and finally Signor Ascanio. They all
seemed a little nervous and uneasy.

Poirot was in his element. He beamed upon them all, and made them
as comfortable as possible. Then, when everyone was settled, he
began to speak.

first it seemed simple enough—a straightforward case of murder.
