And who would that be? The murderer, of course.

“Graves killed his master at about eight o’clock, just after the
dinner had been served. He then ate a little of the dinner himself—to
make it look as though three people had dined there. He drank the
coffee—which he made very black to hide the fact that there were
only two cups used instead of three. He left the rice soufflé
almost untouched, because he didn’t like it. And then he went out,
leaving the window open to make it look as though the murderers
had escaped that way.

“But he had forgotten one thing. He had forgotten that he had been
seen. Miss Rider had seen him. She had come to the house to see
the doctor, and she had seen Graves leaving the flat at about
half-past eight.

“And so, to protect himself, he had to involve her in his plot. He
telephoned her, pretending to be the Count, and told her that he
had been attacked. He knew that she would tell the doctor, and
that the doctor would come to the flat and find the body. And he
knew that the time of the message would be taken as the time of the
murder.

“It was a very clever plot, Graves. But you made one mistake. You
forgot that Hercule Poirot has eyes that see everything. You
forgot that I would notice the little things—the black coffee,
the rice soufflé, the open window. And you forgot that I would
check your story about the music hall.

“And now, Graves, I think the game is up. The police are waiting
for you outside.”

As Poirot finished speaking, Graves made a sudden dash for the
door. But he was too late. Two burly constables were there to
intercept him.

“Well done, Poirot!” cried Dr. Hawker. “I never would have
guessed it. A most ingenious plot.”

“It was indeed,” said Poirot, with a modest smile. “But as I
always say, it is the little things that count. The little things
are everything.”

Signor Ascanio came forward and shook Poirot by the hand.

“I cannot thank you enough, Monsieur Poirot. You have saved my
reputation and perhaps my life. I shall never forget what you
have done for me.”

“It was a pleasure, Signor,” said Poirot. “And now, Hastings, I
think we might have a little supper. All this talk of food has
made me quite hungry.”

A few days later, Inspector Japp dropped in to see us, looking
decidedly crestfallen. He flung his hat onto the table and
sank into a chair. “This Foscatini business is a wash-out,”
he grumbled. “The Italian Embassy has intervened. It turns
out that Signor Ascanio is a personage of considerable
importance—a sort of unofficial diplomatic agent. And what is
more, he has an alibi that is absolutely cast-iron. At 8:47,
the very moment the Count was telephoning for help, Ascanio
was at a formal reception at the Embassy, surrounded by
witnesses who can swear to his presence there since eight
o’clock.”

The morning after the arrest, Poirot received a visit from
Inspector Japp. The latter was looking somewhat crestfallen.

“I’m afraid we’ve got to let that fellow Ascanio go,” he said
disconsolately. “He’s got an alibi for the evening of the murder.”

“Is that so?” asked Poirot.

“Yes. He was at the Italian Embassy from half-past eight till
nearly eleven o’clock. He’s a big man in his own country, it
seems, and his story is that he came over here on some private
mission of a very delicate nature.”

“And the murder?”

“Well, his story is that he was at the Embassy when the murder took
place. That seems to be an undisputed fact. There was a reception
there that night, and dozens of people must have seen him.”

“How about the morning visit?”

“There he sticks to his guns. He says he never saw the Count in
his life, and never was at Regent’s Court. He’s a very clever fellow.”

“But Graves says he was there?”

“Graves’s story is a bit thin. He may have been mistaken in the
man. He only saw him for a minute or two, remember.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And so we are just where we were.”

“Not quite. There’s the younger man. We’re doing our best to get
on his track. He may have been the actual murderer, and Ascanio
the instigator.”

“But Ascanio says he doesn’t know the Count?”

“Of course he says that. He would. But Graves is positive.”

“Is he?” asked Poirot. “I don’t think he is.”

“What do you mean?”

“Just this. That Graves is lying.”

“Lying? What for?”

“That is what we have to find out. But there is one thing that I
am sure of—that Ascanio never was at Regent’s Court that morning,
nor that evening either.”

Japp stared.

“How do you know that?”

“The coffee, my friend—the very black coffee.”

I saw that Japp was as much at sea as I was.

“And the rice soufflé,” added Poirot. “You should have looked at
it, Japp. It was a most interesting dish.”

“Well,” said Japp, “I’ll admit that I didn’t think much of it. I’m
afraid I’m not as observant as you are, Poirot.”

“It is not a question of observation. It is a question of
deduction. The coffee and the rice soufflé tell us quite a lot.”

“What do they tell you?”

“They tell me that the dinner was not what it seemed. Let us go
back to the beginning. Count Foscatini is a man of method. He
orders his dinner for three. Three people sit down to it. But did
three people eat it? I think not.”

“You mean that only two people dined?”

“On the contrary, I mean that only one person dined.”

“One person? But there were three plates—three coffee-cups—three
half-empty glasses of port!”

“Exactly. But did you notice the _quantities_? There was the rice
soufflé, for instance. A fair amount was left. Now, if three people
had been dining, would they have left any of that soufflé? It is
a light dish, and very popular. But if only one person had been
eating it, he would probably have had enough by the time he came
to the last course.”

“But the coffee-cups?”

“They were all used, it is true. But only one man had taken milk.
That is a very significant fact. And then there were the cigars
and cigarettes. One man smoked a cigar, and the other two
cigarettes. That is a very common arrangement when three men are
dining together. But it is also a very common arrangement when
_one_ man is trying to make it appear that three men have been
dining together.”

“But the waiter said that three people had dined?”

“No, the waiter only said that he had sent down dinner for three.
He did not see who ate it.”

“Then you think that Count Foscatini was alone?”

“I am sure of it. And I am also sure that he was dead long before
eight o’clock.”

“Dead? But he telephoned at 8.47!”

“Ah, did he? That is the question. Someone telephoned. Someone
who called himself Count Foscatini. But was it the Count?”

“But Miss Rider recognized his voice?”

“Miss Rider had only heard the Count’s voice once before, and then
it was over the telephone. It is not difficult to imitate a voice
over the telephone, especially if you have a good deal of the
same accent.”

“But why should anyone want to make it appear that the Count was
alive at 8.47 when he was really dead?”

“Because that gave the murderer an alibi. If the Count was alive
at 8.47, then the people who were with him at dinner could not
have killed him, because they were seen to leave the flat at 8.30.”

“But who was the murderer?”

“That is what we have to find out. But I think we shall find that
he is someone who had a very good reason for wanting to get rid
of Count Foscatini, and also someone who knew all about the
Count’s arrangements for the evening.”

“You mean Graves?”

“Graves is a possibility. But there is someone else. Someone who
was in the flat that evening, and who had a very good reason for
wanting it to appear that the Count was alive at 8.47.”

“Who do you mean?”

“I mean the person who telephoned to Dr. Hawker.”

“Miss Rider?”

“Yes, Miss Rider. She was the one who received the telephone
message. She was the one who told us what the Count said. And she
was the one who had the best opportunity of imitating the Count’s
voice.”

“But why should she want to kill him?”

“That is what we have to find out. But I think we shall find that
there was some connection between her and the Count that we know
nothing about.”

“But what about the blow on the head? She couldn’t have done that.”

“Why not? She is a strong woman. And the statuette was not very
heavy. A sudden blow from behind would have been quite enough.”

“But why should she go to your place and tell you about it?”

“Because that was the best way of diverting suspicion from herself.
She knew that if she were the one to discover the murder, she
would be the first person to be suspected. But if she could make
it appear that she was only a messenger, then she would be safe.”

“It’s a clever theory, Poirot, but have you any proof?”

“Not yet. But I think we shall find it. In the meantime, I suggest
that we pay a visit to Dr. Hawker’s house. I should like to have
a little talk with Miss Rider.”

We found Miss Rider at home. She seemed a little surprised to see
us, but she showed us into the doctor’s consulting-room.

“I am sorry the doctor is out,” she said. “He has gone to see a
patient.”

“It is not the doctor I want to see,” said Poirot. “It is you,
Mademoiselle.”

Miss Rider looked surprised.

“Me? What can you want with me?”

“I want to ask you a few questions about the telephone message
you received the night of the murder.”

Miss Rider’s face turned pale.

“I—I have told you all I know,” she stammered.

“Have you?” asked Poirot. “I think not. I think there is something
you have forgotten to tell us.”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean the rice soufflé, Mademoiselle. The rice soufflé that was
eaten by only one person.”

Miss Rider stared at him.

“I don’t know what you’re talking about,” she said.

“I think you do. I think you know very well that Count Foscatini
was dead long before eight o’clock that night. And I think you
know who killed him.”

Miss Rider’s face was now ashen.

“I—I don’t know anything,” she gasped.

“Then why are you so frightened?” asked Poirot. “If you have
nothing to hide, why should you be afraid?”

Miss Rider did not answer. She sank into a chair and covered her
face with her hands.

“Come, Mademoiselle,” said Poirot kindly. “It will be better for
you if you tell us the truth. We know that you were at Regent’s
Court that evening. We know that you were the one who telephoned
to Dr. Hawker. And we know why you did it.”

Miss Rider looked up. There was a look of defiance in her eyes.

“You know nothing,” she said. “You are only guessing.”

“Perhaps,” said Poirot. “But I think my guesses are very near the
truth. Shall I tell you what I think happened?”

Miss Rider did not answer.

“I think,” said Poirot, “that you were in love with Count Foscatini.
I think that you had been seeing him secretly for some time. And
I think that on the night of the murder you went to see him, and
found him with someone else.”

Miss Rider gave a cry.

“It’s not true!” she cried. “It’s not true!”

“Is it not? Then perhaps you will tell us what is true.”

Miss Rider was silent for a moment. Then she began to speak in a
low, hurried voice.

“It’s true that I knew the Count. I’d known him for months. We
met by accident, and—and we fell in love. But he was afraid of his
family. He said they would never consent to his marrying a
commoner. So we had to keep it secret.”

“And on the night of the murder?”

“I went to see him. I had a key to the flat. He’d given it to me
so that I could come and go as I liked. When I got there, I found
him at dinner. He was alone. He seemed glad to see me, but he was
worried about something. He said he was expecting some men to
come and see him, and he wanted me to go.”

“And did you go?”

“No. I—I was jealous. I thought he was seeing another woman. I
stayed and we had a quarrel. And then—and then——”

She broke down and began to sob.

“And then you killed him?” asked Poirot.

“No! No! I didn’t kill him! I swear I didn’t! I was angry, and I
picked up that statuette and hit him with it. But I didn’t mean
to kill him! It was an accident! I didn’t know he was dead until
I saw the blood.”

“And then?”

“I was terrified. I didn’t know what to do. I knew that if the
police found me there, they’d think I’d murdered him. So I tried
to make it look as if someone else had done it. I knew he was
expecting those men, so I thought I’d make it look as if they’d
killed him. I set the table for three, and I ate some of the
dinner myself to make it look as if three people had been there.
And then I went back to the doctor’s and telephoned from there,
pretending to be the Count.”

“And the voice?”

“I’d heard him speak so often. It wasn’t hard to imitate him. And
I knew that if I told the doctor he was dying, he’d come at once
and bring you with him. And I thought that if you were there, no
one would suspect me.”

“It was a clever plan,” said Poirot. “But you forgot one thing.”

“What was that?”

“The rice soufflé, Mademoiselle. You should have eaten all of it.
If you had, I might never have suspected the truth.”

Miss Rider bowed her head.

“I suppose you’re right,” she whispered. “I—I didn’t think of that.”

“And now,” said Poirot, “I think you had better come with us to
the police station. It will be better for you to tell them the
truth yourself.”

Miss Rider rose slowly to her feet. She looked like a woman who
had suddenly grown old.

“I’ll come,” she said. “It doesn’t matter now. Nothing matters
any more.”

As we led her away, I looked at Poirot.

“You’re a marvel, Poirot,” I said. “I don’t know how you do it.”

Poirot smiled.

“It is very simple, my friend. One has only to use the little grey
cells. And to remember that even the cleverest criminal always
makes one little mistake.”

Ascanio, however, was not sent for trial. No less a personage than
the Italian Ambassador himself came forward and testified at the
police-court proceedings that Ascanio had been with him at the
Embassy from eight till nine that evening. The prisoner was
discharged. Naturally, a lot of people thought that the crime was
a political one, and was being deliberately hushed up.

I was not surprised when Inspector Japp dropped in one evening to
discuss the case. He looked somewhat disgruntled, as was his wont
when a "straightforward" case turned out to be nothing of the sort.

"It's a teaser, Mr. Poirot," he confessed, pulling at his pipe.
"That Italian fellow Ascanio is out of it—the Ambassador’s word is
good enough for any court. And yet, who else is there? The valet,
Graves, seems honest enough, and his alibi for the music hall
checks out. We’ve found the second man, by the way—a young hothead
named Count d'Arpazio—but he was at a bridge party in Chelsea all
evening. It leaves us with a dead man who telephoned for help
while he was being murdered, and no one to have done the deed."

“A political crime?” said Poirot. “What do you think, Hastings?”

“Well, it looks like it, doesn’t it?” I suggested.

“You have no better explanation? It does not occur to you that
it’s all a little too simple?”

“Simple? I should have called it just the opposite.”

“In some ways, my friend, you are right. But there are certain
points that do not please me. The telephone, for instance. Why did
the murderer leave it? And why did the Count not cry for help?
Then there is the coffee, and the rice soufflé. It is all very
puzzling.”

“It’s a complete mystery to me,” I confessed.

“Not a complete one, Hastings. There are certain things we know.
We know, for instance, that the Count was a man of method. We know
that he was an Italian. We know that he spoke English perfectly.
And we know that he was murdered.”

“We know all that, certainly,” I agreed.

“Then let us see what else we know. We know that he had two guests
to dinner. We know that they were Italians. We know that they had
some business with the Count. We know that they arrived at eight
o’clock. We know that Graves went out at half-past eight. We know
that the murder was committed at 8.47. And we know that Ascanio
has an alibi.”

“Which means that he couldn’t have done it.”

“Does it, Hastings? Does it? That is just what I am not so sure
about.”

I stared at him in amazement.

“But the Ambassador——”

“Exactly. The Ambassador. A most important witness. And yet—I
wonder. Let us go and see Graves.”

We found Graves at the flat in Regent’s Court. He was busy packing
up the Count’s effects. He seemed surprised to see us, but was
quite ready to talk.

“Yes, sir, it’s a sad business. A very sad business. The Count was
a good master, sir.”

“You are leaving, I suppose?” said Poirot.

“Yes, sir. I’ve got another place. With a gentleman in the City.
A Mr. Smith.”

“A very good name,” said Poirot. “And now, Graves, I want to ask
you a few questions. About the dinner that night. You said the
guests were Italians?”

“Yes, sir. At least, I took them to be so. They spoke a foreign
language to one another.”

“Did they speak Italian to the Count?”

“I couldn’t say, sir. They spoke English while I was in the room.”

“And the Count? Did he speak Italian to them?”

“No, sir. He always spoke English.”

“Even when they were alone?”

“I don’t know, sir. I didn’t hear them.”

“But you listened at the door the morning before?”

“Yes, sir; but they were speaking very low.”

“I see. Now, about the coffee. You brought it in, you say?”

“Yes, sir.”

“How did you bring it?”

“On a tray, sir. Three cups.”

“And you set them down on the table?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Did you notice if anyone took sugar?”

“I don’t think so, sir. I didn’t notice.”

“And the Count? Did he take sugar?”

“Yes, sir. He always took two lumps.”

“And did he take it that night?”

“I—I really couldn’t say, sir.”

“Think, Graves. It is important.”

The man thought for a moment.

“I believe he did, sir. Yes, I’m almost sure he did.”

“Ah! And the other two? Did they take sugar?”

“I don’t know, sir. I didn’t notice.”

“Well, it doesn’t matter. Now, one more thing. About the rice
soufflé. You say there was a good deal of it left?”

“Yes, sir. About half, I should say.”

“And the Count? Did he have some?”

“Yes, sir. He had a helping.”

“And the others?”

“They had some too, sir.”

“I see. Well, that’s all, Graves. Thank you.”

As we went out, Poirot turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of it?”

“I don’t see that we’ve learnt much,” I said.

“No? And yet Graves has told us a very important thing.”

“What was that?”

“He has told us that the Count took sugar in his coffee.”

“Well, what of it?”

“My dear Hastings, do you not see? If the Count took sugar in his
coffee, why was there no sugar in the cup from which he had been
drinking?”

“How do you know there wasn’t?”

“Because I tasted the remains of the coffee in the three cups. Two
of them were sweetened, but the third—the one from which the Count
had been drinking—was not.”

“Then—then it wasn’t the Count who drank it?”

“Exactly, Hastings. It was not the Count.”

“Then who was it?”

“That is what we have to find out. But I think I can guess. Come,
let us go and see Dr. Hawker.”

We found the doctor in his surgery. He was delighted to see us.

“Well, Poirot, any news? Found the murderer yet?”

“I think so,” said Poirot.

“You don’t mean it! Who is it?”

“Before I tell you that, I want to ask you a question. About that
telephone call. You say it was Miss Rider who answered it?”

“Yes.”

“And she told you that a voice said, ‘Help. They’ve killed me’?
And then ‘Foscatini—Regent’s Court’?”

“That’s right.”

“And you are sure she said ‘they’?”

“Yes. I remember it distinctly.”

“‘They.’ Not ‘he’?”

“No. ‘They.’”

“Ah! That is very interesting. Very interesting indeed.”

“Why? What does it mean?”

“It means, my friend, that the Count was not alone when he was
murdered. There were two of them.”

“But we knew that. Ascanio and the other man.”

“Yes, we knew that. But I am not thinking of Ascanio and the other
man.”

“Then who are you thinking of?”

“I am thinking of the two people who were in the flat when the
murder was committed.”

“But there was only the Count.”

“Was there, Hastings? Was there? I wonder.”

“But Graves said——”

“Yes, Graves said. But what did Graves say? He said he went out
at 8.30. He said the two guests were there then. He said he went
to the music-hall. But did he? That is what we have to find out.”

“You suspect Graves?”

“I suspect everyone, Hastings. Even you!”

“Me?” I cried.

“Yes, even you. But in this case I think we can narrow it down.
There were two people in that flat. One was the Count. Who was the
other?”

“The murderer, of course.”

“Yes, the murderer. But who was the murderer? Was it one of the
guests? Or was it someone else? Someone who was already in the
flat?”

“You mean Graves?”

“Perhaps. But there is someone else. Someone who had access to the
flat. Someone who knew the Count’s habits. Someone who knew that
he was an orderly man. Someone who knew that he took sugar in his
coffee.”

“But who?”

“Think, Hastings. Who else was there?”

“The manager? The lift-man?”

“No, no. Someone else. Someone we have seen. Someone we have
talked to.”

“Not—not Dr. Hawker?”

“No, not Dr. Hawker. Though he is a very good friend of ours.”

“Then who?”

“Think, Hastings. Who was it who first told us about the murder?”

“Miss Rider?”

“Exactly. Miss Rider.”

“Miss Rider! But she wasn’t even there!”

“Wasn’t she, Hastings? Are you sure?”

“But she was here, with us!”

“Was she? Let us think. She came into the room. She was very
agitated. She told us about the telephone call. But did she really
receive a telephone call? Or did she only say she did?”

“But why should she lie about it?”

“That is what we have to find out. But let us suppose for a moment
that she did lie. Let us suppose that there was no telephone call.
What then?”

“Then—then the whole thing was a plant!”

“Exactly. A plant. But why? To give someone an alibi? To make it
seem as though the murder had been committed at a certain time?”

“But the clock! The clock stopped at 8.47!”

“Yes, the clock. A very convenient clock, Hastings. A clock that
could be stopped at any time. And the telephone. A telephone that
could be used to tell a story. A story of a dying man’s last words.”

“But the Count! He was dead!”

“Yes, he was dead. But when did he die? That is the question. Did
he die at 8.47? Or did he die earlier? Much earlier?”

“But Graves said——”

“Yes, Graves. We must not forget Graves. What if Graves and Miss
Rider were in it together?”

“But why? What motive could they have?”

“Money, Hastings. Money. The Count was a rich man. And Graves was
his servant. Perhaps he knew where the Count kept his money. Or
perhaps he was being paid by someone else. Someone who wanted the
Count out of the way.”

“But who?”

“That is what we are going to find out. Come, let us go back to the
flat.”

When we arrived at Regent’s Court, we found the door of Flat II
open. We went in. The flat was empty. Graves was gone.

“Aha!” said Poirot. “The bird has flown. But he has left something
behind him.”

He went to the writing-table and picked up a small piece of paper.
On it was written a name and an address.

“Mr. Smith, 14, Bishop’s Gate.”

“The new master!” I cried.

“Perhaps, Hastings. Perhaps. Let us go and see Mr. Smith.”

We took a taxi to Bishop’s Gate. No. 14 was a large, gloomy-looking
office building. We went in and asked for Mr. Smith.

“Mr. Smith?” said the clerk. “Which Mr. Smith? We have several.”

“The one who has just engaged a new valet. A man named Graves.”

“Oh, you mean Mr. Samuel Smith. His office is on the third floor.
Room 302.”

We went up to the third floor. Room 302 was at the end of a long
corridor. Poirot knocked on the door. A voice told us to come in.

We entered a small, poorly furnished office. Behind a desk sat a
middle-aged man with a sharp, shrewd face. He looked up as we
entered.

“Well, gentlemen, what can I do for you?”

“Are you Mr. Samuel Smith?” asked Poirot.

“I am.”

“And have you just engaged a new valet named Graves?”

“I have. Why? Is there anything wrong?”

“We are not sure yet,” said Poirot. “We would like to speak to him,
if we may.”

“I’m afraid he’s not here. He doesn’t start until tomorrow.”

“I see. And where is he now?”

“I haven’t the slightest idea. I suppose he’s at his old place,
packing up.”

“We have just come from there,” said Poirot. “He has already left.”

“In that case, I don’t know where he is. Is there anything else?”

“Yes,” said Poirot. “I would like to ask you a few questions. About
your connection with the late Count Foscatini.”

The man’s face changed. He looked suddenly guarded.

“I had no connection with him. I never heard of him until I read
about his death in the papers.”

“Indeed? That is very interesting. Especially as Graves seems to
think you were his friend.”

“Graves is mistaken. I never met the man in my life.”

“I see. Well, thank you, Mr. Smith. We won’t take up any more of
your time.”

As we went out, Poirot was smiling.

“Well, Hastings, what do you make of Mr. Samuel Smith?”

“He’s a liar,” I said. “He knew the Count, all right.”

“I agree with you. He is a very accomplished liar. But he is not the
murderer.”

“Then who is?”

“I think I know, Hastings. But I must be sure. I must be quite
sure. Let us go back to our rooms. I have a little experiment to
perform.”

When we got back to our rooms, Poirot went straight to the
telephone. He called a number and spoke for a few minutes in a low
voice. Then he hung up and turned to me.

“It is as I thought, Hastings. The pieces are beginning to fit
together.”

“What is it? What have you found out?”

“I have found out that Signor Ascanio is not the only person with
an alibi.”

“Who else has one?”

“Dr. Hawker.”

“Dr. Hawker! But we were with him!”

“Exactly. We were with him from half-past eight until we went to the
flat. And the murder was committed at 8.47. So he couldn’t have
done it.”

“Of course he couldn’t! I never thought he did!”

“No, but it is always well to be sure. And now, there is only one
person left.”

“Who?”

“Miss Rider.”

“Miss Rider! But I told you, she was with us too!”

“Was she, Hastings? Think. When did she arrive?”

“At about a quarter to nine.”

“Exactly. At about a quarter to nine. And the murder was committed
at 8.47. She could have committed the murder and then come
straight to our rooms.”

“But the flat is several streets away! She couldn’t have got here in
time!”

“Perhaps not. But what if the murder wasn't committed at 8.47? What
if it was committed earlier? Much earlier?”

“But the clock! And the telephone call!”

“Yes, the clock and the telephone call. Both of them part of a very
clever plan. A plan to make it seem as though the murder was
committed while she was with us.”

“But why would she do it? What motive could she have?”

“That is what we are going to find out. Come, let us go and see Miss
Rider.”

We found Miss Rider at Dr. Hawker’s house. She seemed surprised to
see us, but she showed us into the doctor’s study.

“The doctor is out,” she said. “Is there anything I can do for you?”

“Yes, Miss Rider,” said Poirot. “You can tell us the truth.”

The woman’s face turned pale.

“The truth? I don’t know what you mean.”

“I think you do. I think you know very well. I think you know that
there was no telephone call from Count Foscatini.”

“But there was! I swear there was!”

“No, Miss Rider. There was no telephone call. You made it all up.
You made it up to give yourself an alibi. To make it seem as though
the Count was still alive at 8.45.”

“That’s not true! Why would I do such a thing?”

“To cover up the fact that you had already killed him.”

“Me? Kill the Count? Why should I?”

“For money, Miss Rider. For the money he was keeping in his flat.
The money that you and Graves were going to steal.”

“It’s a lie! A wicked lie!”

“Is it? Then perhaps you can explain why there was no sugar in the
Count’s coffee-cup? The Count always took sugar, Miss Rider.
Always. But the cup from which he had been drinking was
unsweetened. Why was that?”

“I—I don’t know! I wasn’t there!”

“Yes, you were there. You were there when the Count was having his
dinner. You and Graves. You killed him, and then you set the stage.
You stopped the clock, you made up the story about the telephone
call, and you came to us to provide yourselves with an alibi.”

The woman was trembling now. Her face was ashen.

“It wasn’t me! It was Graves! He made me do it!”

“Aha!” said Poirot. “So I was right. It was a joint effort.”

“He said it would be easy! He said the Count was a miser, and that
he had thousands of pounds hidden in the flat! He said no one
would ever know!”

“But someone did know, Miss Rider. Someone did know.”

At that moment, the door opened and Dr. Hawker walked in. He looked
from one to the other in amazement.

“What’s going on here? Poirot? Miss Rider? What is it?”

“It is the end of a very clever plot, doctor,” said Poirot. “A plot
to murder Count Foscatini and steal his money.”

“Murder? Miss Rider? You don’t mean to say——”

“I’m afraid so, doctor. Miss Rider and Graves were the culprits.”

The doctor sank into a chair. He looked as though he had been
turned to stone.

“I can’t believe it,” he whispered. “I simply can’t believe it.”

“It is hard to believe, I know,” said Poirot. “But the evidence is
quite clear. The coffee-cup, the clock, the telephone call—they all
point to the same conclusion.”

“But what about Ascanio? And the Ambassador?”

“Ascanio was a convenient scapegoat. He had been to see the Count,
and he had been seen by the lift-man. It was easy to throw the
suspicion on him. But his alibi was too strong. Even for a clever
pair like Miss Rider and Graves.”

“And the money? Did they find it?”

“No, doctor. They didn’t. Because there was no money. The Count
was not a miser. He was a very wealthy man, but he kept his money
in the bank. Not in his flat.”

“So they killed him for nothing?”

“For nothing, doctor. For absolutely nothing.”

Poirot turned to Miss Rider.

“And now, Miss Rider, I think you had better come with us. The
police will be very interested in what you have to tell them.”

The woman didn't resist. She seemed to have collapsed completely.
As we led her out, I looked at Poirot.

“You are a marvel, Poirot. A positive marvel.”

“No, Hastings. I am only a man who uses his grey cells. And who
remembers that a man who takes sugar in his coffee will always
take sugar in his coffee. Even when he is about to be murdered!”
