Poirot was not at all surprised at the turn of events. He sat in his
armchair, his eyes closed, and a faint smile playing on his lips.
“It was to be expected,” he murmured. “The alibi of Signor Ascanio
is exactly what I anticipated. It was a diplomatic necessity,
perhaps, but it also happens to be the truth. He was not at
Regent’s Court at the time of the murder. But that does not mean
the case is closed, Hastings. On the contrary, it is only just
beginning.”

Poirot was not satisfied. He shook his head over the newspaper report and paced the room with restless steps. “It is not clear, Hastings,” he murmured. “The Ambassador’s word, it is final. Ascanio was at the Embassy from eight till nine. But the dinner? The three coffee cups? The plates? Someone ate that dinner, but was it three men? I think not. I wish to see this Monsieur Graves once more. There is something in his story that does not ring true—or rather, there is something in the dinner that rings *too* true!”

The discharge of Signor Ascanio was a blow to the official police, but Poirot received the news with a strange lack of surprise. He sat for a long time in his favorite chair, his eyes closed, his fingers joined at the tips.

“It is as I thought,” he murmured. “The alibi, it is solid. And if Ascanio was at the Embassy, he was not at Regent’s Court. Yet the dinner was eaten—or so it appeared. Let us reconsider those three plates, Hastings. Three people are supposed to have dined, yet only one man—a man of very large appetite—could have consumed what was sent down from the kitchen. And even he, you will observe, was forced to leave the rice soufflé!”

Poirot had taken a keen interest in all these points. Nevertheless,
I was somewhat surprised when he suddenly informed me one morning
that he was expecting a visitor at eleven o’clock, and that that
visitor was none other than Ascanio himself.

“He wishes to consult you?”

“_Du tout_, Hastings. I wish to consult him.”

“What about?”

“The Regent’s Court murder.”

“You are going to prove that he did it?”

“A man cannot be tried twice for murder, Hastings. Endeavour to
have the common sense. Ah, that is our friend’s ring.”

A few minutes later Signor Ascanio was ushered in—a small, thin
man with a secretive and furtive glance in his eyes. He remained
standing, darting suspicious glances from one to the other of us.

“Monsieur Poirot?”

My little friend tapped himself gently on the chest.

The little Italian took a seat and looked at Poirot with a wary eye. “You sent for me, Monsieur? I do not understand why. The law has finished with me.” Poirot leaned forward, his eyes shining with a sudden green light. “The law, yes. But the truth, not yet. You were at the Embassy at eight o’clock on the night of the murder. That is true. But it is also true that you visited Count Foscatini the morning before. You went there to recover certain documents—documents that involved a high personage in your country. Foscatini was a blackmailer of the worst type, was he not?” Ascanio started, his hands trembling. “How do you know this?” he gasped.

“I have come at your request, Monsieur Poirot,” said Ascanio in a low, cautious voice, “but I do not know what you can possibly have to say to me. The matter is closed. My alibi is beyond dispute.” Poirot leaned forward, his eyes shining with that peculiar green light. “Precisely, Signor Ascanio. It is because your alibi is so excellent that I know you were not at Regent’s Court at eight o’clock that evening. And if you were not there, then no one was there—except the Count and his killer. You did visit him the morning before, did you not? To discuss certain... documents? Documents that the Italian Government was anxious to recover from a man who was, shall we say, a high-class blackmailer?” Ascanio started, his face turning a pasty grey. “How do you know that?” he whispered.

“I have been cleared by the authorities, Monsieur Poirot,” Ascanio
began in a low, guarded voice. “The word of my Ambassador is
final. I do not see what further business you can have with me.”

Poirot smiled agreeably. “It is not of your whereabouts on the
night of the murder that I wish to speak, Signor Ascanio. I know
quite well that you were at the Embassy. It is of your visit on the
_previous_ morning that I am curious. You were there to recover
certain documents, were you not? Documents that the so-called
Count Foscatini was using for the purpose of blackmail?”

Ascanio started, his face turning a sickly grey. “How did you know
that?”

“I guessed it,” said Poirot. “Foscatini was no Count. He was a
scoundrel, a man of many aliases. You went there to buy back the
papers. He invited you to dinner to conclude the bargain. But you
did not go to that dinner, Signor Ascanio. You thought better of
it, and went to your Embassy to seek official protection instead.”

“I have invited you here, Signor Ascanio,” began Poirot, “because I am of the opinion that you have not been entirely frank with the police. You did visit Count Foscatini on that Tuesday morning, and you were to dine with him that night. Is it not so?”

Ascanio’s face went a shade paler, his eyes darting toward the door. “I have said all I have to say to the authorities,” he muttered in a low, vibrating voice. “The word of my Ambassador was sufficient. I was not at Regent’s Court at the hour of the crime.”

“I do not dispute it,” said Poirot calmly. “But you were there in the morning. Why lie about it? Unless, of course, the business you discussed was of such a nature that even a hint of it would be ruinous. You came to buy certain papers, did you not? Papers that the Count, a man of—shall we say—irregular political involvements, had in his possession.”

“I am at your service, Monsieur,” said the Italian, his voice low and cautious. “But I have nothing to say. The police, they have questioned me, and they have been satisfied. My alibi, it was complete. From eight o’clock until nine I was with my distinguished countryman, the Ambassador. It is a matter of record.”

“I do not doubt it for a moment,” replied Poirot, waving him to a chair with an air of grandeur. “It is not the time of the murder that interests me so much as the menu of the dinner. Tell me, Monsieur Ascanio, do you like the rice soufflé?”

“Be seated, signor. You received my note. I am determined to get
to the bottom of this mystery. In some small measure you can aid
me. Let us commence. You—in company with a friend—visited the late
Count Foscatini on the morning of Tuesday the 9th——”

The Italian made an angry gesture.

“I did nothing of the sort. I have sworn in court——”

“_Précisément_—and I have a little idea that you have sworn
falsely.”

“You threaten me? Bah! I have nothing to fear from you. I have been
acquitted.”

“_Précisément_,” said Poirot, “and I have a little idea that you have
sworn falsely. It is not the police you have to fear, signor. It is
the truth. On Tuesday morning, you went to that flat to recover
certain papers—at a price. You paid that price. You were not there
at dinner. The dinner for three was a farce—a comedy played for the
benefit of the lift-man and the service-phone. There was only one
man at that table—the man who ate as much as he could and then
found himself unable to finish the rice soufflé!”

“True. But there is a point. I have evidence that you were at the
Count’s flat on the Tuesday morning. My friend, the valet-butler,
testified to it. Now, you will tell me what passed at that
interview.”

The Italian laughed.

“His word against mine, eh? Why should I tell you?”

Poirot leant forward.

“Because I know—already.”

“_Davvero?_”

“Shall I tell you?”

The Italian made a contemptuous gesture.

“Proceed, then.”

“You were there to negotiate a—what shall we say?—an exchange of
certain documents. Is that not so? They were—how do you say
it?—compromising documents. You and your friend represented—shall
we say—the Italian Government? And the Count—he was a blackmailer.
He had stolen those papers and he was holding them at a very high
price. Is it not so?”

The Italian’s face was a study.

“How do you know this?” he asked.

“Because I am Hercule Poirot. And you had no intention of paying
that price. You intended to recover those papers by—other means.
On Tuesday morning you were there to make a final offer. It was
refused. You were told to come to dinner on Wednesday. You came
accordingly. Is that not so?”

Ascanio hesitated.

“I was not there on Wednesday evening,” he said at last. “I was
at the Embassy. You have the Ambassador’s word for it.”

Poirot smiled.

“The Ambassador is a very great man. He would do much for his
country—even to the extent of—shall we say—stretching a point or
two in his evidence? It was a political matter, was it not? The
honour of a great family was involved?”

Ascanio rose.

“I have nothing to say to you. Your talk is all of moonshine. I
wish you good day.”

And he walked out of the room.

“True, but there is always the risk of a third person. I am a very
particular man, signor. I have a habit of looking at a problem
from all sides. Now, I will put it to you what I think really
happened. In the first place, you _did_ visit Count Foscatini on the
morning of the 9th. In the second, you _did not_ visit him on the
night of the 10th.”

Ascanio’s jaw dropped.

“How do you know that?”

“The coffee-cups, for one thing—the rice soufflé for another. The
Count was alone when he died. It was he who ate the dinner for
three.”

Ascanio looked at him.

“I was at the Embassy,” he muttered. “The Ambassador himself swore
to it.”

“I am aware of it. That is why I knew you were not at the flat at
eight o’clock. But you were there on Tuesday morning, was it not
so?”

Ascanio nodded.

“The Count was a blackmailer, a spy, and a scoundrel. I was
commissioned by my Government to buy from him certain documents
stolen from our Embassy. It was a matter of fifty thousand lire.
I gave him the money, and he gave me a large envelope which he said
contained the papers. I did not open it at the time, but when I
got back to the hotel I found only blank sheets of paper. I went
back to his flat in a fury. The valet said he was out. I called
again on Wednesday morning, but with no better success. That
evening I had to go to the Embassy on business. The Ambassador
kept me there until nine o’clock. Next morning I heard of the
murder. I was terrified. If I told the truth, the whole story of
the stolen documents would come out. So I denied everything.”

“One thing more,” said Poirot. “The young man who was with you
on Tuesday morning?”

“My secretary. He had nothing to do with it.”

“I see. Well, signor, I wish you a very good morning.”

“What is the meaning of all this?” I asked, when the door had
closed behind the Italian. “If Ascanio didn’t do it, who did?”

“_Ma foi_, Hastings! You are of a simple nature. You believe
everything you are told. Now, I—I look for the little things that
are not right.”

“And what were they?”

“The dinner, Hastings—the dinner! Three people sit down to dinner.
One of them is a Count. He is a man of the world, a man of
aristocratic tastes. He orders a good dinner. And what do we find?
A dinner for three—and only one of those people exists! The other
two are myths! The Count dined alone. Then why did he order dinner
for three? To suggest that he had guests. Why did he want to
suggest that he had guests? To provide an alibi for the person who
was going to kill him! And who was that person? The only person
who could have been in the flat at the time! The man who had been
there all the time! The man who told us that he went out to the
music hall!”

“Graves?”

“Graves. He killed the Count, then he set the scene. He ate a
portion of all the dishes, he soiled the three plates, he used the
three coffee-cups. But he made one mistake. He was not a man of
large appetite. He could not finish the three portions of rice
soufflé. Then he went out, and at 8.47 he rang up his own house,
and, in a disguised voice, gave the message that Miss Rider
received. Then he went to the music hall, and came back later to
find the body.”

“But the voice on the telephone?” I asked. “Miss Rider said she
recognized it as the Count’s.”

“My dear Hastings, she had never heard the Count’s voice. She only
said it was a ‘terrible’ voice. And Graves had only to mention the
name ‘Foscatini’ and ‘Regent’s Court’ for her to jump to the
conclusion it was the Count. It was a very clever plot. If it had
not been for the rice soufflé, and the fact that I happen to know
that no Italian ever takes milk in his coffee, Graves would have
gone scot-free.”

“But what was his motive?” I asked.

“The fifty thousand lire, Hastings. The Count was a blackmailer,
but he was also a man who kept a large sum of money in his flat.
Graves knew that. He saw his chance, and he took it. A very simple
case, after all.”

“Well,” I said, “it’s lucky you were there. I should never have
suspected Graves.”

“_Mon ami_,” said Poirot, “it is the little things that count.
Always remember that. The little things!”

“Certainly. But you see, my friend, it is not you that I suspect
of the crime. Not at all. I know better than that.”

The Italian stared.

“What do you mean?”

“I will tell you. You were at the Italian Embassy from eight till
nine on the Tuesday night, so much is true. It is also true that
on the Tuesday morning you, and another, did call upon Count
Foscatini. It is also true that you did not dine with him on the
Wednesday night. In short, all the Count’s guests on that night
were—imaginary.”

Signor Ascanio’s jaw dropped.

“I will tell you what I think happened,” continued Poirot. “The
Count was a man of some importance in your country, but he was
also—how shall I say it?—a black sheep. He had in his possession
certain—shall we say—incriminating documents. You were sent to
England to buy them from him. You called upon him on the Tuesday
morning. You did not reach an agreement. He told you to return on
the Wednesday, and he would give you his final answer. But on the
Tuesday night some one else—a man who also wanted those
papers—visited the Count and—killed him.”

“How did you know all this?” Ascanio’s voice was a whisper.

“It was simple. The Count was a very orderly man. On the Tuesday
morning he had no engagement for Tuesday evening. He had an
engagement for Wednesday evening. It was for Wednesday that he
invited you to dinner. When you went to his flat on Wednesday,
thinking to find him alive, you found him—dead. You were
horror-stricken. You saw that if you were found there you would be
suspected of the murder. You fled. Then you saw that your only hope
of safety was to prove an alibi for the Wednesday night. With the
influence of your Government behind you, you succeeded.”

“It is true,” Ascanio said. “We found him—dead. We took the papers,
for they were what we had come for. We could not allow them to fall
into the hands of the police. Then we fled.”

“You have been acquitted,” said Poirot, “of the murder. But of the truth? That is another matter. You were there on Tuesday morning. You went to see Count Foscatini because he was a blackmailer. He had in his possession certain documents of a very sensitive nature—papers that your Government was anxious to recover. You reached an agreement as to the price, and you were to return on Wednesday evening to complete the transaction. Is that not so?”

Ascanio’s face changed. The furtive look was replaced by one of sheer astonishment. He sank into a chair. “How did you know?” he gasped. “It is as you say. But I did not go on Wednesday. I swear it! I was at the Embassy, as the Ambassador himself has testified.”

“Exactly; and as I am not an imbecile, it is not with the gallows
I threaten you—but with publicity. Publicity! I see that you do
not like the word. I had an idea that you would not. My little
ideas, you know, they are very valuable to me. Come, signor, your
only chance is to be frank with me. I do not ask to know whose
indiscretions brought you to England. I know this much, you came
for the especial purpose of seeing Count Foscatini.”

“He was not a count,” growled the Italian.

“I have already noted the fact that his name does not appear in
the _Almanach de Gotha_. Never mind, the title of count is often
useful in the profession of blackmailing.”

“I suppose I might as well be frank. You seem to know a good deal.”

“I have employed my grey cells to some advantage. Come, Signor
Ascanio, you visited the dead man on the Tuesday morning—that is
so, is it not?”

“Yes,” admitted Ascanio. “I will tell you the truth. That man
possessed certain papers—they were of a political nature. I
visited him on Tuesday morning to arrange the terms. I returned
later that day and paid him the sum he demanded. I have never been
to the flat since. As for the dinner on Wednesday night, I know
nothing of it. I was, as the Ambassador stated, at the Embassy.
And further, there was no young man with me on Tuesday. I was
alone.”

“_Précisément_,” said Poirot. “I thought as much. You have been
most helpful, signor. I thank you.”

Signor Ascanio bowed and withdrew.

“I will tell you,” the Italian said at last, his voice dropping to a low, guttural hiss. “That man—he was a scoundrel, a blackmailer of the worst description. He had in his possession certain papers—important papers—belonging to a high official in my country. I came to London for the sole purpose of recovering them. On the Tuesday morning, I went to see him. I offered him a sum of money, a large sum. He laughed at me. He demanded more—a price so ruinous that I told him I must communicate with my superiors. But as for the dinner on Wednesday night—I know nothing of it! I never went there. I was, as the Ambassador himself has stated, at the Embassy from eight o’clock onwards. I have never seen the man again, alive or dead.”

“I was there on Tuesday morning,” Ascanio admitted at last, his shoulders sagging. “Foscatini—if that was his name—had certain papers in his possession, documents of a political nature that would have caused a grave scandal in my country. I came to London for the express purpose of buying them back. The price was high, but I paid it. I left him on Tuesday morning, and I have never seen him since. As for the dinner on Wednesday, it was a complete fiction. I was at the Embassy, as His Excellency has testified. I know nothing of any dinner, nor of any ‘Signor Ascanio’ who was supposed to be there.”

“I saw him on Tuesday morning, as you say,” Ascanio admitted. “I was
sent by certain people in Italy to buy back some papers that this
Foscatini—who was nothing but a low blackmailer—had obtained. We
reached an agreement. I returned that afternoon, paid him the money,
and received the documents. I never saw him again. The story of the
dinner is a lie from beginning to end. I was never there on
Wednesday night, as the Ambassador has testified.”

“I will be frank,” said Ascanio at last. “I did visit the man on Tuesday morning. He was no Count, but a dangerous rogue who lived by his wits. He had obtained certain papers—I will not say how—that were of a highly sensitive political nature. I went to him to buy them back. We could not agree on the price. He told me he would think it over and that I should return on Thursday morning. As for Wednesday night, I was at the Embassy, as His Excellency has stated. I have never seen the man since Tuesday, and I was never at Regent’s Court on the night of the murder. The valet’s story of my dining there is an absolute fabrication.”

“Yes; but I never went there on the following evening. There was
no need. I will tell you all. Certain information concerning a man
of great position in Italy had come into this scoundrel’s
possession. He demanded a big sum of money in return for the
papers. I came over to England to arrange the matter. I called upon
him by appointment that morning. One of the young secretaries of
the Embassy was with me. The Count was more reasonable than I had
hoped, although even then the sum of money I paid him was a huge
one.”

“Pardon, how was it paid?”

“In Italian notes of comparatively small denomination. I paid over
the money then and there. He handed me the incriminating papers.
I never saw him again.”

“Why did you not say all this when you were arrested?”

“In my delicate position I was forced to deny any association with
the man.”

“And how do you account for the events of the evening, then?”

“I can only think that some one must have deliberately impersonated
me. I understand that no money was found in the flat.”

Poirot looked at him and shook his head.

“I think, signor, you had better tell me the name of the man who
informed you of the count’s death. You said, I believe, that you
did not know it?”

“That is so. The news came to me by telephone. A voice—an English
voice—spoke to me. It said: ‘The Count is dead. Do not let
yourselves be drawn into it.’ I stayed in my hotel. Next day I
was arrested. That is all I know.”

“You are certain that the voice was an English one?”

“_Ma si_, signor. Perfectly.”

“Thank you, signor; you have told me exactly what I wanted to
know.”

He rose. Signor Ascanio lost no time in taking his departure.

“Well, Poirot, what is the meaning of it all?” I asked. “Is it the
man-servant Graves, after all?”

Poirot smiled.

“_Mon ami_,” he said, “there are several points that I should like
to have cleared up. I am expecting another visitor. Let us see
who it is.”

“No, Signor Ascanio, it was not an impersonation. There were three
men there that evening. One of them was the man who was murdered.
The other two were—his murderers. Oh, no, you were not there. I
never for one moment believed that you were. You had the alibi of
the Embassy. Your Excellency—if I may so address you—it is my
little friend Japp’s fault. He is too sure of himself. If he had
only examined the table with a little more attention he would have
perceived that only two men had dined there. It was all a little
mistake, you see.”

“Three men were seen to enter, and the waiter at the kitchens sent
down dinner for three.”

“Yes; but one man could easily eat the portion of two. A little
heavy for the digestion, perhaps, but quite possible. I ask
myself, ‘Why?’ And the answer is—to give the impression that three
people have dined there. Why should they wish to give that
impression? Only one reason—to create an alibi for someone who
was not there.”

“Then you think it was the manservant?”

“Exactly. Graves. He killed his master, after his master had
received a large sum of money. Then he hid the money, and
deliberately planned the whole thing. He goes out, and he comes
back with two friends. They go into the dining-room. He serves a
meal for three. He himself eats the food, and makes his two
friends smoke and drink.”

“But the third man? The man who was seen to enter with Ascanio?”

“There was no Ascanio. There were only two men. They were Graves’s
friends. He let them in himself. One of them was a young man. The
other—well, I have a little idea that the other was not a man at
all.”

I stared at Poirot.

“What do you mean?”

“I am thinking of the voice that spoke on the telephone. The
terrible voice. ‘Help,’ it said. ‘They’ve killed me.’ Now, if a
man is being killed, he does not usually have the time or the
inclination to go to the telephone and call up his doctor. But if
someone else wants to create the impression that he is being
killed at a certain time, then the telephone is a very handy
instrument. And who was the person who received that telephone
message? Why, Miss Rider!”

“Miss Rider?” I cried. “But she is Dr. Hawker’s housekeeper.”

“Exactly. And also, as I have since discovered, the sister of
Graves. It was a very clever little plot. Miss Rider is at the
doctor’s house. She ‘receives’ a telephone call. She rushes in to
us with the news. We all hurry to the flat. We find the body.
Everything points to the murder having just been committed. The
stopped clock—the telephone call—the evidence of the lift man—all
join to fix the time. And Graves, of course, has a perfect alibi.
He was at the music-hall.”

“But the two men?”

“There were no two men. There was only one—the young man who was
seen to enter. The other ‘gentleman’ was Miss Rider herself,
disguised. She and the young man (who I suspect is her nephew)
entered the flat. Graves let them in. They stayed there for a
while, then she slipped out, changed her clothes, and went to the
doctor’s. Later, she and the young man ‘left’ the flat—or rather,
he left, and she was already gone. It was all very well thought
out. But they made one mistake.”

“What was that?”

“The coffee. It was very black. Now, if three people have been
dining, and have all taken coffee, it is unlikely that the cups
would be so full of black coffee. It suggested that it had been
poured out but not drunk. And then there was the rice soufflé.
Only a little of it was eaten. A man who is eating two dinners
cannot manage everything! And lastly, there were the curtains. If
a man is having a dinner party, he usually draws the curtains.
The fact that they were not drawn suggested that the whole thing
was a stage-play—to be seen from outside if necessary, though in
this case it was the evidence of the table that was important.”

“And the money?”

“I think that if the police search Miss Rider’s ‘gloomy old house’
thoroughly, they will find the Italian notes. Graves could not
afford to have them on him.”

“_Mon ami_,” said Poirot, turning to me, “it was a pretty little
case. It shows the importance of the trifles. The coffee, the rice
soufflé, and the curtains. They all told the same story.”

Signor Ascanio rose.

“I am much indebted to you, Monsieur Poirot. You have done me a
great service.”

He bowed and left the room.

“A very clever couple, Graves and his sister,” remarked Poirot
meditatively. “But they did not account for Hercule Poirot.”

“No, signor, I do not believe a word you say. Not a word. Now,
I have another little idea. You saw this man on the morning of
the 9th; you paid him a certain sum of money; but you did _not_
get those papers. Is that not so? He was a man of his word, the
late Count Foscatini, and he told you that if you would dine with
him the following night, he would then give you the papers. You
came there at eight o’clock, and you and your friend partook of
dinner. Then, having got the papers, one of you struck him down.
You then left the flat together. You are safe now, but if you do
not tell me the truth, I will go to the Italian Embassy and
denounce you. The Ambassador, I take it, was a friend of your
father’s and wished to help you; but if he finds that you have
committed a murder, he will not continue his protection.”

The Italian went ashy-white.

“No, no! I did not kill him. I swear it. I will tell you the truth.
We went there at eight o’clock, as you say. We had dinner—a very
good dinner—and afterwards we had coffee and port. Then the Count
went to his desk and gave me the papers. We left the flat at once.
He was alive and well when we left him. I swear it.”

“At what time was that?”

“It was just after half-past eight.”

“Then you must have met the valet as you went out?”

“No, we saw no one.”

“And you did not telephone?”

“Telephone? No, why should we? We had what we wanted.”

“Very well, signor, you may go. I believe your story this time.”

When the Italian had departed, I looked at Poirot.

“You believe him?” I asked.

“I do, Hastings. His story has the ring of truth.”

“Then who killed the Count?”

“A very simple question, my friend. Let us see. Who remains?”

“The valet—Graves?”

“Is it not a little difficult for a man to be in two places at
once? At 8.47 Graves was at the Metropolitan Music Hall, according
to his own account. And then there is the telephone call. If the
Count was dead at 8.47, who was it that telephoned?”

“But he wasn’t dead then. He telephoned himself.”

“Wait a minute, Hastings. At 8.47, the Count was, according to
Graves, sitting at dinner with his two guests. He could not,
therefore, have been telephoning from the writing-table in the
same room.”

“Then it must have been one of the two guests who telephoned?”

“_Ma foi_, Hastings, you are not very brilliant this morning. If
one of the guests had killed him, would he have been likely to
telephone to the doctor and give his own name, and then wait
patiently for the police to arrive?”

“It is certainly very difficult,” I said. “Who can it have been?”

“Let us think,” said Poirot. “Who else is there?”

“There’s the doctor’s housekeeper, Miss Rider,” I suggested
facetiously.

“_Pourquoi pas?_ It is she who hears the voice on the telephone.
Suppose there was no voice? Suppose she only _said_ there was?
What then?”

“But she had no motive!”

“_Précisément_. She had no motive. Now let us look at the case
from a different angle. What was the most remarkable thing about
it? The dinner, Hastings, the dinner! For three people, remember.
Soup, fish, an entrée, and a rice soufflé. Now, when I went up to
the kitchen, the cook told me that the dishes were all empty, with
the exception of the rice soufflé. That is to say, those three
people had between them eaten a meal intended for at least four or
five! Now, that is very remarkable. Count Foscatini was a small
man, and the two Italians were also small men. They would not be
likely to have such enormous appetites.”

“Then what do you deduce?”

“I deduce that there were not three people at dinner, but only
one—one man with a very large appetite. The plates were soiled,
the dishes were emptied, to create the illusion that three people
had dined. But why? To provide an alibi for the two guests? No,
because they had no need of an alibi. It was the _time_ of the
murder that was the point. If the murder had taken place earlier,
say at eight o’clock, then the two Italians were still at their
hotel. If it had taken place later, say at half-past nine, then
they had already left the flat. But at 8.47 they were supposedly
at dinner with the Count. Therefore, the murder was committed at
8.47.”

“But by whom?”

“By the man who had most to gain by it. Who was that?”

“I don’t know.”

“Think, Hastings. There is one person who has been very much kept
in the background. A man who was supposedly out at the time, but
who could easily have been in the flat all the time.”

“You mean—Graves?”

“Exactly. Graves. Let us suppose that he kills his master at
eight o’clock, just as the dinner is being sent down. He then sets
to work. He has to eat that dinner—every bit of it. It must have
been a high trial for him, poor man! Then he soils the plates,
arranges the coffee-cups, and finally, at 8.47, he telephones to
the doctor, imitating the Count’s voice. Then he slips out and
goes to his music-hall, arriving there in time to establish his
alibi.”

“But the two Italians? They say they were there!”

“Of course they were there. They were there on the Tuesday morning.
The whole story of the dinner was a fabrication on the part of
Graves. He knew they had been there that morning, and he used that
fact to build up his story.”

“But the doctor’s housekeeper?” I cried. “She said she heard the
Count’s voice!”

Poirot smiled.

“She heard a voice, Hastings. She did not know the Count. Any
foreign-sounding voice would do for her. Now, I have a little
plan. I want you to go to the doctor’s house and see if you can
get hold of Miss Rider. Tell her that the doctor has had an
accident, or anything you like, but get her to come with you to
the flat at Regent’s Court. I shall be there with the inspector.”

I did as I was bid. Miss Rider was only too ready to come. She was
a person who thrived on excitement. When we arrived at the flat,
the inspector and Graves were already there. Poirot was standing
by the window.

“Ah, you have arrived! Now, Miss Rider, I want you to tell the
inspector exactly what you heard on the telephone.”

Miss Rider repeated her story.

“And you are sure it was the Count’s voice?” asked Poirot.

“Oh, yes, sir. A sort of foreign-sounding voice, it was.”

“Like this?” asked Poirot.

He began to speak in a high-pitched, affected voice, with a
strong foreign accent.

Miss Rider started.

“That’s it! That’s it exactly!”

Poirot turned to the valet.

“You see, Graves? It is a very good imitation, is it not?”

The man’s face changed. He made a sudden bolt for the door, but the
inspector was too quick for him.

“It’s no use, Graves,” said Poirot. “I have been to the Italian
Embassy. I know that Signor Ascanio was there from eight till nine
that evening. He never came to this flat at all. The whole story
was a lie. You killed your master for the sake of the money you
knew he had in his possession—the money that had been paid to him
that morning by Signor Ascanio.”

He turned to me.

“You see, Hastings? The rice soufflé! No man would eat a whole
rice soufflé if he could help it! It was that which first aroused
my suspicions. And then the coffee. Why was it so black? Because
it was not coffee at all, but only the grounds, to make it look
as though it had been drunk. Graves had no time to make fresh
coffee.”

“A very ingenious criminal,” I remarked.

“_Pas du tout_,” said Poirot. “He made one very great mistake. He
forgot that a man who has just been murdered does not usually
telephone to his doctor to say so! It is not—how do you say
it?—natural.”

And with a little bow, Poirot led the way out of the room.

“It is all very simple, is it not? But there are just one or two
points—the black coffee, for example, and the rice soufflé.
They have a tale to tell, Signor Ascanio. You say you were never
at the Count’s flat on the Tuesday evening? I believe you.
I believe also that the Count was already dead when you visited
him on the Tuesday morning. The telephone call to Dr. Hawker
was a ruse, a very clever ruse, but it did not deceive Hercule
Poirot!”

“No, Signor Ascanio, it will not do. You are not a very good liar.
One thing is certain: you were not at Regent’s Court on Tuesday
evening. At that hour you were at the Embassy. That I know. It is
not only the Ambassador who says so.”

“What did you want with me, then?” asked the Italian, with a
sullen look.

“I wished to see for myself that my little ideas were correct.
You have been of great service to me.”

When he had gone Poirot turned to me with a twinkle in his eyes.

“You see, Hastings, the case is really very simple. Ascanio did
not do the murder. He was at the Embassy between eight and nine
on Tuesday evening. Count Foscatini was murdered at 8.47. It is
physically impossible for him to have been at Regent’s Court.”

“Then who did do it?”

“Let us consider the facts. Two men are seen to go in at eight
o’clock. At 8.47 the Count is murdered. At 9.0 Graves, the man,
comes in and finds him dead. Is that not so?”

“No,” I corrected him. “Graves did not find him. He was out until
nearly eleven.”

“Ah, I had forgotten that. Let us re-examine the facts. Ascanio
denies having been at the flat at all on that Tuesday. Is it
likely that his double should have been there?”

“No, I should think it most unlikely.”

“Then we have to ask ourselves: who saw these two men? Only Graves,
the valet. No one else. The lift man did not see them.”

“But he heard from Graves that there were two gentlemen to dinner.”

“Ah, he heard from Graves! Everything comes back to Graves. He
alone saw them. He alone said that they were there. And it was he
who was out for the evening.”

“Then you think it was Graves?”

“But we must not forget the telephone call,” said Poirot
reprovingly. “The call that Dr. Hawker’s housekeeper received.”

“Well, surely that proves——”

“It proves that _someone_ telephoned. It does not prove that it was
Count Foscatini.”

“But he said his name.”

“Does a man who is dying—a man who has been struck a terrific
blow on the head—tele-phone to his doctor? No, Hastings, he does
not. If he could move at all, he would stagger to the door and
cry for help.”

“Then who did telephone?”

“Some one who wanted to fix the time of the murder. Some one who
wanted to be sure that the doctor would be there to see that it
had been done. Now, let us look at the dinner. Three people dine
together. There are three of everything—three plates, three
knives, three forks, three coffee-cups. But—and this is the point,
Hastings—only one man eats!”

“What do you mean?”

“The rice soufflé. It is a very light dish. If three people eat
it, it is finished. But there was a fair amount left. That means
that only one person had eaten of it. And then the coffee. The
Count, we are told, was a man of regular habits. He takes his
coffee black. But one of the cups contained milk. Why? Because
Graves, the valet, likes milk in his coffee! And the window.
The curtains were not drawn. Why? Because no one had been dining
there. It was all a _mise en scène_.”

“But why? What was the object of it all?”

“Money, my friend, money! The Count had just received a large sum
of money in small Italian notes. Graves knew this. He killed the
Count, probably about seven o’clock, before he was supposed to
have gone out. Then he set the stage. He ordered a dinner for
three, and when it came down he ate enough of it to make it appear
that three people had dined. He soiled the plates and the glasses.
He himself had the coffee and the port. Then he changed into his
master’s clothes—he was about the same build—and he telephoned.
The voice was muffled, but it was enough to deceive a woman like
Miss Rider. He knew the doctor was with us, so he could safely
telephone there. Then he changed back into his own clothes and
went out, leaving the front door slightly ajar. At eleven o’clock
he comes back and ‘discovers’ the body. It was a clever plot,
Hastings.”

“And Ascanio?”

“Ascanio was a godsend to him. He had overheard the conversation
in the morning, and he knew that Ascanio would be the first person
to be suspected. He knew, too, that Ascanio could not easily clear
himself without compromising the person he had come to see.”

“But how did you know, Poirot?”

“My friend, I have told you. The coffee and the rice soufflé. And
there was one other thing—the teeth. The Count’s teeth were
exceptionally white. The man I saw on the sofa had one front tooth
stopped with gold. It was a small point, but it was enough. I
was sure then that the man on the sofa was not the man who had
dined.”

“But he was! It was the Count’s body.”

“Precisely. But the man who ‘dined’ was Graves. He had the dinner
sent down, he ate it, and then he killed his master.”

“But you said he killed him at seven o’clock?”

“_Mon Dieu_, Hastings, use your little grey cells! If he killed
him at seven, he could not be the man who was seen dining at
eight. It was the other way about. He killed him _after_ the
dinner had been sent down—about 8.15. Then he had half an hour
in which to set the stage and telephone to the doctor. It was all
very simple, really.”

“And what did you do?”

“I have done nothing. I have merely seen Signor Ascanio. He is a
brave man, and I respect him. He has been through a great deal.”

“But Graves? Is he to go free?”

“Not at all. I have already sent a little note to my friend Japp.
I think he will find the Italian notes in Graves’s possession.
The man is not as clever as he thinks.”

I looked at Poirot with admiration. His methods were certainly
unique.

“You are a wonderful man, Poirot,” I said.

“I am,” he replied, with his usual lack of modesty. “But even I
cannot work without my ‘grey cells.’”

I laughed. Poirot was himself again.

“Strange,” he murmured. “We all have the little grey cells. And so
few of us know how to use them. Good morning, Signor Ascanio. I
believe your story. It is very much as I had imagined. But I had
to make sure.”

After bowing his guest out, Poirot returned to his arm-chair and
smiled at me.

“Let us hear M. le Capitaine Hastings on the case?”

“Well, I suppose Ascanio is right—somebody impersonated him.”

“My dear Hastings! That is too much to swallow. No, let us rather
look at the facts. They are three in number. The first is that
Foscatini was a man of very regular habits. The second is that
Ascanio visited him on Tuesday morning, and not on Wednesday
evening. The third is that it was Graves, the valet, who said
the visit had taken place on Wednesday evening.”

“You mean that Graves was the murderer?”

“I do not say so, Hastings. But let us look at the facts as I see
them. The Count was murdered between eight and nine o’clock—let
us say at 8.47. It was at 8.47 that the telephone message was sent
and the clock stopped. But was it the Count who sent the message?”

“Miss Rider said it was his voice.”

“A man who is being murdered does not stop to reflect on the
timbre of his voice. He would be lucky to get out any sound at
all. Let us see what else we have. A dinner for three had been
eaten—eaten, mark you. And yet, if the Count were a man of such
regular habits as he was reported to be, would he have eaten a
heavy dinner if he were expecting guests? Then there is the
coffee. Very black coffee. Now, why should a man have his coffee
so very black? To keep him awake? Perhaps. But there is another
reason. It might be to hide the taste of a certain drug.”

I stared at him. “A drug? But he was killed by a blow on the
head.”

“Was he? That is the question. Dr. Hawker said he was ‘stone dead.’
But even a doctor may be deceived. Let us suppose that the Count
was already dead when the blow was struck.”

“But the telephone message?”

“Ah, the telephone message! Who sent it? Not the Count. He was
already dead. Then it must have been the murderer. And why? To
fix the time of the death. But why did he want to fix the time of
the death? To provide himself with an alibi, of course. And who
had an alibi for that time? Graves! He was at the music-hall. But
who else had an alibi? Ascanio! He was at the Embassy. The
murderer, then, must be some one who knew that Ascanio would have
an alibi for that time. And who would know that better than the
man who had been listening at the door on Tuesday morning? Graves!”

“But how could he have managed it? He was at the music-hall.”

“Was he? He went out at 8.30. He could have been back in ten
minutes. He had the key of the flat. He enters, strikes the dead
man a blow on the head, rings up Dr. Hawker’s house, and then
departs for his music-hall. It was all very simple.”

“But the dinner?”

“The dinner was the most clever part of the whole business. Graves
himself ate that dinner! He ate the dinner for three, and then
soiled the plates and glasses to make it look as though three
people had dined. That was why he ate so little of the rice
soufflé—he was already full to bursting! And that was why he had
his coffee so black—to counteract the effects of such a large
meal.”

“But why did he kill him?”

“For the money, of course. The Italian notes that Ascanio had paid
over that morning. They were never found. Graves had them all the
time. He had hidden them safely away.”

“But what about the voice on the telephone? Miss Rider said it
was the Count’s.”

“My dear Hastings, have you never noticed how easy it is to
deceive anyone over the telephone? A few words—a groan—a
whisper—and the thing is done. And remember, Miss Rider had never
heard the Count’s voice. She only knew it was a ‘terrible voice.’
Naturally it would be, under the circumstances.”

“It’s incredible!” I exclaimed.

“It is very simple,” said Poirot. “I knew it as soon as I saw that
dinner table. No man, however hungry, could have eaten three
dinners. And yet the plates were all soiled. It was a physical
impossibility. Therefore, only one person had eaten, and that
person was Graves. He is a man of method, as I said.”

“And the clock?”

“He set it at 8.47 and then knocked it over. It was all part of
the same plan to fix the time of the murder.”

“Well,” I said, “it’s a wonderful case. I should never have
thought of it.”

“That,” said Poirot, “is because you do not use your grey cells,
my friend. You should try it some time. It is very stimulating.”

He smiled at me, and then, reaching out, he took a chocolate from
the box on the table.

“After all,” he murmured, “it is the little things that matter.
The little things are always the most important.”

“And who should do that? Some friend of the Count’s—no, for then
he would have known. It must have been some one who knew of the
appointment Ascanio had made. Who was that?”

“The valet, Graves,” I cried.

“_Precisely_, my friend. Graves, the valet, who listened at the
door. It was he who knew the money was in the flat. He killed his
master and took it. Then he had to make an alibi for himself. He
gave himself the evening off, and then—what? He could not be in
two places at once. So he invented the dinner party. He himself
played the part of the two guests. He ordered the dinner for
three, and when it was sent down he ate it—all three portions!
Think of that, Hastings. It was a feat, indeed! No wonder there
was only a little of the rice soufflé left! And he had to be quick.
Then he soiled the plates, used the three coffee-cups, and
smoked the cigar and the cigarettes. Then he struck his master
down, and—this was his master stroke—he rang up the doctor from
the flat and, imitating his master’s voice, gave the alarm. He
even thought of the little detail of the clock. But he made three
mistakes.”

“Three?”

“Yes. The first was the window. It was a cold night, and yet the
curtains were not drawn. Why? Because Graves had to keep an eye
on the hall to see when the doctor arrived. He would see him from
the window, and that would be his cue to slip out of the front
door. He was a little too late, and had to hide in the hall, but
eventually he got away. The second mistake was the coffee. It was
_very_ black. Graves is not a coffee drinker; he did not know that
if you pour three cups of coffee from a small pot it will be
practically all sediment. And the third mistake—the greatest of
all?”

“What was that?” I asked.

“He was too careful. He wanted to make it clear that the three
men had had a long talk. But he forgot that he had to do it all
in an hour. He should have known that no three men could have
eaten a four-course dinner and had a long talk in that time.”

“But the voice,” I objected. “The voice on the telephone. Miss
Rider recognized it as a man’s voice, but she didn’t say it was
Foscatini’s. She said it was a ‘terrible voice’.”

“_Exactement_! It was a voice disguised—a voice meant to sound
like a dying man’s. And who had the best opportunity to know the
Count’s voice, and to know the doctor’s habits? Why, the man who
lived in the house. But there was another person who knew the
doctor’s habits even better.”

I stared at him. “You don't mean...?”

“I mean, Hastings, that we must look at the person who brought the
news. Who was it that came running to us? Miss Rider. She told us of
a telephone call that no one else heard. She claimed the Count said
‘Foscatine’—a name she could only have known if she were part of the
plot. And why was she so agitated? Not because of a voice, but
because she had just come from Regent’s Court herself.”

“My dear Hastings! That is too simple. Consider the facts. A
telephone message at 8.47. A clock smashed at 8.47. Very neat,
is it not? But wait. What did the man who ordered the dinner
say? He said that the Count had eaten his dinner—all of it, with
the exception of the rice soufflé. Now we know from the doctor
that the Count was killed at 8.47. That is only three-quarters
of an hour after the dinner was served. Is it possible for a
man to eat a four-course dinner, even a light one, in that time?
No, it is not. Besides, we have the coffee. It was very black.
Now, as you know, I always take my coffee with much sugar. The
Count, it seems, took his very black. But there were three cups.
The two visitors had their coffee black also. Is it likely?”

I was beginning to see light.

“You mean that there was no dinner?”

“_Précisément_. There was no dinner. The dishes were soiled, the
food was thrown away—but it was never eaten. And why? Because
the Count was already dead!”

“Already dead?”

“Exactly. He was probably killed on the Tuesday morning, shortly
after Ascanio’s visit. The murderer then had all day to prepare
his stage. He was a man of method, as I said. He must have
resembled the Count in height and build. He put on the Count’s
clothes, he even, I suspect, wore a false moustache to heighten
the resemblance. He was seen by the lift man at eight o’clock.
He ordered the dinner. He soiled the plates. He was even
sufficiently a man of detail to leave a little of the rice
soufflé—a dish which, as every one knows, is never eaten to the
last morsel. Then, at 8.47, he telephones to Dr. Hawker,
smashing the clock to provide himself with a perfect alibi.
Then he changes his clothes, and walks out of the flat.”

“But the man Graves said he saw the two visitors!”

“Exactly. The man Graves.”

Poirot’s eyes twinkled.

“The elusive Signor Ascanio was a godsend to him. He had only to
say that he had seen him on the Tuesday morning, and that he had
returned on the Wednesday evening. But, as we know, Ascanio did
not return.”

“Then Graves was the murderer?”

“Who else? He knew of the money that had been paid to his master.
The Count was a blackmailer; his valet was probably one too.
He killed his master, and then set to work to provide himself
with an alibi. It was a clever scheme. But for one thing.”

“And what was that?”

“The coffee, my friend. He made it much too black. It was a little
error, but it was enough. And then, there was the telephone
call. He should have known that a man who has just been
murdered cannot telephone for the doctor.”

I must confess that I was still a little confused.

“But the voice on the telephone—Miss Rider said it was the
Count’s?”

“How should she know the Count’s voice? She had never heard it
before. She heard a voice—a man’s voice—and she jumped to the
conclusion that it was the Count’s. Graves, no doubt, did his
best to imitate an Italian accent.”

“But the doctor—he knew the Count?”

“He had only seen him once, and then when he was ill. He would
hardly have recognized the voice in any case. No, it was a
shrewdly planned crime. Graves is a clever man.”

“Then you’re going to denounce him?”

“My friend, I have already done so. I had a little talk with
Japp this morning. He was very much impressed by my
deductions.”

“My dear Hastings! Think. Is it possible for a man to be
impersonated in that way? There were two of them—two foreigners.
Who was the second man? Let us consider his position. He was
unquestionably a foreigner. He spoke Italian, as did the other
man. The lift-boy saw them. They were seen by the Count’s servant.
They were seen by the man from the kitchen. All these witnesses
agreed that they were foreign. If we are to believe Ascanio, he
was never there on the Wednesday evening at all. Then who were
these two men?”

“I don’t know,” I said. “I’m sure I don’t.”

“But it was very simple, Hastings. Think. All the evening we were
presented with the evidence of a dinner for three. But what if
there were only two?”

“Two? But there were three plates, three coffee-cups, three——”

“Exactly. And the rice soufflé? What did I say about the rice
soufflé?”

“You said there was a good deal of it left.”

“Precisely. It was a dinner for three, and yet only two people
had partaken of it. The third man—the Count himself—had eaten
nothing. Why?”

“Because he was dead?” I suggested.

“Exactly, Hastings. He was dead before the dinner was even ordered.
He was killed, not at 8.47, but much earlier—probably between
seven and eight o’clock. The whole dinner was a plant. The
murderer, having killed the Count, then ordered the dinner, and
when it was sent down he and his accomplice—a man who could talk
Italian—ate enough for two, and soiled the third plate to make it
look as if three people had dined.”

“But what about the telephone call?”

“The most ingenious part of the whole business. The murderer,
knowing that the doctor would be with me, rings up the doctor’s
house. He knows that the doctor is out, and that his housekeeper
will answer the phone. He gives a message in a choking voice,
‘Help! they’ve killed me!’ and then adds the name of the place.
The housekeeper, of course, repeats this to the doctor when she
sees him, and the doctor, in all good faith, repeats it to the
police. It fixes the time of the murder to a minute. It was a
clever idea—a very clever idea.”

“Then who was the murderer?” I asked.

“Who was the only person who could have carried out such a scheme?
Who was the only person who knew the Count’s habits, who knew that
he would be alone that evening, and who could have easily gained
admittance to the flat?”

“Graves!” I cried.

“Exactly. Graves. He killed the Count, probably for the sake of
the money he knew he had in his possession—the money Ascanio had
paid him that morning. He then went out, met his accomplice, and
together they returned to the flat and carried out the comedy of
the dinner. It was Graves who ordered the dinner, Graves who
telephoned to the doctor’s house, and Graves who, after the dinner,
quietly walked out of the flat, leaving his accomplice to do the
same a few minutes later. It was a well-thought-out crime, but he
made one mistake.”

“What was that?”

“The coffee, Hastings. He forgot that a man of the Count’s
luxurious habits would never drink his coffee with milk. He took
it black. But Graves, being a servant, was used to taking his
coffee with milk, and so, when he came to the third cup—the one
intended for the Count—he added milk to it without thinking. It
was a small mistake, but it was enough to show me the truth. And
then there were the curtains. A man like the Count, who was so
particular about his comfort, would never have sat down to dinner
without the curtains being drawn. But Graves, in his hurry, had
forgotten them. It is the little things, Hastings, that always
give the murderer away.”

I was silent for a moment, marveling at my friend’s insight.

“But what about the clock?” I asked. “The one that was stopped at
8.47?”

“That was also a part of the plant, Hastings. Graves simply set
the hands of the clock to 8.47 and then knocked it over. It was
all very simple, once you have the key to it.”

“And what are you going to do now?”

“I shall place the facts before Japp. I think he will find that
Graves’s alibi for the time of the murder—8.47—is not quite so
unshakable as he thought.”

And Poirot was right. Graves was arrested, and, faced with the
evidence against him, he eventually confessed to the crime. It
was, as Poirot had said, the little things that had been his
undoofing.

“You really believe that, my friend? Do you not see the absurdities
of that theory?”

“I don’t know. I’m quite at a loss.”

“That is because you will not think. It is all so simple. If
Ascanio was telling the truth, and he had already paid the money
over that morning, why should any one want to impersonate him on
the following evening? No, my friend; it is the servant—the valet,
Graves—who is the culprit. He is a very clever man, that Graves.
_Ma foi!_ he had a brain. He did it all. It was he who was the
murderer.”

“Graves? But he was out.”

“Was he? Think. He had seen the money paid over that morning. He
knew it was in the flat. The Count had been very lucky. Graves,
on the other hand, was probably in low water. He killed the Count
that morning, and سپس (then) he spent the rest of the day in
making his preparations.”

“But the dinner—the three people——”

“There was no dinner. One person—Graves—ate it all. That is why
he ordered such an enormous meal. He wanted to make it appear
that three people had dined there. It was he who ate the three
plates of soup, the three soles, the three helpings of beef—all
except the rice soufflé, of which he had only a small portion.”

“The coffee-cups?”

“Exactly. He drank the three cups of coffee. One of them—his
own—he took with milk. The other two he took black, as Italians
usually do.”

“But the telephone message?”

“Graves again. He must have known that the doctor was at my flat,
and he rang up and gave that message. He knew that I should
immediately set out for the Regent’s Court. He timed it
beautifully. Then he slipped out and went to his music-hall.”

“But the voice on the telephone?”

“His own, of course. He is a bit of an actor, that Graves. He
even went so far as to give himself an alibi.”

“But the body?”

“The body had been dead some hours when we found it. That is why
I was so interested in the rice soufflé. It was the only dish
that had not been entirely consumed. I felt sure that there must
be some reason for that. And there was. It was because Graves had
already eaten as much as he could manage. I also noticed that the
window curtains were not drawn. Now, a man who has guests to dinner
is almost certain to have his curtains drawn. But a man who is
playing a part might easily forget such a detail. Graves is a
clever man, but he made that one little mistake. He is also the
man who smashed the clock and set it at 8.47. A very clever man,
but not quite clever enough for Hercule Poirot.”

“Never, never will you use the brains the good God has given you.
Recall to yourself some words I uttered after leaving the flat that
night. I referred to the window-curtains not being drawn. We are
in the month of June. It is still light at eight o’clock. The light
is failing by half-past. _Ça vous dit quelque chose?_ I perceive
a struggling impression that you will arrive some day. Now let us
continue. The coffee was, as I said, very black. Count Foscatini’s
teeth were magnificently white. Coffee stains the teeth. We reason
from that that Count Foscatini did not drink any coffee. Yet there
was coffee in all three cups. Why should anyone pretend Count
Foscatini had drunk coffee when he had not done so?”

I shook my head, utterly bewildered.

Poirot’s eyes sparkled with the light of the hunter. “Consider the stomach of a man, Hastings! To eat three portions of soup, three of fish, three of the tournedos—it is a feat, is it not? But even the most gluttonous assassin must draw the line somewhere. Thus, the rice soufflé remained largely untouched. The dinner was a farce, staged to provide a false timeline. The Count was already dead when that meal was ‘served’ through the lift. One person alone had the opportunity to play all three parts at the table, to stain the coffee cups, and to ensure the lift man saw three dirty plates return to the kitchen.”

“You are still in the dark, Hastings? Then let us illuminate. The dinner was ordered for three, and the plates were soiled to suggest that three people had eaten. But consider the stomach of a man! Could one man eat three helpings of soup, three of fish, and three of beef? No, he would be—as you say—bursting! Therefore, he must dispose of the food. The service lift, Hastings! He sent the food back to the kitchens, course by course, having merely dirtied the plates and moved the cutlery. But he made a mistake with the rice soufflé. It is a light dish, yes, but even a hungry man cannot easily dispose of three portions of it without leaving a trace. And the coffee! He filled three cups, but he forgot that the Count, with those white teeth, would never have drunk his coffee so black and so strong. He drank the coffee himself to keep his courage up, and then distributed the dregs.”

“Because,” said Poirot, his eyes shining with the green light I knew so well, “the man who ate that dinner was not three men, but one man! A man with a very large appetite—but even he could not finish three rice soufflés! That is why some was left. He ate three helpings of soup, three of fish, three of meat—it is a feat, but possible for a hungry man. He soiled three sets of plates. He poured coffee into three cups. But he forgot to drink the third cup because he was not really a coffee drinker, or perhaps he was too full! And the curtains, Hastings! In June, at eight o’clock, it is broad daylight. No one would draw the curtains. But at nine o'clock, they would be drawn. The fact that they were not drawn proves that the ‘dinner’ was a stage-managed affair, and that the Count was already dead.”

“_Mon ami_,” said Poirot, “it is all so very simple if one uses
the little grey cells. Consider the dinner. An order for three.
Soup, fish, meat, and a rice soufflé. We are told the plates were
soiled and the dishes empty—with the exception of the rice
soufflé. Now, a hungry man might manage three portions of the
earlier courses, but three helpings of a rice soufflé? It is a
physical impossibility! Therefore, the meal was not eaten by
three people, but by one. And that one person was not the Count,
for his teeth were white, yet the coffee in the cups was black.
He had drunk no coffee. The entire dinner was a farce, staged to
give the impression that the Count was alive and well at eight
o’clock.”

“Because,” Poirot’s voice was silky, “there was only one person who dined in that flat. The two guests were a myth, invented to provide a motive and a pair of mysterious assassins. One man ate a little from each of the three plates of soup, the three plates of fish, and the three plates of meat. Small wonder he had no room for the rice soufflé! And having finished his gluttonous task, he soiled the three coffee cups, but neglected to consider the Count’s white teeth. He then struck the fatal blow, set the clock back, and prepared his exit. He had already seen Ascanio on the Tuesday morning and knew of the money. The money, Hastings! The Italian notes that Ascanio paid—they were not in the flat because the murderer had them in his pocket.”

“Come, I will help you. What evidence have we that Ascanio and his
friend, or two men posing as them, ever came to the flat that
night? Nobody saw them go in; nobody saw them go out. We have the
evidence of one man and of a host of inanimate objects.”

“You mean?”

“I mean, Hastings, that the dinner was a farce! There were no guests. One man alone sat at that table—the murderer. He had killed the Count much earlier, probably shortly after Signor Ascanio’s morning visit, and secured the bundle of Italian notes for himself. But he needed to fix the time of death later to provide himself with an alibi. He ordered dinner for three through the service lift and then, with a truly prodigious effort, he ate all three meals himself! That is why the rice soufflé was not finished—even his appetite had its limits. He soiled the plates and filled the coffee cups, forgetting in his haste that the Count’s white teeth proved he never touched the beverage. He then set the clock to 8:47, shattered it to fix the time of the supposed ‘struggle,’ and departed at 8:30 to establish his alibi. The telephone call to the doctor’s house was his final masterstroke, made from a public booth at the appointed time to create a witness of the Count’s ‘dying words.’ The ‘man of method,’ Hastings, is none other than Graves!”

I mean Graves. Graves told us of the two Italians. Graves told us he was given the evening off. It was Graves who, having killed his master for the money Ascanio had paid that morning, proceeded to eat three dinners so that it might appear that three persons had dined together! A man of method indeed! He even remembered to soil the plates and the coffee-cups. But he could not bring himself to eat three portions of rice soufflé—that would have been too much even for his appetite! And the curtains—had they really been dining at half-past eight, the curtains would have been drawn. They were not drawn because the room was empty and the “guests” were a myth of Graves’s invention.

“I mean Graves. It was Graves who killed the Count. He saw the money pass on Tuesday morning, and his cupidity was too much for him. He killed the Count early in the evening, and then set to work to create the necessary atmosphere. He staged that dinner for three, eating what he could of the three portions—it was the rice soufflé that was his undoing; he was already full to bursting! He poured the coffee into the cups to make it appear that the meal was over, but he dared not let it touch the dead man’s teeth. Then, having moved the clock back and left the flat, he telephoned Dr. Hawker’s house at the appointed time, imitating the Count’s voice to provide himself with an alibi and to point the finger of suspicion at Ascanio.”

“I mean Graves,” said Poirot. “Graves is the only person who tells us those two men ever arrived. He killed the Count on Wednesday evening, probably just before eight o’clock, to secure the money paid by Ascanio the day before. He then ordered dinner for three and—an extraordinary feat—ate as much of it as he could to soil the plates. But he was not quite equal to the task; he managed the soup, the fish, and the beef, but his appetite failed him at the rice soufflé! He did not draw the curtains because, being alone and in a hurry to consume three portions, he forgot that a valet would normally do so as the light failed. Finally, at 8:47, he telephoned the doctor’s house from a public booth, faking the Count’s voice to establish a time of death that provided him with a perfect alibi at the music hall.”

“I mean the evidence of the dinner-table, Hastings. I asked myself: ‘Why should three men, two of whom are supposedly guests, leave a table so neatly?’ The answer is that there were no guests. One man ate that dinner—a man with a truly remarkable appetite. He ate the soup, the fish, and the beef, but by the time he reached the rice soufflé, his capacity failed him. He then carefully dirtied the other plates and glasses to suggest a party of three. He poured coffee into three cups, but he forgot that Count Foscatini, with his magnificent white teeth, would never have touched such black, staining liquid. It was the valet, Graves, who killed his master to possess himself of the notes Ascanio had paid. He staged the scene, left the flat at 8.30 to establish his presence elsewhere, and at 8.47 he rang the doctor’s house from a public booth, gasping out the dying message he had so carefully rehearsed!”

“I mean knives and forks and plates and empty dishes. Ah, but it
was a clever idea! Graves is a thief and a scoundrel, but what a
man of method! He overhears a portion of the conversation in the
morning, enough to realize that Ascanio will be in awkward position
to defend himself. The following evening, about eight o’clock, he
tells his master he is wanted at the telephone. Foscatini sits
down, stretches out his hand to the telephone, and from behind
Graves strikes him down with the marble figure. Then quickly to
the service telephone—dinner for three! It comes, he lays the
table, dirties the plates, knives, and forks, etc. But he has to
get rid of the food too. Not only is he a man of brain; he has a
resolute and capacious stomach! But after eating three tournedos,
the rice soufflé is too much for him! He even smokes a cigar and
two cigarettes to carry out the illusion. Ah, but it was
magnificently thorough! Then, having moved on the hands of the
clock to 8.47, he smashes it and stops it. The one thing he does
not do is to draw the curtains. But if there had been a real dinner
party the curtains would have been drawn as soon as the light began
to fail. Then he hurries out, mentioning the guests to the lift
man in passing. He hurries to a telephone box, and as near as
possible to 8.47 rings up the doctor with his master’s dying cry.
So successful is his idea that no one ever inquires if a call was
put through from Flat II at that time.”

“Except Hercule Poirot, I suppose?” I said sarcastically.

“Precisely. I made inquiries. No call was made from that flat at 8.47. It was Graves who, having found the money Ascanio had paid over, decided to make it his own. He was arrested this morning while attempting to change some of the Italian notes. A man of method, as I said, but he did not account for the fact that three dinners are a great deal for one man to consume—even a man as robust as Mr. Graves! And so, the mystery of the Italian Count is ended, and once more the ‘little grey cells’ have triumphed.”

“I did not even need to do that,” said Poirot, with a twinkle in his eye. “The logic of the stomach, it does not lie. When the police, acting on my suggestion, searched Graves’s belongings, they found the Italian notes concealed in the lining of his trunk. A man of method, as I said, but he failed to realize that while one may deceive the ears and the eyes, one cannot so easily deceive the digestive system. And now, my friend, let us go and dine—but I think we will avoid the rice soufflé. The very mention of it gives me a most unpleasant sensation of repletion.”

“Precisely. And when I suggested to the inspector that he might find a large sum in Italian notes hidden in Graves’s quarters, the matter was settled. The poor Graves—he had the stomach of an ox but the heart of a thief. He is now safely in the hands of the law, and I believe Dr. Hawker has at last regained his faith in my ‘moonshine.’ It was the black coffee that did it, Hastings. Always remember: the teeth, they do not lie!” He smiled at his own reflection in the hallway mirror and adjusted his moustache with a touch of pride. “And now, my friend, let us go. The case is closed, and I find that, unlike the late Count’s valet, I have a very simple desire for a single cup of chocolate—served, if you please, without the accompaniment of a rice soufflé.”

“Precisely,” Poirot replied, his eyes twinkling. “I confirmed with the exchange that no such call originated from the flat. When the police, acting on my suggestion, searched Graves’s lodgings, they found the Italian notes hidden in the lining of his trunk. The poor man’s digestion, I fear, was his undoing; even a murderer should know his limits when it comes to a rice soufflé. It was a clever comedy, but he forgot that while a man may lie, the inanimate objects—the plates, the coffee, the undrawn curtains—always speak the truth to those who know how to listen.”

“Precisely,” said Poirot. “I made inquiries at the exchange. No call had been put through from Flat II at that time. Graves, of course, had the money—those Italian notes of which Ascanio spoke. A very clever man, Graves, but he did not reckon on the little grey cells of Hercule Poirot. He is now, I believe, safely in the hands of our friend Japp. It was a well-planned crime, Hastings, but for one thing: he forgot that while a man may have the heart of a murderer, it is a rare individual indeed who possesses the capacity to consume three entire dinners in the space of a single hour!”

“Not even Hercule Poirot,” said my friend, with a smile. “I am
about to inquire now. I had to prove my point to you first. But
you will see, I shall be right; and then Japp, to whom I have
already given a hint, will be able to arrest the respectable
Graves. I wonder how much of the money he has spent.”

Poirot _was_ right. He always is, confound him!
